Once the catalyst for those shifts was, say, a splinter clan trying to steal a powerful scroll, but now it's an economic bubble emerging from an influx of cheap foreign money. Either way loyalty and fraternity are the only things that end up having real, intrinsic value.

Woo and Tsui are the directors of this franchise respectively, but when Tsui fully takes the reigns A Better Tomorrow becomes something else entirely, not necessarily better, but different. John Woo has become a man known for graceful violence in gunfire, but Tsui doesn't really treat these moments with artistry, but rather harder truth. The closest he gets to graceful in this film is when characters jump out of the way of bullets or twist around their partner who is also engaged in gunfire. They worked together one more time on The Killer, but parted ways for the final part of the A Better Tomorrow trilogy, with Woo taking his screenplay off and making it as Bullet In The Head, while Tsui also used the idea of a prequel set in the Vietnam War to make and direct A Better Tomorrow III. Chow Yun Fat started the trilogy as Mark, became his twin brother Ken in the sequel, and now returns as Mark again in this prequel, which boils down to an origin story…

reviews.author: Avalyn Wu
reviews.text: Like if Mikio Naruse made his version of a Better Tomorrow film, tying the dissolution of a relationship to the end of an imperialist occupation. Simultaneously the most richly stylized and the most grounded film of the three, focusing more on expressive shadows and dense hues of blue and orange rather than sheer explosiveness, all in the service of a political and historical awareness that had previously not existed. The mythic-melodramatic tinge of the preceding two films is brought back down to earth, as our heroes quickly realize that they cannot outpace the movement of the masses, stand above the common rabble as an autonomous petite bourgeois. They chase the conditions of free enterprise only to find that they are slowly collapsing everywhere. Hinging the stability of your Third World country upon friendliness with the United States is the biggest non-choice there is.

reviews.text: The other day, at the library, I suddenly found myself in the basement, in an archive where you could browse through newspapers from every day all the way to the 1930s and beyond, and since I was there I decided to look for an issue from the day of my birth. I was especially interested in the TV program: I was curious to see whether they were showing any old movies that day, and what it would be. In the afternoon Laurel and Hardy were on, and in the evening they were showing this film, the very fittingly titled A Child Is Waiting.

reviews.text: Won’t bore you with the details behind the production, but clearly the camerawork and staging in every scene in Cassavetes’s work. Just watch any other Kramer-produced work from this era and it’s clear a real director is there - the camera is more mobile and the staging more pronounced. That opening scene is a complete killer, almost like the emotional equivalent of the opening to a Sergio Leone film in the way it builds its tension. Lot of great dollies, ground-level shots, and nicely placed zooms, and an emphasis on faces that really allows one take in these kids. Much of it is basically economical, but it’s the kind of good economic directing that makes Jacques Becker a great director.…

reviews.text: Ronald Colman was superb! He won the Oscar for his performance which can be described as Othello within Othello. A dark wander into dementia for a stage actor slowly losing control over his mind and starts living the character he portrays in the play. Such a heavy-handed atmospheric execution that still manages to keep some of Colman's natural gentlemanly charm. Only thing holding A Double Life (1947) back was the rather weak investigation. Felt like it was just patched on without much though. And what it did was take one out of the torment and make the movie feel ordinary. Such a shame after such a deep and passionate focus on the rest of the production.

reviews.author: Lawrence Garcia
reviews.text: "A ship is the finest nursery in the world." The underlying subject of Richard Hughes' novel is also that of Johan Huizinga's contemporaneous study Homo Ludens: the primacy of play in civilization and society. The unique thrill of this adaptation is that it dispenses with any attempt to recreate the children's subjectivity, instead rendering their "innocent voyage" according to the particular rules and logic of their sundry amusements, for which both the seafaring adventure genre and Mackendrick's vigorous, propulsive direction—near-constant orchestrations of thrumming activity; dynamic foreground-background compositions that even Richard Fleischer would envy—prove ideal. Thus, the children's games and the crew's undertakings are equally worthy of serious attention: a scene of parental abandonment plays out again as a doll ceremony;…

reviews.author: Scott McCullough
reviews.text: This is my kind of western. It's a mean, vicious, cruel brawl through barren landscapes and border towns. George "The Tan" Hamilton plays a malicious Confederate captain who wants one more victory even though the war is ending soon. He really strikes the right balance between in control and manic spitefulness as his ragtag soliders make a daring escape from their Union captors and head for Mexico. The whole crew of Confederates are kind of nasty and vile but fun to watch. Harry Dean Stanton, Max Baer, Tim Carey all have great moments. Dick Miller shows up and he's in a different movie all together which is my only gripe.

reviews.author: Jacob Knight
reviews.text: The Blaxplo IN THE HEAT OF THE NIGHT. Almost singularly angry heist procedural where racial tensions practically (and literally) explode into horrific violence in each scene, repulsing even those who are participating. It’s all fire and chaos in Harlem, and we're either riding shotgun with the fatalistically doomed stick-up men, or the sweaty, bigoted cops, savagely tearing into suspects. Progress is what frightens these crews - the Mafia is scared of the blacks, the old dicks of their hungry young successors. “When are you gonna start looking at me like a cop?” Yaphet Kotto screams at one point, and you realize almost none of these individuals view the others even as human beings. You only get to see a few movies this good in your lifetime.

reviews.author: Rafael "Mister Movie" Jovine
reviews.text: Another movie that, at first glance, seems like any other action thriller from the 1970s. Among the intriguing behind-the-scenes details are Quinn's having to accept the main part after being unable to secure John Wayne, Burt Lancaster, or Kirk Douglas. Also, Sidney Portier was supposed to play the lead, but the people of Harlem didn't want him because they didn't think he was "urban" enough. Also, director Barry Shear's ordeal of filming in New York despite widespread warnings against doing so on account of the city's high production costs, the difficulty of securing a filming permit, and the widespread belief that Harlem was the most lawless slum in the United States at the time.

reviews.author: WraithApe
reviews.text: I think this was a pretty apt choice for MLK day; a politically charged Blaxploitation banger that bars no holds and in true 70s style, is gritty af to the bitter end. I haven't seen enough of the genre to say for sure, but I can't imagine many top the very high bar this sets. Tight script, committed, heartfelt performances from all involved, low-key dazzling cinematography that taps the vein of grimy, down-at-heel Harlem and a deep-in-the-groove funk score featuring Bobby Womack's eponymous funk soul standard.

reviews.text: I love a good disaster film. If you’re a fan of horror, how could you not like them? That one tiny little piece of set-up in every Final Destination film likely drew some inspiration from this genre. Better still, an entire film that centers on a horrific event, SIGN ME UP. The 70s created a grandiose blueprint for this genre and Airport led the first wave.

reviews.author: Dave Edwards
reviews.text: Representing the birth of the 70s disaster movie cycle, Airport was a huge hit upon its release in 1970. Looking back 50+ years on, the genre obviously evolved, fine tuning the tropes, characters, and plot mechanics, which would all calcify by the close of the decade. While Airport’s pacing might be off a smidge and the script is more interested in developing character dynamics than providing the type of thrills associated with a disaster picture, Airport’s third act is satisfying when the crisis transitions from a simmer to a boil. Dean Martin, George Kennedy, and Helen Hayes (who won an Oscar for her work here) deliver some great performances to help you through the down time and get your pulse racing as Airport reaches its climax.

It's a disaster film with barely any disaster and instead what feels like melodrama for a huge portion, and melodrama which I personally didn't find interesting at all. I don't really understand how this was nominated for so many awards back in the day, but I guess I understand why some enjoy this due to nostalgia, but for me, it's quite a crap one.

reviews.text: For me, Alice is one of writer-director Woody Allen’s more disappointing films. Usually, when he goes full-tilt at Magic Realism, the results are good (Midnight In Paris), if not excellent (The Purple Rose Of Cairo). Alice’s central conceit is promising: rich but bored housewife Mia Farrow gets more than she bargains for when she visits acupuncturist Keye Luke in Manhattan’s Chinatown. Luke’s various “herbs” are not just the psychosomatic tools of an alternative medicine; they give Farrow actual magical powers, such as the ability to speak to the ghost of a long-dead lover (Alec Baldwin), to revisit her own past, or to turn invisible so she can spy on her husband (William Hurt) and potential lover (Joe Mantegna). reviews.text: in its way the closest to relatively grounded and thematically ambitious since the original. the bullied kid's fantasy of traveling to Monster Island and helping Minilla fight his own tormenter Gabara is genuinely cute and, for a movie like this, spirals appropriately out of control when he gets kidnapped in real life by bank robbers. the film actually implies that the socioeconomic hardship of having two working parents is rotting away at some kids' moral fiber, contributing to both a bullying problem and the deeper issue of crime in general. it's both sweet and telling that he imagines his kaiju counterpart Minilla getting the quality time with his father that he himself craves. i'd dock it more for recycling a good chunk of the monster fights from previous films if the framing device didn't integrate it so well, with simple dual kid- and adult-friendly themes. also it's funny that little Ichiro imagines himself flying commercial to Monster Island.

reviews.text: A young boy who lives in a blasted toxic wasteland is left alone at home for days on end. The child is bullied and only finds solace in electrocuting himself unconscious and hallucinating that he's hanging out on a monster island with his drunken friend Minilla, who cheers with him as they watch Godzilla rip the arms off monsters. A duo of robbers, weakened and desperate in the current economic climate, captures the child because they need some information, but the child feels no sympathy for their plight and sics the police on them. Might makes right. The son beats up his bully, gains the respect of a bunch of loser kids, and then humiliates a painter for no reason. And so, the child learns that the only way to survive is by punishing the innocent. He is the monster now. The cycle of violence continues.

reviews.text: Almost Dead feels like a 90s time capsule. It’s a psychological thriller wrapped in low-budget, TV movie aesthetics that plays almost like a proto-It Follows: a woman is relentlessly haunted by a spectral figure (her mother), unsure if it's real, a projection, or something in between. The sense of dread is slow and creeping, and there's an eerie repetition to the haunting that gives it a dreamlike feel. It's not nearly as refined or stylish as It Follows, but the DNA is there for a while, if you look closely enough.

reviews.author: Joe Wawrzyniak
reviews.text: An expertly done thriller short that works like unnerving gangbusters because it doesn't really seem like a thriller until the last 30 seconds in which there's a big creepy reveal. Prior to said reveal, this short instead plays like a neatly observed slice of urban life concerning a young woman who desperately needs some relief from the grinding hustle and exhausting bustle of basic everyday big city existence. Director/cowriter Rod Blackhurst does an excellent job of contrasting the stressful calamity of the city with the soothing serenity of nature. Rose Hemingway gives a fine and credible performance as our weary protagonist. As for that aforementioned big creepy reveal, well that shit comes across as genuinely unsettling because it's something that can happen and alas does happen to women with depressingly appalling regularity. Vey highly recommended.

reviews.text: The most eccentric gallery of artists embarks on a cruise ship named Gloria: distinguished members of the opera world — sopranos, baritones, prima donnas — as well as musicians, comedians, and politicians, all gathering to pay their final tribute to the diva Edmea Tetua whose ashes are to be dispersed on her native island of Erimo. She was revered and often referred to as the greatest singer who ever lived. Given that music is perhaps the art form closest to perfection that humanity has ever achieved, the odyssey takes on the dimension of a pilgrimage into the soul of a goddess-like figure who embodied the very perfection of music.

reviews.text: Fellini's early studies on decadence draw heavily from their specific moments as time passes, he moved towards a more allegorical space. And the Ship Sails On does nothing to hide its actual subject matter, the end of aristocratic Europe at the start of the great war, but it is very dependent on the ship as symbol, an imagined field for its tension to play up as large as possible right down to ending by going behind the curtain. A triumph of artifice as history. It is also a far more sorrowful film than his other work on this vein. Even the colors are more muted.

reviews.text: And The Ship Sails On may not be Fellini's most famous or emotionally impactful film, but I couldn't help seeing the influence it had in it's wake. Comparisons to contemporary "eat the rich" dramadies such as Mark Mylod's The Menu, and Ruben Östlund's Triangle of Sadness danced through my head. That's because all three films are about how the privileged elites are so enraptured by their own superiority, that they don't even realize how disconnected they are from "normal" people. However, just like those aforementioned films, I find myself more enthralled by the concept rather than the final product.

reviews.text: On the surface, Martha Coolidge’s ANGIE seems like a strange film to choose to talk about from a watershed year that also gave us PULP FICTION, THE HUDSUCKER PROXY, THE LAST SEDUCTION, AMATEUR, CROOKLYN, and many of my other all-time favorites. In 1994, I was fifteen going on sixteen. I loved movies. I’d gotten very serious about them, writing a couple of terrible scripts, and watching as many movies a week as I could, usually around ten, most of them rented from my neighborhood video store or borrowed from the library. reviews.author: Peter Labuza
reviews.text: "It’s one thing to attempt to mimic the greats, but it’s another thing to signal to your audience you know you are a pale imitation. Kahn and Reynolds don’t shy from their off-key voices—they embrace them with drunken abandonment. They move their bodies with taps in their steps and shout for the rafters, and there’s a genuine charm to their attempts to succeed. Shepard’s voice is perhaps the most classical, but she’s also the most silly! A constant smile on her face, though occasionally a stern pout, she turns herself into a ragdoll of an actress as she charms her way through."

reviews.text: What should be a cracking tale of rampaging barbarians and twisted imperial politics is a staid and platitudinous attempt at a historical epic. Pietro Francisci treats it like a lost Shakespearean play, so there's lots of declaratory scenes where one of the main actors, mostly Anthony Quinn as Attila, invariably stands around shouting at everyone else, or pouts, or blankly stares at something off screen for an eternity. Clearly, it's material ripe for a HBO Game of Thrones treatment, instead of this overly serious attempt at a poor man's Macbeth. It's not a complete waste: Quinn is in his element and chews up the scenery; Sophia Loren lends her statuesque presence to the character of the scheming Honoria, largely undeveloped…

reviews.author: Film at Lincoln Center
reviews.text: The second (of three) Universal adaptations of Fannie Hurst’s turn-of-the-19th-century-set novel stars Margaret Sullavan and Charles Boyer (possessors of two of the best voices in classic Hollywood: she with her musical rasp, he with his luxuriantly accented baritone) as adulterous lovers whose brief encounter stretches into a decades-long affair, with her forever living in the shadows as the “other woman.” One of the few films made under the Production Code to deal sympathetically with marital infidelity, this elegant tearjerker overflows with dreamily romantic moments: the couple lounging under a cloud-filled sky, a chance meeting on a snow-shrouded New York sidewalk, and the quietly devastating liebestod of the climax.

And here, he’s paired with the ever competent Margaret Sullavan - their voices together in harmony, make for a wonderful melody. After this film, I'm already halfway through Maggie’s filmography and it's such a shame she didn't do more films, she was a great beauty but more importantly, a great talent. reviews.author: Bruno Andrade
reviews.text: "Barrabás é um filme totalmente original. Pegue a maioria dos filmes bíblicos: eles vão geralmente de A a Z. São cíclicos e terminam sempre fechando um círculo perfeito. Ora, Barrabás só vai de A a B. Cabe ao espectador fazer o resto do caminho, se ele quiser. E contrariamente aos filmes bíblicos, que são fundados sobre a afirmação, é um filme sobre a dúvida. Nenhuma sequência se fecha sobre si mesma, pelo contrário. Todas permanecem abertas. Há uma progressão dramática, mas não intelectual, pois os fatos se contradizem, se neutralizam, são interpretados de dez maneiras diferentes sem que essa liberdade seja vista como um erro. E você não considera isso original no domínio do filme religioso?! É quase revolucionário!"

reviews.author: Diogo Serafim
reviews.text: The material man haunted by the world of ideas. Chained to the brutality of life, doomed to it, until the light frees him to a path towards death. reviews.author: harrylime66
reviews.text: In a crowded square, Pontius Pilate gives the people the opportunity to save one of the two men who are going to die by crucifixion: Jesus, the so-called son of God, or Barabbas, the criminal. Many of you know what comes next and the playwright Christoper Fry (who wrote the screenplay) and Richard Fleischer do not want to provide us with the usual pastoral colossal where the incredulous people are flashed with the light and blind people get their sight back. In this sort of progressive negation, the film associates action with darkness and incomprehension as if personal liberation went through mistakes… doubts… maybe an overt blasphemy. After being praised by the crowd, Barabbas is released from the underground prison…

reviews.author: John_Lehtonen
reviews.text: Moving perpendicular to history, Barabbas cannot be reconciled. Of an invisible and generally unmentionable underclass — bandit, highwayman — his movement is as property, through literal hells of sulfur mines to the gaudy excesses of Rome, surveying, as it were, a full breadth of empire, from colony to slave camp to capital. Fleischer's alienated form, his distance, unnerves where other Biblical epics cloy, dramatizing a schism imparted by Christian morality in a "barbaric" mind. His only tool for potential freedom, his physical strength, now condemned, a confrontation between impulse and a new kind of reason play out on the expressive face of Quinn. Seen through the rising arc of a mass inversion in values, it cant help resemble the end of a world; the darkness encroaching in the religious sequences, the anxious rumbling of the score, all culminate in Barabbas' crucifixion, a spiritual pledge to darkness. The body's flight from salvation, if salvation means negation.

reviews.author: Seer
reviews.text: Cinema passes through Mondrian and finds Fleischer. It's not just These Thousand Hills; we find it in films before (Violent Saturday) and after (Barabbas). One must believe in the line: it describes a movement of the hand (the painter and their brush, the filmmaker and their camera), and prescribes a movement to the eye, following this line. As Fleischer made popular cinema, he understood what Jean-Claude Rousseau would years later, that depth in composition is the just relation of lines on a flat surface. Conflict and tension are the movement to and from the vertices; Fleischer draws boldly and confidently along the abscissa and the ordinate, which is why he sometimes appears an invisible author. The nervous are clumsy and…

reviews.author: jeliben
reviews.text: Fleischer does a Hegelian religious epic, presenting history as a battle of ideas, where elements of polytheism are absorbed (aufgehoben) by the then burgeoning Christianity (and vice versa). One priest describes these processes as “a wrestling back and forth, a laboring of the world spirit like a woman in childbirth” (emphasis added). Christian heretics are skewered alive in droves by the all-powerful Roman State Apparatus, but we sense that their deaths are a form of sacrifice to the Angel of History.

reviews.author: samwm
reviews.text: There's a lot I still have to understand about how Fleischer weathered the particularly difficult period his career spans and managed to make excellent films from the start to the end, but aside from economic and international questions, what is striking about a film like this, made at a terribly inauspicious moment for a Hollywood director, is how uncompromising it is. Other American directors had perhaps made films as existentially, philosophically and even theologically complex as this but had any made a film that was so uninterested in disguising its own complexity? Fleischer mobilises every surface, every particle of the earth, and every feature of his actors' faces to conjure the materiality of ideas, but none of this has the…

reviews.author: nathaxnne [goodbye <3]
reviews.text: A tale of love gone both right and wrong within and without a family. How monsters are defined, not born. How good intentions sometimes cannot divert disaster. Why letting your ex-conjoined twin talk you into a campaign of murderous revenge is more than likely a terrible idea, with lasting consequences beyond what may or may not have been intended. A warm and lovingly rendered portrait of early 1980's NYC Times Square Culture, from low-rent hotels with stairwells full of trash to adult theatres that show Kung Fu Triple Features to grimy bars that are a home away from home to seedy doctor's offices with poor lighting. Basket Case is not a film that offers any answers to how we should be with ourselves, our families, our loved ones, our neighbors, but it is one which honors the difficulties in mediating the tensions within all of our relationships, and does so with honesty and compassion.

Rains threatens to devour the scenery with his over-the-top performance, leaving the cast of young scientists that surround him to “Ooh!” and “Ahh!” like the kids who used to help Don Herbert with his experiments on Mr. Wizard’s World. Benson gets to deliver the disastrous news when “The Outsider” starts to inexplicably orbit Earth. He seems to be the only person who realizes the horrifying implications of that defiance of calculus.

reviews.text: Made a year after Ishirō Honda smashed Japan to smithereens with Godzilla, Half Human (or Monster Snowman) is a much less earth-shattering affair. It doesn't help that the only prints of the Japanese version of this film are borderline unwatchable. The film floats about in a weird state of semi-nonexistence, as Toho locked down its own property after concerns about its racism toward the Burakumin people. Pretty silly considering how later Toho properties would feature far worse racism. Free from its surrounding historical importance and controversy, Half Human is an okay but ultimately unremarkable watch. We get a somewhat sluggishly told Abominable Snowman story that if cut to seventy minutes would have been a banger. There are some really cool…

reviews.author: Colin the dude
reviews.text: There is one impressive scene which is when they get shot down "behind enemy lines". The sound design, the emergency of it, the whipping past the camera of the jet and the missiles actually looks pretty great, including a cream-dream shot of the jet brushing the treetops of a forest and throwing all the snow off its branches. It's the only time I'll backhandedly compliment the direction of John "Die Hard 5" Moore. The rest of the movie is this pre-9/11 (though released post-9/11) jingoistic romanticism of American brashness that may or may not have played well in 2001 but just doesn't play anymore. Not to mention a plot that is an insult to plotting. And Owen, come on. I know you were testing the boundaries of your dramatic chops like your buddy Vince Vaughn at the time, but stick with Wes. In fact, write something new with Wes prontisimo, we miss your synergy.

reviews.text: Saw this on 35mm for the first time tonight and it was even more of a thunderclap sensory explosion than I’d expected. Gorgeous, proud, brilliantly lit and staged, sometimes incoherent, funny, tragic, genuinely apocalyptic and end-of-the-millennium poetic. As bad as Nas is, DMX is that good. And the soundtrack is unusually smart—intermingling boom bap with dancehall, Southern rap with jazz and cleverly leaning on a capella renditions of R&B songs for a wildly operatic effect during Hype Williams’ orgy-of-light slow motion set pieces. Who wants to raise some money for Hype’s long-awaited follow up?

reviews.text: Lamberto Maggiorani (who plays the lead role of Antonio) was laid off from his job as a factory worker shortly after the film was complete. The factory required budget cuts and decided to fire Maggiorani because everyone assumed he was a millionaire movie star when he actually made only 600,000 lira (a little over 30,000 US dollars today, counting inflation). He pretty much spent the rest of his life as a bricklayer desperately trying but failing to land more acting gigs; even de Sica wouldn’t rehire him. Eventually, he died poor, having never regained the success of his first role.

reviews.text: John Milius' coming-of-age drama Big Wednesday seems to be still criminally underseen here on LB. A seminal 70's film that captures the spirit of the 1960's, and focuses on three surfers and their journey of self discovery against the backdrop of the Vietnam War. Milius' film is about the end of an era, but also about the bond of friendship that could never be broken. Featuring Gary Busey at his craziest, just watch his draft-dodging escapade for the proof, Jan-Michael Vincent at his most sun-tanned, and William Katz as the calming influence on both of them, the end of innocence and the death of the 1960's is played out among the swells of Malibu.

reviews.text: What an absolutely miserable film this is. Every frame is despondent with the kind of hopelessness that could've made it a struggle to behold. Every bleak thought it spits out equally so. But somehow, its darkness is inviting. Exploring faith, the loss of it, and the emptiness of spiritual isolation with a healthy dose of merciless violence, Christopher Smith's film packs a mean, often exhilarating punch. The desolate setting, paired with a good eye for grim motifs, imbue this pic with the atmosphere it needs to feel eerily resonant now and accessible regardless of the time in which it is viewed. It's not perfect by any stretch but it's got the kind of introspection usually reserved for more restrained features.…

reviews.text: Blackthorn has the bones of a good western. Squint hard enough and you might even see the shape of great film. Unfortunately, it’s saddled with uneven dialogue, bad flashbacks, and uninspired direction. A shame because I loved the setting—dazzling Bolivian vistas, the likes of which I’ve never seen on screen. And it has a great Sam Shepherd performance playing an elderly, ruminative Butch Cassidy. Thematically, there’s a little bit of meat on the bone as Cassidy wrestles with his past and the code by which he’s lived, but not enough to stick to the ribs.

reviews.text: Blackthorn ist eine Weitererzählung der Butch Cassidy & Sundance Kid Geschichte.Der inzwischen in die Jahre gekommene Cassidy (Sam Shepard) lebt in Bolivien und hat vor demnächst aus privaten Gründen für immer in die Staaten zurück zu kehren, Auf dem weg dorthin begegnet er Eduardo (Eduardo Noriega) und ab diesem Zeitpunkt entwickelt sich eine spannende Geschichte, in der auch immer wieder kleine Rückblenden in die Vergangenheit Cassidy’s gezeigt werden.Viel mehr möchte ich aber hier nicht zur Handlung sagen, außer das sie auch einen unerwarteten Twist bietet. Insgesamt hat Regiesseur Mateo Gil hier einen ruhigen aber atmosphärischen Western geschaffen, bei dem Oscarpreisträger Sam Shepard natürlich die herausragende Rolle spielt und der zum Teil fantastisch gefilmt wurde, hier sind z.B. die Szenen in der Salzebene zu erwähnen.Insgesamt ein Film den ich weiterempfehlen kann und den es auch noch kostenlos und legal zu schauen gibt.

reviews.author: Quiller
reviews.text: There’s a lot that’s good about this Technicolor remake of the silent-era classic. Chief among those qualities is Ernest Palmer and Ray Rennahan’s often breathtaking cinematography. Director Rouben Mamoulian wanted to pay homage to Spanish art — notice the enlarged details of Velázquez‘s Las Meninas that adorn the walls of Rita Hayworth’s home — and Palmer and Rennahan are up to the challenge. Jo Swerling’s adaptation also picks up on the underlying class tensions in Vincente Blasco Ibáñez’s novel. Tyrone Power sees exactly what awaits him in the pathetic figure of over-the-hill matador J. Carrol Naish, yet he lacks the education to protect his own economic interests. Power isn’t even literate.

Hayworth is forced into being the icy beauty again, which is always a pity. I don't like her cold. Linda Darnell, in a better role, kicks ass. She shares something with Tyrone, an air of innocence, something unspoiled and childlike, they always blend beautifully. Tyrone, whose birthday is tomorrow, carries himself like a proper Taurus, with graceful determination he faces a fellow bull. And he's angry, too.

reviews.author: Fint
reviews.text: Holy moly. To experience the early 40s Technicolor tones of Blood and Sand in an original nitrate print was to luxuriate in a sublime velvety richness. Rouben Mamoulian's visual sense was exquisite, notwithstanding the uniqueness of the event, his evocation of Spanish masters breathtaking, his shadows resonant, his reds vibrant. Beyond the visual, the film is suffused with a Spanish sensualness that juxtaposes sex and Catholicism with intensity, and contains electrifying musical interludes. Tyrone Power struts with conviction as the matador, Linda Darnell copes well with the difficult part of the good girl, Nazimova is magnificent as the mother whose tragic history is repeating itself.

reviews.text: I think with a lot of Burton's '70s films, you have to expect them to be pretty crap, and I went into this expecting the same, but honestly, it was a slight step above some of his other features. It's just all over the place; it feels like it wants to delve more into Bluebeard at times, and often at other times, it delves into exploitation, excess, and morbid violence.

reviews.text: A man who has murdered every one of his previous six wives and keeps their corpses on display should not be trusted. Anne, played by Joey Heatherton, discovers this firsthand when her handsome war hero husband, Kurt Von Sepper, an Austrian aristocrat played by Richard Burton, gives her free rein of his beautiful castle, with the instructions that she has access to all of the rooms except for one. Richard Burton is at the height of his alcohol-soaked hammy glory here as a pompous fascist who kills off his various paramours through stories told to his latest bride, the anachronistic and delightful Joey Heatheron (who I don't think closes her mouth once during the running time). The real fun kicks in during the second hour with a parade of outrageous vignettes as welcome guest stars like Virna Lisi, Raquel Welch, Agostina Belli, and Marilu Tolo drive our titular villain to homicide, though we ultimately find out the real reason for his behavior.…

reviews.author: Michael Shawn
reviews.text: I really wasn't sure what to expect from this but it wasn't what I got. And that was a terrific surprise! For one, in keeping with the obsession with psychology in the '60s & '70s, it takes a psychoanalytical approach to a folktale character and it works beautifully. The conclusion drawn brings the character to life in an ingenious way for modern sensibilities. Another thing I had no inkling of was that the film is a comedy — a black comedy, but absolutely hilarious at times. The many wives that Bluebeard has killed are each uniquely idiosyncratic and wildly amusing. It made the rather long runtime bearable to discover a new and delightful, and remarkably beautiful woman in each flashback sequence.…

reviews.text: It's not very often that you go into an "action" movie and come out with a dramatic arthouse-esque film, but that's what happened to me with Blunt Force Trauma. There is definitely a classic western motif that is utilized for the film, particularly in the almost nihilistic tone of the film with its wandering protagonist, but really the film plays out more akin to the approach Monsters took to science fiction than a normal action spin. The results are shockingly effective. The minimal exposition, the quiet characters, and the mysterious way the plot plays out are all benefits to the style. I will say though, the ending will leave quite a few folks pissed off - even if it was ridiculously fitting and well executed.

reviews.text: Andrew Dice Clay starring in an Albert Pyun movie? It happened! "Brain Smasher" is the nickname of the Diceman's character - a bouncer who finds himself protecting supermodel Teri Hatcher as she is pursued by Shaolin monks trying to find a rare lotus flower. The key creative touchstone here seems to be Big Trouble in Little China, but there's a police interrogation scene that's lit like a film noir, with everyone dressed in '40s garb. Why? Because Pyun thought it would look cool. You don't watch an Albert Pyun movie for a coherent vision - what it for nifty stuff. This movie isn't as propulsive as it needs to be, and the action isn't too exciting, but it's beautifully shot…

Breach tells the story of the investigation and exposure of Robert Hanssen, who while never as famous as his contemporary in spying for the Soviet Union and then Russia, the CIA's Aldrich Ames, may have caused even more damage and cost more lives. Ironically Hanssen escaped detection for several years after Ames' 1994 arrest in part due to intelligence leaks being blamed on Ames rather than him. Hanssen was also a most unlikely ally of Moscow, as he didn't fit anyone's idea of a potential spy: he was politically conservative, a devout Catholic, a gun enthusiast and a vocal anti-communist.…

reviews.text: When faced with nuclear annihilation, sometimes fondling a little angora helps. The ideas in Bride of the Monster existed decades before the film was shot and were thought up by people that were not Ed Wood. Motivations and character in Bride of the Monster are plugged in based on the costume - emotionless cop, mad doctor, plucky journalist, monstrous henchman - and we know what they all stand for based on the films of previous generations. But, Wood can’t put the puzzle together in an expected way and that’s why we remember him, he turned tropes into his personal cyphers, each film a roman à clef where every character represents a different side of Wood. Every character comes across as an outsider struggling with a past they can’t control, a past set in motion decades before Ed Wood was born.

reviews.author: Matteo
reviews.text: Bruceploitations were always wacky, but were they wacky enough to justify a title like Bruce Lee Fights Back from the Grave? Sure, plenty of wild, off-the-wall titles surfaced during the martial arts boom that followed Bruce Lee’s death, but only one was a Bruceploitation flick shot mostly in L.A.—and not even a Hong Kong production, but a Korean one. This one doesn’t feature the familiar icons we fans of Lee’s exploitation legacy love—no Dragon Lee, Bruce Li, Bruce Le, or Bruce Liang and the countless linguistic mutations of “Lee” that populated grindhouse marquees—just an unknown impersonator who literally rises from the grave. It looks like it’s going to be completely bonkers—exactly what that poster sells—but it’s not. It’s more limp…

The business, violence and Cary Grant schtick doesn't really come together. Barry Levinson was out of his depth when not doing chamber-comedy and his state-of-the-studio style dates badly. Self-mythologising subway flasher James Toback gets lost whenever it's more than one guy jerking off too, though his script is eager to please PUA hero Warren. As is usual with Beatty films, the highlight is a well-chosen supporting cast. Here Annette Bening gets to do Barbara Stanwyck, though…

reviews.text: Potentially my favorite of the three shorts in Memories. What these protestors want is not an end to the phantom war continuing on in perpetuity against an unknown foe, nor are they asking to reimagine and realize the totalitarian society dismantled. What they’re asking for is safer gunpowder to be used in firing the cannon. Marginally better conditions in service to the same great machine.

reviews.text: It's nice to be reminded once in a while that anime is a medium, not a genre or an art style. Cannon Fodder is a cool anime short with a unique art style that uses really creative "camerawork" to push the medium. This is a story about the world more than the characters, and the camera knows it. It floats around this cool militarized city whose whole society is based around the firing of giant cannons against an unseen enemy, focusing on the daily life of a family in it. Shots are connected by zooms, pans, and rolls that you rarely see in 2D animation, reinforcing this feeling that you're just seeing a tiny slice of a huge, moving city.…

reviews.text: Beginning with an appearance from Edgar Allen Poe, Danse Macabre builds into a brilliantly atmospheric slice of Italian Gothic. The plot focuses on a writer who agrees to stay in a haunted castle for a wager. He meets various characters while there, and naturally there's more than meets the eye! It's the style and atmosphere that is the standout of this one. Director Antonio Margheriti (who apparently took over from Sergio Corbucci) gives the film every ounce of style he can. The film delights in showcasing the Gothic sets, and the languid plotting gives plenty of opportunity for that. It almost verges on German Expressionism at times (was the Four Devils at the start a tribute to FW Murnau?) The…

reviews.text: High Gothic Terror! Love From Beyond The Grave! Musty Crypt Exploration! So Many Cobwebbed Candelabras Characters Literally Trip Over Them! A Fake E.A. Poe Intro/Outro Story! Castle Of Blood stands between not only Life and Death, but also at The Height Of Italian Gothic Horror on the precipice of its Psychedelic, Bloody Future. It required the combined talents of Sergio Corbucci AND Antonio Margheriti to pull off this chiller! There are so many elongated sequences of characters lighting candelabras or torches or candles and going up and down staircases in the otherwise full dark into libraries or tombs or bedchambers that even I was almost satisfied with how much of that sort of thing there was! No line of dialogue is wasted setting up this ghost story and mood. Poe and the others discussing the afterlife and love staying immortal through sharing and writing stories. reviews.author: Bleeding Skull
reviews.text: In a 1963 interview, actress Barbara Steele was asked what her plans were for the future. She replied, “I want to f*ck the world!” With movies like CASTLE OF BLOOD, that’s exactly what she did. A lonely traveler meets Edgar Allan Poe (!) in a pub. Poe issues a challenge: Spend the night in an abandoned castle and win a pile of money. The wager is accepted. But when the stranger arrives at the castle, he finds that it’s not so deserted after all. Dripping with gothic ectoplasm, CASTLE OF BLOOD feels like a wish-list of everything we expect from a stylish French-Italian co-production in 1964. Graveyards! Ghosts! Zombies! Sex! And of course, the incomparable presence of Barbara Steele in a career-defining role. Prepare for the spookiest sleepover of your life. (Joseph A. Ziemba)

reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"
reviews.text: "Danza Macabra" or "Castle of Blood" is a 1964 horror film directed by Antonio Margheriti. The film focuses on a journalistic personality named Alan Foster who takes a bet to spend the night within the walls of an old, haunted castle. This all comes about due to his skepticism, eagerly placing even a minor bet on surviving the night but for a sum of money that makes little financial difference. Upon arriving, he finds a night of interacting with spirits who recount for their violent last moments on earth withing the living. Then as the film goes further, even more devious truths arise, making for quite the haunting spectacle but one that also makes you ponder about the afterlife.

reviews.text: How does it feel to be the object of the female gaze, Mastroianni? The same question could be asked of Fellini, a director who was always accustomed to smother his male characters with beautiful, voluptuous women. From LA DOLCE VITA (1960) to 8½ (1963), from JULIET OF THE SPIRITS (1965) to FELLINI'S CASANOVA (1976), women have always been portrayed as seductive mysteries onto which debonair men have projected their dreams and fantasies. These films are strongly autobiographical in nature, almost behaving like extensions of how Fellini feels about himself. The sheen of cool that once defined his male characters, like Marcello, Guido, and Giogio—each, you'll recall, presented as if they could tantalize and possess any woman they desired —feels faded and…

reviews.author: john semley
reviews.text: My god I love this movie. Many American films try, but none romance the life of the nothing-to-lose itinerant like this one. I lose $60 playing online blackjack and have a panic attack that I'll never recover financially. Frank bets his home and whole life on two pissed-off roosters battling and doesn't make a peep. It invites the contemplation of whole other worlds teeming underneath the surface of everyday American life, where hard men are sent gilded invitations to exclusive cock-fighting tournaments. Beautiful, touching, mean filmmaking. Incredible to think of Néstor Almendros going from shooting Rohmer to filming slo-mo cockfights in dingy motel rooms in Nowheresville, USA to winning an Oscar for Days of Heaven. Talk about a life lived. Jesus Christ I feel like I need a drink of water I'm so worked up.

reviews.text: Rex Allen died in 1999. He suffered a coronary and collapsed face down in his driveway just as his secretary was backing his gold Cadillac out of the garage to drive him to a doctor’s appointment. She accidentally ran over him and, when the ambulance arrived, the Cadillac’s wheel was still on his torso. Allen died two weeks before his 79th birthday. Dawes) brings back most of the cast (and props, hello again flame-throwing helicopter, my old friend) of Codename: Wild Geese for second go that’s more revolutionary saga than “men on a mission” thriller. No Ernest Borgnine or Lee van Cleef this time, but we do still get heroic Lewis Collins and Manfred Lehmann, and Klaus Kinski as a hissable villain. It’s mostly pretty weak sauce, other than a couple of truly outstanding set pieces, in particular the missile destruction of a commercial airplane that looked so good I found myself wondering if Margheriti had reused actual news footage. Kudos on that one.

reviews.text: Auf den ersten Blick ein ordentlich produzierter B-Flick, auf den zweiten ein Namedropping, das einem das Fan-Herz, vor allem das deutsche, hochschlagen lässt. Hinter der Produktion Antonio Margheriti, Erwin C. Dietrich, Peter Baumgartner, vor der Kamera, und, um nur einige zu nennen, Klaus Kinski, John Steiner sowie, besonders interessant, die Synchronisations-Legenden Thomas Danneberg und Manfred Lehmann. Skurril, Danneberg spricht in der deutschen Synchro Lewis Collins und wird dann selbst gesprochen von Rainer Brandt.Sicher, die hohen Erwartungen werden nicht erfüllt, wann schon mal bei dieser Art Film, aber das Tempo stimmt, die Darsteller wirken motiviert und die Effekte passen. Ordentlich Knall-Bumm, viel Pyrotechnik und sehr überzeugende Miniaturen. Kurzer Break im Mittelteil, da gibt es Handlung. Löblich, aber gefährliches Terrain bezüglich…

reviews.text: I haven't seen nearly as many "macaroni combat" films as giallo or spaghetti westerns, but Commandos is currently my favorite. The premise is your usual "men on a mission" "behind enemy lines" set up, this time in the harsh North African desert. While our erstwhile heroes aren't recruited straight from the brig as is typical for the genre, there is a nod to the idea that some of the commandos tasked to masquerade as Italian soldiers have a checkered past as Italian-American mob goons. This mission briefing is the first of several bits that seem to have inspired Tarantino's Inglourious Basterds, much more so than its namesake.

The narrative is enthused with ideas of serving justice versus enforcing the law - the limitations of the latter in the realisation of the former.…

reviews.text: Above and beyond its myriad other pleasures, this is straight-up the most well-plotted Italian crime movie I've ever seen, foregoing all false, twisty, or confusing melodramatic incident for novelistic narrative clarity. But it also makes for very engaging entertainment, where the violence really hits you both in the gut and in the heart.

When the law exists purely as an instrument of capitalism and it's only there to protect the interests of the powerful, the only principled position is to tear it down by any means necessary. A way deeper kind of Italian flick with the adjacent theme work of say Street Law or Revolver. Damiani stays away from the violence 90% of poliziotteschis mess with. As I've recently learned, this film belongs to the "high brow" strain. I'm chomping at the bit to return to Contraband.

An assassination plot of a powerful construction magnate goes awry and a sprawling investigation ensues. The intensity is felt from the first frame itself, but the plot unfolds gradually and with a thoroughly dramatic approach.

reviews.text: When was the last time a director created a cinematic study of the civil war? If you are director Ronald Maxwell then perhaps “you” are the last person to probe this conflict in American history. “Copperhead” is actually Maxwells third trip down memory lane and herein lies an underside to that conflict. Set in upstate New York in 1862, the story is a personal conflict of conscience for Abner Beech a Democrat and pacifist. He comes into conflict with his Republican neighbor Jee Hagadorn an abolitionist and his own son who has joined the fight. The film is a slow build to an interesting resolution in the final two reels of the film. Questions raised by Jees’ son Ni Hagerdorn…

reviews.author: Sara Michelle Fetters
reviews.text: "Gettysburg" and "Gods and Generals" director Ron Maxwell goes the moderately fictional route with this tale of a Northern family living in New York State who do not believe in the war (aka 'Copperheads') and the effect this belief has on their close-knit community as well amongst members of the clan itself. The heavy-handed nature of the melodrama gets a little too much to bear by the climax, and the sprawling nature of the narrative feels a little more fitting to a two-part miniseries than a two-hour feature film, but for the most part this story is treated with intelligence and respect, never belaboring any of the issues Maxwell is trying to make while also assuming the audiences can navigate the more inherently personal portions without any extraneous embellishments.

reviews.author: Matthew Christman
reviews.text: Tolstoy wrote, "Happy families are all alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way." That goes double for movies. Good movies, no matter how different in tone or subject matter, all display a similar set of recognizable traits. Bad movies can suck for a million different reasons. One of the most common causes of film suckiness is the unspoken but all-pervasive assumption that every movie, regardless of genre, must contain the following elements: 1.) a plausible plot 2.) sympathetic, realistic characters and 3.) relationships between said characters that change over the course of the film. Now, most movies need these elements to really grab an audience, but for others, they just get in the way.

Влюбленная пара, которая не может быть вместе из-за разного социального статуса, соглашается на предложение незнакомца совершить преступление в обмен на возможность сбежать из города.Спродюсированный Корманом перуанский клон "1984", на удивление пристойно выглядящий, но напичканный ужасно играющими актерами, в том числе задублированной Шерилин Фенн, еще не снявшейся в "Твин Пиксе" и поэтому вынужденной раздеваться и уворачиваться от хватаний себя за промежность. Идущий первым в титрах Кэррадайн, вплывает в кадр на отметке получас и проводит на экране в общей сложности минут десять. Его функция - без всякой причины предложить бывшему охраннику и проститутке стать грабителями, с чем правда связан неплохой сюжетный твист, на котором фильм ожидаемо не может капитализировать. Вообще не самая плохой история, местами напоминающая адекватную бумажную антиутопию, совершенно не работает, поскольку зажата и разыграна между тремя неприятными персонажами, полностью отбивающими желание следить за их проблемами.

reviews.author: Josh Larsen
reviews.text: Sword of Destiny serves as an interesting case study on the difference between choreographing a fight scene and directing it. Yuen Woo-Ping is the director here, after working as action choreographer on the first Crouching Tiger, as well as on The Grandmaster, The Matrix and Quentin Tarantino’s Kill Bill films. Although Yuen has directed nearly 30 films, including the entertaining Iron Monkey, it’s revealing to compare the fight scenes in Sword of Destiny with those in Crouching Tiger (it should be noted that the two movies also have different editors). The choreography itself is dazzlingly inventive, but there is something too emphatic about the ways the sequences are filmed and assembled. Intentions are overstated, glances are held a beat too long, pauses take up too much space and slow motion is overly employed. In short, the action sequences in Crouching Tiger were at once clear and enigmatic; here, they’re explained.

Lenny is a fascinating character; everything he does feels like he’s flying by the seat of his pants and performing tasks for the first time. reviews.text: Cybill Shepherd never gets the credit she deserves. I am in the middle of reading the Henry James story this is based on, and one thing that immediately becomes clear from reading even a few pages of the text is that her interpretation of the character is quite bold, although it remains accurate to James' conception. Most actresses would attempt to generate sympathy for the character by either playing her as naive and innocent, completely unaware of the social boundaries she is crossing, or as defiant and rebellious, knowingly bucking the rigid conventions of the bourgeoisie. Of course, Winterbourne's dilemma is attempting to identify which of those two positionalities she actually occupies, but what Shepherd does that's really tricky is…

reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"
reviews.text: "Daisy Miller" is a 1974 film directed by Peter Bogdanovich. By any general assertion this would be considered a period drama within general form, but it actually holds itself up with quite a bit of its quirky comedic elements. The narrative follows an upper-class American by the name of Frederick Winterbourne who has fallen somewhat smitten by Daisy Miller while vacationing at a Swiss hotel. Miller, equally from an American well-to-do family, enjoys living a bit on the fringe and driving Winterbourne a slight bit mad by being flirtatious all over. This challenges Winterbourne's societal notations, as many of his associations seem opposed to him giving Miller any further of his time. In the true nature of affluent society, this…

The cocksure, young director and former movie critic, who ditched his wife and little daughter for a much-publicised affair with model turned actress Cybill Shepherd, had long been a thorn in the side of the critical establishment. Mixing beautiful original drawings by Topor, original shots and stock images, he creates a depressive yet accurate depiction of human existence through an ironical lense. It seriously features some of the most puzzling, creative and symbolic images I've seen in animated films, plus the mournful music gives it a timeless, sort of grand proportion. If you have ten minutes to watch a beautiful work of art, spend them here.

I swear, if you ever wanted to summarize 60s London, all you'd have to do is say "Beatles or Stones" and you’d fit right in. This film gets that. reviews.text: Giallo is not exactly an over-easy genre to get into, but I do consider myself a hard-boiled connoisseur of the form. That being said, Death Laid an Egg leaves me feeling scrambled, clutching at ephemeral clues like dander tossed by the breeze, my brain beaten, basted and fried. I sit back, trying desperately to piece together this odd bucket of inexplicably winged scenes, struggling to remember which came first. Director Giulio Questi poaches refreshingly little from his peers, serving up an experience unique in its cockiness, nuggets of cinematic perfection liberally doused in the sauce of exasperation. A few more like this and he would be near the top of my directorial pecking order. This movie is like bread, bread that is all meat.

As a retired hitman, Brynner’s Peter Marciani is pulled out of that retirement when a local mob boss Gennare Gallo (Giancarlo Sbragia) spots Sal Leonardi, an American Mafioso in Naples, collecting his winnings at the race track, kills him on the spot. reviews.author: Dennis Vehlen
reviews.text: Antonio Margheriti's only real Eurocrime film (not counting 'Killer Fish') teams retired hitman Yul Brynner up with a younger sidekick and love interest Barbara Bouchet to avenge the death of his brother. While 'Death Rage' isn't the most action-packed Italian crime film, Margheriti still directs some excellent shoot-out and chase scenes and makes them count. Brynner has a strong presence as always and sells the aging mafia killer perfectly, and his relationship with a younger protege is definitely the heart of the film. It reminded me a bit of Lee Van Cleef and Giuliano Gemma in 'Day of Anger' and may also be inspired by Bronson in 'The Mechanic' but actually has more warmth. The ending was especially good and actually finally turned my rating up to 4 stars. The De Angelis brothers also deliver another memorable soundtrack and we get plenty of tiny J&B bottles to top it off.

reviews.text: This was a decent crime / action flick. The lead actor, Yul Brynner, was really good. Also the plot was a simple revenge plot. In fact it was so simple that the bits that weren't action sequences seemed to mostly be filler that did little for the advancement of the plot, such as the protagonist's romantic sequence. There was also this arc where he takes on an assistant or apprentice, plans to have the apprentice kill the main bad guy at the end, then takes over himself in the last minute. The point of going through all that to just do it himself was lost on me. But hey, that didn't make the film all bad by itself, I did actually enjoy parts of it even if I did find certain parts a bit pointless.

reviews.author: laird
reviews.text: As I started to nod off, this Eurohorror-Gothic-mad-doctor-Edgar-Allan-Poern-revenge-from-beyond-the-grave movie got better. It's like my mind needed to sink down a level of consciousness to get onto its wavelength. The compression of time and intercutting between flashbacks and fantasy combined with the lazy dubbing and sloppy censorship edits (that were maybe made by a rogue projectionist) just added to the overall weird dream state vibe. At some point we as movie audiences allowed "making sense" to have some sort of supremacy status on the list of criteria for a "good movie." Screw that noise, I'd rather experience something first and understand it later, if ever (In that respect, this movie is more like GOODBYE TO LANGUAGE than I would have ever imagined).

reviews.text: Deathstalker 3 uses a third actor to play the lead role as Deathstalker, and he's hands down worse than the second. The sword fights here are routinely acted better by ten year olds in front yards all over the world. I've seen more realistic larp videos. There's even significantly less action here, likely because their actors were so bad at filming the action. This one doesn't even have the comedy tag or themes that the second used to try to boost its entertainment value. It wasn't all terrible, there are a couple decent ideas, like the undead warriors, and a few of the set pieces were decent. Yet honestly if you thought the second Deathstalker was bad, this one is clearly worse in many ways.

reviews.author: shookone
reviews.text: It looks a bit like The Wind That Shakes the Barley transformed into an action movie, this Defiance, and yet it doesn't. Different time, different place. The Polish/Belarusian partisan struggle against the Nazis in the early 1940s, filmed in the Lithuanian forests. It is precisely these elements, the costumes, and indeed the attention to historical detail that are reminiscent of The Loach. And yet, Defiance is a thrilling action film set against a historical backdrop, although the weighting and interest in the characters are thankfully given careful consideration.

reviews.author: MrPPeeps
reviews.text: "Defiance" is a gripping World War II drama that tells the incredible true story of the Bielski brothers, played brilliantly by Daniel Craig, Liev Schreiber, Jamie Bell, and a young George MacKay, who selflessly led a group of Jewish refugees to safety in the Belarusian forests. The film features terrific performances, great characters, and strong writing. My only real gripe is that, despite the powerful and emotional story being depicted, the film doesn't quite convey that emotion as effectively as it should.

reviews.author: Travis Lytle
reviews.text: With "Defiance," Edward Zwick assembles the type of film that has become his stock in trade: a rousing, emotionally alive story about war and its effects on those fighting it. Zwick weaves together humanity and explosive spectacle, and, though "Defiance" is not as passionate and exhilarating as "Legends of the Fall," "Glory," or "The Last Samurai," it is a memorable and impactful piece of work.

reviews.text: A great story with a loaded cast that has some powerful moments but also underwhelms in aspects. At its core, the connection between the brothers and how they are trying to save hundreds while also looking out for themselves and each other is very intriguing. I started to lose interest as it delved a bit into Fiddler on the Roof territory with forest wives for each of the brothers. There were many points in the film where I felt that Defiance didn’t exactly know what it wanted to be. Still, as with any film dealing with the atrocities of the Holocaust, it is powerful and will certainly leave an emotional impact.

reviews.text: There have been many documented films about The Holocaust. What they all have in common is the power to educate. How many people aside from historians had heard about Oskar Schindler before Thomas Keneally's book and Steven Spielberg's film? The same would apply to the Bielski brothers, a group of partisans who rescued Jews in Eastern Poland at the height of the Nazi's occupation. A true story, this has Daniel Craig, Liev Schreiber, and Jamie Bell as the main protagonists battling against overwhelming odds in the Naliboki Forest. This film dispels the notion of Jewish passivity, but also upset historians who accused director Ed Zwick of more than a few mistruths. Controversial in Poland and Belarus upon its release, this…

reviews.author: ButtNugget
reviews.text: A radio news broadcast informs listeners that the following day is the anniversary of the bioterror attack in Tokyo by religious extremists from a cult, which left over a hundred people dead and thousands poisoned. Four individuals seem to have taken special notice of the date. And so begins Hirokazu Koreeda’s profound and thought-provoking mood piece Distance. This is just phenomenal work by a great director at the top of his game. What follows is an intricate tale about loss and regret, and I honestly think that this might very well be Koreeda’s best movie.

Lá, encontram um homem que havia pertencido ao grupo, mas que sobreviveu por ter saído antes do desastre. Quando se preparam para ir embora, descobrem que o carro que os trouxe desapareceu, junto com a motocicleta do sobrevivente. Sem saída e com a noite se aproximando, são obrigados a se abrigar em uma cabana abandonada usada pelo grupo anos antes. É nesse isolamento forçado que memórias e tensões começam a surgir, e o encontro entre familiares e sobrevivente se torna…

reviews.author: Ben
reviews.text: Hirokazu Kore-eda's third feature, Distance, differs slightly in style from his earlier works, Maborosi and After Life, but not at all for the worse. While the documentary-like approach makes it difficult to understand the characters' actions and motivations, it still vividly captures aspects of the human condition. What I had loved most about the other films I had seen from Kore-eda before this was his ability to create characters and situations that felt genuine. Distance might not have tugged on my heartstrings like Maborosi's depiction of grief or After Life's exploration of memories and death, but it certainly had a strong impact on me and left me with lots to think about.

reviews.author: Enfant du Siècle
reviews.text: On the shores of a peaceful lake, as they do every year, a group of people gather to remember and mourn loved ones who committed mass suicide in that place. They are relatives of members of a sect who, three years ago, planned an attack by sabotaging the city's water supply that claimed the lives of several people. By chance of fate, they meet the only surviving member of the sect and are forced to spend the night with him; during this time doubts and concerns arise as well as a need to inquire into the past to try to elucidate what happened.

reviews.text: The Unhappy Place. A hallucinatory spaghetti nightmare tale of greed and corruption, loaded with gruesome violence as a revenant stranger serves as our guide through a homoerotic gothic spaghetti odyssey apocalypse where gold = greed and greed = suffocation by molten gold. Bleak, surreal, grim, and filled with horror tinged setpieces, gay cowboys, and trippy editing. The acid western, could be about 15 minutes shorter but I really can’t complain—naturally a movie with a town called “The Unhappy Place” and a man called “Sorrow” came from Guilio Questi of Death Laid an Egg fame.

reviews.author: Rafael "Mister Movie" Jovine
reviews.text: The ambition on display here deserves high praise. It presents a spectacular visual feast—gory, bloody, and violent—filled with striking and terrifying imagery. Many of the creatures (what on earth were those black, humanoid, energy beings?) and some character designs, particularly the villain, stand out remarkably. The animation overall, along with the production design and cinematography, is top-notch and incredibly imaginative, improving with each new chapter. Initially, I was somewhat concerned that the narrative might become repetitive, but they skillfully manage to refine it, introducing fresh elements while remaining true to its central themes—the eternal battle between good and evil.

Covering the same material as the first live-action film, this OVA greatly benefits from not being compressed into a two-hour runtime. It allows for a more in-depth exploration of its broader narrative. Granted, this is still the first third of a 10-book epic, mind you, so not everything is tied up as neatly as you’d like, and threads that seem essential can be left behind without a care. It can be beyond confusing at times, as it has a habit of introducing plot lines and characters that are unwanted or unneeded,…

reviews.text: "Dragon: The Bruce Lee Story" is a 1993 film directed by Rob Cohen. A biographical feature focused on the life and times of the infamous Bruce Lee, most of the context for the film was taken from the 1975 book "Bruce Lee: The Man Only I Knew" written by Lee's widow Linda Lee Cadwell. This obviously includes the growth of Lee from his humble beginnings to his relationship with Linda directly, also observing his entrepreneurial and showmanship side that grew him into the magnetic cultural icon in timeless form.

reviews.author: AD917
reviews.text: This Bruce Lee biopic is probably about 90% fantasy, 10% something approximating reality. A lot of it can seem downright silly—especially in its more melodramatic beats, or when Bruce is doing literal battle with his inner demons—and maybe such a standard “rise and fall” formula isn’t the ideal way to capture the spirit of a true iconoclast. But one thing it has to help elevate it above the genre conventions the script shamelessly deals in is a genuinely magnetic lead performance by Jason Scott Lee. Whether he’s in a fight scene, a love scene, or just peeling out on a motorcycle, you can’t take your eyes off him. Everything he does just screams “movie star!” If there was such a thing as justice in this world he’d have had a career on the level of Keanu Reeves or somebody of that stature.

reviews.text: Through Akira Kurosawa’s Dreams you notice a profound reflection of the director’s ideals and values he had during his life. This is probably his most experimental work and adding all the hallucinatory sequences, surrealism, post-apocalyptic visions and an exuberant display of nature really helped enhancing the whole experience to a whole other level. While some of the dreams might be more enticing to watch than others, they all have a deep significance attached to them. At the end of the day, this is a fascinating celebration of life and death that will certainly stick with you.

reviews.text: Dreams is a unique concept for a film, consisting entirely of short films inspired by Akira Kurosawa's recurring dreams. It is unlike anything else in his filmography and pure surreal arthouse. The images are beautiful and abstract, the storytelling often formless and wordless but forever hypnotic. All the sections are interesting in their own way, but the dreamy and slow presentation makes for something much more. Whilst Dreams is somewhat like Dodes'ka-den in having multiple stories, it is all structured and separated clearly here.

reviews.text: Driven is a notoriously (and criminally) maligned, high-octane car wreck of a movie you have to see to believe. Tracking the CART open-wheel circuit, Renny Harlin (an underrated auteur of wildly sloppy dad-movie extravaganzas) adapts Sly Stallone's bloated script and delivers ADHD-addled thrills from start to finish. This thing peels out at 200+ mph and refuses to let you breath or think — only pulling over to recharge at a few well-timed soapy, melodramatic pit stops (ludicrously saucy moments punctuated by pouty-eyed moues, smooth jazz flourishes, and over-embellished dissolves).

reviews.text: To's grace is replaced by a caustic bluntness more to-the-point than even the Category III films he ghost-directed for Patrick Yau in the '90s. But do not mistake this ostensible calming of form for acquiescing to Chinese censors; it instead gets one over them, mirroring the no-nonsense approach taken by police to drugs until it becomes a savage, uncompromising attack on that myopia. It's telling that, for all the planning and swift execution of the cops to put down a drug lord's operation, the generic upheaval of the final act comes out of nowhere to show how much they've missed.

reviews.author: Sean Gilman
reviews.text: From the beginning, it explains that this is not your typical heroic bloodshed Triad film, concerned more with codes of honor and brotherhood and the mirroring of good and evil than anything else. No, instead this is going to be a straight police procedural, with no metaphysical mumbo jumbo: "You're a drug dealer, I'm a cop. I didn't betray you, I busted you," explains Sun Honglei's Captain Zhang, and with that 25 years (at least) of Hong Kong genre convention, from John Woo's A Better Tomorrow and The Killer to To's own cop/Triad movies (Breaking News, PTU, Mad Detective, etc) is summarily dismissed.

reviews.text: 100-word review: Taking you on a nostalgic adventure with Scrooge McDuck and his nephews, DuckTales: The Movie introduces a plot centred around a genie and a magical lamp — a premise that, while familiar, predates Disney's Aladdin by two years. The film stays true to the spirit of the beloved TV series, capturing the humour and adventurous spirit that fans cherish. As a result, it feels like an extended episode rather than a fully distinct cinematic experience. While the animation quality is solid and the voice acting remains top-notch, the storyline doesn't quite push boundaries beyond what fans already expect from the show.

reviews.author: ratbastard
reviews.text: Spaghetti Western from Antonio Margheriti. Agent ‘Joe Ford’ is tasked to protect a run of gold shipments from a looming ambush. Ford’s preferred method of dealing with the ambushing bandits is dynamite. Quirky, energetic, and generally playful - though tonally muddled, and oddly paced. The photography, costumes and sets are decent. While the performances are generally fine, the characters are fairly stock and the dubbing is hit or miss. Rik van Nutter does his best to channel ‘The Man with No Name’, his character choosing explosives over conventional sidearms. The opening act is engaging, though the momentum dips in the second act, while the third act is a lot of fun. The set pieces and (fairly frequent) explosions are well executed - boasting some solid miniature work, all punctuated by a fun / breezy score.

reviews.author: Dennis Vehlen
reviews.text: A super fun spaghetti western by the great Antonio Margheriti starring Rik Van Nutter as a dynamite slinging special agent who almost feels a bit like you're putting a mixture of James Bond and Sylvester Stallone from 'The Specialist' in a western. His charming, womanizing ways reminded me of Dean Reed in 'God Made Them, I Kill Them' if I had to compare it to any other spaghetti western protagonist, and that's not a bad thing because I always enjoy when the genre tropes get shaken up a little like this. As you would expect from Margheriti the movie has a few great action scenes and obvliously a whole lot of dynamite, and it's kind of a blast.

reviews.author: rickrock
reviews.text: Every October, I dive into my annual old-school horror movie marathon. It often ends in January or February. But this year, my marathon has been hijacked by dozens of sphaghetti westerns. Sure they are somewhat limited- they mostly feature repeat and predictable conflicts: gold, search for outlaws or vengeance. So while Dynamite Joe is not particularly great, and a bit preposterous (as most low budget Italian westerns are), it's a nice change from the normal gunslinger lead. It's funny at times and there is a enough creativity to hold interest. Don't expect "Duck You Sucker", but for any fan of Italian produced westerns, it's a pleasant view.

reviews.text: The last entry in the Black Emanuelle series proper starts off with the sexy photojournalist in Kenya on the hunt for an Italian gangster who has taken refuge there. We then relocate to New York after Emanuelle spots something suspicious at the airport, and eventually gets involved in a sex slave trafficking ring. Emanuelle and the White Slave Trade is much less sleazy than many of the previous entries, with the focus much more on steamy slow motion sex scenes than violence…

reviews.text: You know how lots of films have an angry woman throwing her man's stuff out the window or onto the front lawn? Usually it's a device to show us he's got some character flaws and is in need of growing up and his life is being shaken up to propel the movie forward. That's true here too, but then the entire film stops on the lawn. The dude takes up residence on a comfy chair amidst his life's collection of possessions. What will he sell? What will he refuse to part with? His stuff symbolises his life and his psyche. The screenplay is clever and I really like the ending, which is unexpected and insightful. This film plays with the initial clichè then pretty much avoids all others. Will Ferrell gives a good performance - I actually think I prefer him in drama over comedy.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: drops you into the heat of a middle-aged, middle-class existential crisis not through a coherent psychological point of view but the scattershot emotions, ramblings and rage of a single night on the town in a state of drunken ennui; all captured in cassavetes' signature intense roaming handheld close-ups of high-contrast 16mm. though i think he had an ungenerous read on what cassavetes was ultimately going for (calling it a "dull diatribe against american life" lol) i really like andrew sarris' assessment of its raw spontaneity eventually cohering into an odyssey "of emotional survival through an endless night of loneliness and shattered defenses." i think it's power actually comes from being both of things at once, and lurching from one to the other in a haze of painful emotions and the pursuit of something, anything that might distract from them. anyway this is very good, but it is as grueling and exposed as advertised so mileage may vary.

There aren’t better performances than the ones in Cassavetes films.

reviews.author: Rick Burin
reviews.text: Far From Heaven is an expert pastiche of Douglas Sirk melodramas of the 1950s - particularly All That Heaven Allows and Imitation of Life - that also stands on its own two feet. The gimmick, and there is always one where homages are concerned, is that Haynes deals with themes that were resolutely off-limits for moviemakers during the Eisenhower era, like homosexuality and inter-racial love. Julianne Moore is the smiling housewife whose apparently perfect existence is shattered by the revelation that her husband (Dennis Quaid) is gay. She seeks solace in the company of her black gardener (Dennis Haysbert), but it turns out that small-town housewives of the 1950s will talk...

reviews.text: It is impossible to understand John Milius’ exact thought: he has always refused the label of fascist and he defined himself as a “zen anarchist”, that sounds beautiful, but no matter how you analyse it, it means nothing. I have other options: “stubborn classicist”, “nostalgic for MGM”, “rifleman of screenplay”, “indoor smoker of cigars” and so on. However, his core feature is his intolerance towards modernity. “Farewell to the King” takes place in a lush Borneo that looks more like the Middle-earth than to a specific point on the world map, and his titanic hero must have read Kipling and Tarzan to become the liberator of a tribe as if by magic. The film is exactly what you are expecting,…

reviews.text: John Milius does Lawrence of Arabia, The Bridge Over the River Kwai, and The Man Who Would be King with Farewell to the King, and while it falls short, it is still a nice call back to the days of high adventure. Apparently the film was butchered in the editing stage by the studio, and that could be the film's main problem. There are multiple times when I wasn't completely sure what was going on, and maybe if Milius had the final cut, it would have been better. Still, I feel that Milius' films suffer the most in the editing department, so maybe it wouldn't have been better.

reviews.text: Во время Второй мировой сбитый над тихим океаном английский военный обнаруживает в джунглях дезертира, ставшего королем местных туземцев, которого пытается уговорить помочь в борьбе с японцами.Несмотря на кассовый успех "Красный восход" видимо крепко ударил по репутации Милиуса, потому что вышедший спустя целых пять лет "Прощай король", выглядит почти извинением за предыдущие перегибы вправо и наполен банальщиной и морализаторской пошлятиной, от которой до этого режиссеру хватало ума держатася подальше. Тут у нас правильные аборигены, живущие в райской гармонии с природой и проклятый белый человек, пришедший испортить эту волшебную идилию своей войной. Фильм пытается выстроится вокруг культурного конфликта Короля- беглеца и британского офицера, но это не работает, поскольку Нолти безбожно кривляется, делая вид, будто живет среди туземцев не пару лет, а всю жизнь, а актёр Хейверс вообще никакой. И поскольку минуте к двадцатой ясно практически всё, что случится, смотреть это кино становиться очень скучно, даже несмотря на красивую природу и пару приличных боевых сцен.
