reviews.text: Living in a world where freedom is bought with blood. A rather puzzling exercise, somewhat intimate and elusive while still very frontal and elegiac about its adventurous conception and exotic settings. Milius' unfaltering respect for each human life is seen in the mournful, carefully built sequences of death, but also in the sequences of life, where an isolated microcosm of people learn to live together by the most humane means.

reviews.author: Mark Tinta
reviews.text: Third time I've watched this in the 30 years since its release and it's still a crushing bore. Essentially a retread of a handful of ideas that writer/director John Milius used in his screenplay for APOCALYPSE NOW, FAREWELL TO THE KING has an earnest performance by a fully-committed Nick Nolte as a WWII deserter who becomes the king of an isolated tribe in Borneo. He doesn't quite go full Kurtz but Nolte still gets pretty wild-eyed at times, especially with a look that's equal parts YOR: THE HUNTER FROM THE FUTURE and Celtic Frost frontman Tom G. Warrior.

reviews.text: Cory and I are currently in a state of limbo following our Ernest watch party series. We've explored all the available resources from John Cherry III and Coke Sams' respective filmographies. So, now, we're left digging up the rocks of Jim Varney's other, non-Ernest related efforts, hoping to find something resembling the spark and spirit inside his creative soul, which clearly burned bright throughout his often-middling and underwhelming movies. Sadly, we're left with despicable films like Fast Food, a relic of the late '80s which was left in the sands of time — and one that should very well stay buried.

He is a painter and a storyteller; he is nostalgic and melancholic; he is carnal and sexual; he is a poet and a dreamer and an eccentric; he is a filmmaker afterall. But he is all of this with Love. Love for images, love for poetry, love for dreams, love for family, love for memories, and love for women. That is why Fellini’s Casanova is one of the Italian master’s most riveting and magical films: it is a picture about Love.

reviews.text: Fellini is a traveler, or rather, his films are about travelers. Not simple "road movies," but in the sense that his films never return to the same place where they began, not only spatially or physically, but perhaps mentally as well. Fellini's Casanova resonates throughout his filmography and aligns with the ideas of decadence first in La Dolce Vita and later in Paolo Sorrentino's The Great Beauty. He is a character who boasts of being a joke, a sex machine, and who finds in his arrogance the mockery and misfortune of his life.

reviews.author: Aurora
reviews.text: A solid well-acted police thriller. I think it could've gone even harder with the ending but it walks a fine line of reality and bad luck versus showy set pieces. I feel that Jai Courtney who is great here, has been pigeonholed in Hollywood -- forced to play loud brash crazy characters. But this movie proves he's perfectly capable of playing a more nuanced role. I love how the film shows just how protected a cop is as he constantly makes mistakes. Cops are a gang of their own and I always appreciate films exploring this side of the law. It's a character driven moral dilemma drama with more than enough intrigue to carry the tension. I would also call this movie: Men & Their Mistakes.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: A taut, stark, who's-deceiving-who neo-noir debut with some pretty impressive no-budget mood and style. You can tell the kind of harsher music sounds he gravitated towards even here. Between some of the look and camera movement choices you get the feeling watching it that Nolan thinks he's doing his version of something like Breathless but as is typical for him (around this time especially) it's built around a non-linear, literal-minded, twisty smart-guy plot that kinda stifles it from getting to a place like that. I do like going back to this era for him to see some of the darker, more perverse psychological obsessions and character relationships that got phased out of him after Memento and The Prestige, but will confess to finding this one a bit harder to take as grimly seriously as those two because the "burglar who... makes u think?" concept built into it is just so funny to me.

reviews.author: Kevflix And Chill
reviews.text: The nonlinear story telling here effectively weave some narrative twists into this noir-ish tale. Really enjoyed seeing the genesis of some of Nolan’s filmmaking hallmarks. It’s a little slow at the start playing out seemingly in linear fashion. It’s when Nolan reveals that this is a nonlinear story, that I became totally engrossed. The main character’s hair length changes, bruises appear on his face, we start to witness events that were alluded to in the past tense in previous scenes. Putting the puzzle together makes for a really engaging watch even if it’s not thematically rich. Worth checking out, especially for fans of Nolan’s other films, plus it’s a breezy 70 minutes.

reviews.author: Quiller
reviews.text: The best adaptations of Alistair MacLean’s novels (The Guns Of Navarone, Where Eagles Dare, Breakheart Pass) lean into the source material’s pulpy sense of fun. However absurd the action gets, it’s best to play it straight and let the audience have the most fun, not the characters themselves. The problem with this long-delayed sequel to Guns is that it’s a little too tongue-in-cheek. It’s more in the tradition of boys’ own adventure than pulp fiction. The result is diverting but not particularly memorable.

reviews.text: A sequel to the classic 1961 war action The Guns of Navarone also based (albeit loosely) on an Alistair MacLean novel, about a squad sent to Yugoslavia on a secret mission. It stars Robert Shaw, Harrison Ford and Edward Fox, and despite being a follow up the leads have been recast. The link to the original is fairly minimal but on its own, the film is a solid adventure that benefits from numerous twists and turns. However, the characters aren’t well developed and the special effects are a bit underwhelming, and so while I enjoyed the film I thought it wasn’t as good as similar war movies.

The fact it took 17 years to make a sequel, a fairly awful sequel in fact, said it all. Gone were Peck, Niven, and Anthony Quinn, the elements that helped make the original film work so well, and although Robert Shaw and Edward Fox do their best, this goes downhill…

reviews.author: Niall Urquhart
reviews.text: An interesting wartime film which I think would have been quite effective as morale boosting propaganda. Showing how a house in London has endured other conflicts starting with the Napoleonic wars. An amazing cast of Hollywood based ex-pats and American actors try to bring it all to life. Unfortunately, the film is very gentle and just meanders its way through all the different moments in time. However, there is then a jolt at the end as bombs drop on the neighbourhood in a sequence that is unpleasantly effective. It's fun to spot all the famous faces. reviews.author: Keith G
reviews.text: Middle class Americans Dick and Jane farcically spiral into financial trouble when Dick loses his lucrative aerospace engineering job. When they can't get another job, welfare and their garden is repossessed, the couple turn to crime to pay the bills. This used to be regularly on TV decades ago, my memory was always enjoying it more when the pair turned to crime. What I think now is Jane is a delight, Fonda is very good here, Dick however, is a dick, we're not supposed to root for the unemployment clerk but we do. Social commentary aside, I feel that can only be successful in these circumstances, if we sympathise with both characters. This probably goes down better in 1977. The idea of turning to crime to maintain your social status doesn't work for me. Has some funny moments but overall not a film I enjoyed revisiting.

reviews.author: Felix Atkinson
reviews.text: Ted Kotcheff's "Fun With Dick And Jane" is a wild and riveting film that is overflowing with comedic shenanigans. The film starts when an upwardly mobile couple finds themselves unemployed and in debt, they turn to armed robbery in desperation. This film is laugh out loud funny! The interesting thing about Dick and Jane, is that the film presents them as objectively awful people. They do bad things throughout the film, and it never tries to portray them as earnest or good- it tells it how it is. I think that's a really clever thing, and makes this modern Bonnie and Clyde-esque film oh so much better. The humour is so good, and some of the jokes are just excellent.…

reviews.text: Revisited this one to show Jozlyn and it reminded me just how much I miss movies like this. Trashy, atmospheric, low-budget Alien knockoffs, of which this is probably one of the absolute best, are such a friggin' mood. This kind of stuff isn't even a dying art anymore. It's fucking dead and buried. They literally don't even remember how to make films like this in Hollywood. Films that milk every penny of their meager budget to maximum effect, with tons of amazing sets, gorgeous matte paintings, and goopy rubber monsters. Plus, you get a pre-Nightmare Robert Englund, and Sid Haig as a stoic space-warrior with these awesome crystal throwing star dealies. Upped my rating to 5 stars.

I wouldn't say that Galaxy of Terror is an exciting film, but it gets on with the action straight away and actually manages some surprisingly memorable sequences; the worm rape/disappearing clothes scene being the best of them. There's a handful of goey gory practical effects which is always nice and there's a few memorable faces in the cast. The final reveal is quite interesting aswell...it's really a shame that the overall film isn't better because it has a lot going for it.

The irony of some parodically money hungry goons exploiting a man; with his untimely demise in real life a marketing ploy, a scheme to sell more tickets: meta-fuckery at its absolute worst. Clouse was no doubt promised molti geetus to make Game of Death, and what makes it all the worse is that it’s so shamelessly and crummily made, not only narratively, but in terms of its awful acting, writing and technical specs as well—it is bad enough that the story is so indecorous, did the rest of the movie have to be as well? And yes, the actual Bruce footage is fantastic, but getting to that point was a lot like suffering through a root canal: long and aching, and doubly so considering all the extenuating circumstances surrounding the making of this shitshow.

The film was released posthumously by Golden Harvest 5 years later, and basically constructed a whole story around 11 minutes of actual Bruce Lee footage. The result is undeniably a hack job where the stitching is painfully obvious. Lee's stand-in, despite director Robert Clouse's attempts to shoot him from behind wherever possible or in shadow, is never very convincing. It's actually pretty distracting. With the best will in the world, it's never amounts to more than a guy pretending to be Bruce…

(1976) yesterday, a debut feature that is a documentary with a strong political and narrative element, prompted me to rewatch Australian writer/director John Hillcoat’s Ghosts... of the Civil Dead, a debut narrative feature with strong political and quasi-documentary elements. This film made a huge impression on me when I saw it on its initial cinema release and I have been a Hillcoat fan ever since, particularly liking The Proposition (2005), The Road (2009) and Lawless (2012). It was also a chance to continue my run of watching first features by directors I have come to admire.

It's a little better than average for the genre and has a nice mean streak to it. For instance, a teenager tags along with Richard Harrison's group of warriors and ends up getting caught by the enemy. Harrison refuses to rescue him, saying the mission is more important than one soldier. Yet as he's pontificating, you can hear the kid screaming as he's being tortured. The over-acting that Harrison does to try and convey his inner turmoil at hearing this is hilarious. This one lacks any big monsters which is a shame. Margheriti would correct this with the awesome Yor, Hunter From The Future in his trashy 80's period.

reviews.author: PopcornIdeology
reviews.text: A sentimental farewell to his two most frequent collaborators, Ginger and Fred is a unique film in Fellini’s filmography. Surprisingly it feels much less felliniesque than the other films he made later in his career, yet it has an undeniable warmth and comfort to it. Giulietta Masina and Marcello Mastroianni have amazing chemistry, and there characters seem to represent two separate past lives of Fellini, that have since reconciled with time. I wish Fellini could’ve focused on this more rather than taking some unneeded (yet admittedly still interesting) thematic detours. While the final 30 minutes provided poignant and interesting insight into Fellin’s psyche, I would be lying if I didn’t say I found the first half of the movie unfocused and even a little contrived. With that being said though I was surprised with some of the vulnerability and emotion clearly being exerted by Fellini, someone who in my opinion rarely shows his true emotions effectively.

Everyone is hustling, everyone trying to catch a moment of fame, or live in an old one, once more. Our guide to the carnival chaos is Giulietta Masina as Ginger, who has her own reasons for attending,…

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: It is tired and very honest about it. It is unique among Fellini films in that artifice is equate with commodification in way he never tried before, almost a self-critique while also remaining very harsh about the world around it. Much like in E La Nave Va the reduced means become part of the film subject matter. One might call it an old man's film, but it is also very close to Moretti's Sweet Dreams from a few years earlier. The most contemporary Fellini film and a very sorrowful one. It gets a lot of Massina/Mastroianni paring and it is impressive in how much it manages to both use their star personas and respect the overall concept that should work against it.

reviews.text: The most impressive thing about Fellini’s Ginger & Fred is that, despite being the first time legends Giulietta Masina and Marcello Mastroianni are in a film together, their connection seems profound and deep-rooted. Both in their sixties, they portray a famous couple who, in their prime, impersonated Ginger Rogers and Fred Astaire and who, now, decades later, are reunited for a television show where they’ll perform their number one last time. Fellini paints their relationship with subtlety, hinting at deeper feelings they might have had for each other that went beyond the professional, and how they reemerge with this reunion.

Ginger and Fred also makes for a nice companion piece to City of Women in how Fellini builds the worlds of each movie. The City of Women feels like it's right next to The City of Television.

reviews.author: BrandonHabes
reviews.text: A shame. Fellini missed a golden opportunity of turning this Masina/Mastroianni mashup into a 2-hour, tap-dancing music video. I jest. But really, how cool is it that they finally get to share the screen together after all these years? Problem is, we don't get to see enough of them, let alone their Ginger/Fred act, develop onscreen. Fellini seems far more interested with indicting modern showbiz and Italian television culture, riddling almost every frame with heavy-handed TV screens, bizarre commercials, and other impressionistic hullabaloo that distracts us from their story. Clearly a lampoon of the amphetamine MTV generation, but it all kind of succumbs to the excesses it means to critique. While the "Cheek to Cheek" number is fun and worth the watch, GINGER & FRED is yet another example of Fellini having lost interest in the humanity of his characters.

reviews.text: I've been too hard on this film in the past. Watching it again on 35mm at the Mahoning Drive-In, I could take in the genuinely astounding effects work on display and the heroic attempt at returning the Big-G to his disaster movie roots - without ever losing his personality. Godzilla would get smaller eyes (eventually going full cat) as the Hensei films progressed, but here he's got the big old ping pong browns that he sported in his more money-starved entries, and I love it so much. There's no attempt to hide the fact that the big guy is rubbery as hell, but it's filmed from some breathtaking angles, and the miniature buildings have never looked better.

reviews.text: technically a direct sequel to the original but basically a respectful reboot. and given what was available (though pricey) as far as FX technology in the mid-80s, it's nice that this stayed cheap and aesthetically faithful. while it doesn't have the '54 version's urgent fear, aside from a few flourishes (particularly the Super X, a high-tech anti-Godzilla aircraft) the tone here is fairly dry, so after 15 variously absurd previous entries you might trick yourself into thinking it's kind of humorless. but it does a decent job with the anxiety of a country feeling close once again to a conflict between superpowers, only this time having first hand experience with the likely result. on the other hand there's a downright agonizing 10-minute stretch featuring the Japanese Prime Minister trying to convince the Americans and the Soviets to not use nukes on Godzilla.

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: With numerous shots of dead arms, legs, and heads poking through pools of oily sludge, is this the only Godzilla film to actually show the bodies of kaiju attack victims? The imagery here is panicked, desperate, with whole chunks built out of shots of dozens of talking heads on TV screens shouting at you or screaming babies and skulls mocking us. The inky black color palette is disrupted by slashes of color, whether it's at some psychedelic happening or a cheerfully sinister animated interstitial scene, or even a James Bond-style opening credits sequence. It's maybe trying to jar an audience it sees as oblivious swinging 60s burgeoning Japanese consumers out of their complacency. The sheer urgency of its sincere and simple environmental advocacy is almost disorienting. I'm amazed it doesn't end with Godzilla crying a single tear over a garbage-strewn Monster Island.

reviews.text: GODZILLA VS HEDORAH is often labelled “The Silly One”, but it’s just as serious and committed as Honda’s original, updated to reflect the era of its creation. Environmental collapse replaces nuclear annihilation and Honda’s grim documentary approach is switched out with some freewheeling 70s style: Groovy pop songs decrying the destruction of the earth, playful animated sequences about the murder of innocents, and nervy fourth-wall-breaking tricks that underline the story's consequences: Like when the screen’s colours explode to life when some teens start to party on Mount Fuji, but ghostly figures watch them silently, as the teens ignorant actions lead them to a terrible fate.

reviews.text: A film becomes more interesting if the viewer knows about the directors. If you are not aware of the work of the Taviani brothers, the film would appear to be a fictional biopic of D W Griffith, his film "Intolerance" and his way of making films. If you know about the Taviani brothers, you will realize that they were making a film about themselves, their past films, and their love for cinema and a lot less about Griffith (they never, ever had much to do with Hollywood, at least not up to the making of this film!). A fascinating work--I hope to write a detailed review explaining what most viewers missed out. This Italian filmmaking duo is one of the most talented filmmakers in Europe. Vittorio Taviani died recently--his younger brother Paolo survives.

I am a person that needs a philosophical justification for even mundane actions. I had a good philosophical idea to explain this particular one. reviews.text: Gridiron Gang is a solid, feel-good sports drama that hits because it’s really about second chances, not just football. Dwayne Johnson does a good job playing a tough but caring coach who pushes these kids to believe they can be more than their mistakes. The team chemistry feels real, and the movie shows how discipline and support can change someone’s path. It’s not the most original story ever, but it’s easy to root for, has strong emotional moments, and the message actually lands. Overall, it’s inspiring even though it’s cheesy but it lands for the reason that it’s based on a true story.

It's either a film about how an interracial platoon of soldiers become a brotherhood interspersed with combat, or vice versa., but both parts work. reviews.author: Kevin_Robbins
reviews.text: Hamburger Hill (1987) is a movie I recently watched on Amazon Prime. It tells the story of a battalion that, shortly after completing training and getting their first taste of combat in Vietnam, is sent to a heavily contested location where American forces are suffering severe casualties. The area, nicknamed “Hamburger Hill,” is a brutal stretch of land where U.S. troops are pinned down by relentless guerrilla warfare and sniper fire. As the losses mount, morale deteriorates and the hope of victory fades.

The film eventually limps towards a sort of half-arsed Heart Of Darkness denouement where randomly enough 80's TV siren Glynis Barber makes an appearance. reviews.text: It's not easy to tell where this movie is going. It features sex symbol Raquel Welch as a rape victim who wanders around wearing only a serape, leaving you to sympathize with her for being raped while simultaneously gazing at her as the desert wind blows that serape here and there. Plus "Hannie Caulder" leans spaghetti western, then kind of Peckinpahish, then more like an old-fashioned Hollywood western. Plus Raquel Welch is out for revenge, but being a woman, needs a man to teach her how, kind of a feminist film with masculine leanings. But in spite of the apparent overall lack of commitment to any particular style or message, "Hannie Caulder" is a kick-ass western in the Burt Kennedy vein, since he's the director, violent and well produced, by the British apparently (maybe that explains its multiple personalities). Robert Culp is pretty cool as well.

reviews.text: So very clearly written by men, but Raquel Welch‘s fiery commanding performance transcends the script’s objectifying awkwardness. (Was the dream flashback to the rape really necessary?). Thankfully that same script also has snappy hardbitten dialogue for the entire cast to relish. Hannie Caulder walks a shaky line between rape-revenge exploitation and gritty western adventure, propelled by a central mentorship that may or may not have influenced Tarantino’s Django. The action was unexpectedly robust too, with a scrappy dynamism and surprisingly bloody gunshots. The ending’s deus-ex-machina was annoying though, felt like it deliberately undermined Welch’s arc.

reviews.text: Dismissing the charm, characters, and sports-comedy fun of its predecessor, "The Love Bug," Robert Stevenson's "Herbie Rides Again" runs on empty. Watchable but forgettable, the followup is marked by the same cookie-cutter narrative at work in Disney live-action product from the era: nefarious businessman wants something; nefarious plot ensues. Here, Herbie, the beetle with a mind of its own, finds its way into that plot. Comic beats are forced, characters are uninteresting, and the work's enjoyable set-piece are not long-lasting. It is a strictly mediocre family-friendly outing.

reviews.text: Steve Reeves's original outing as Hercules seems to be one of the earliest Italian-made Peplum films making it a swords and sandals genre monolith. Its success is credited as the reason dozens and dozens of other Italian Peplum films were pumped out through the mid-60's. I enjoyed it, but not as much as I likely would have in 1958. In fact the hero could have been named anything, there wasn't much in the story that linked him to his divine heritage other than his immense strength. There were several entertaining sequences, but nothing over the top or that stands out. It's an easy watch, but modern swords and sandals flicks just seem better at almost everything this one tried.

reviews.author: Travis Lytle
reviews.text: Engaging horror let down by its final moments, Rod Blackhurst's "Here Alone" is a still-respectable genre entry. Revolving around five characters but with its sharpest focus on one, the story sees the survivors of a disease escaping civilization to eke out an existence away from the threats presented by the virus's flesh-eating victims. Stark and mannered, the film is neatly put together; it is minimal yet emotionally broad. Blackhurst and his leads build something taut where danger lurks around every corner. Its story may descend into genre cliche in the final act, but the film is a, nonetheless, watchable piece of work.

reviews.text: This was my first time seeing a prime era Wiseman, as opposed to his later, more sprawling documentaries, and the tighter thematic focus really sings out. Here, it's all about how even in The Freest Country On Earth we seem to be hopelessly obsessed with guiding children towards obeying authority, staying in line, and following the rules. The final scene, showing an assembly reading of a letter from a former student being written just before the writer goes to fight in Vietnam, capped off by the teacher or administrator doing the reading saying something like "whenever we get a letter like this, we feel we've done a good job," is one of the most chilling things I've ever seen in any documentary.

reviews.text: Hiroshima Mon Amour is both a great film and some of the most pretentious clap trap I've ever seen.It is as much a beautiful ode to overcoming the despair of utter destruction as it is a terribly misguided self-important comparison between the main character's lost love and the world's most horrific disaster.It is beautifully photographed and scored, and so melodramatic at times that it is laugh out loud funny.It's poetic dialogue sings, but the dreariness is too heavy.It wants to be passionate but the "come here, go away, come here, go away" antics of the cut-out cardboard character turn it into a farce.Hiroshima Mon Amour is a great innovative film that makes me appreciate Hollywood.

reviews.author: Matt Singer
reviews.text: "It’s cool to be Agent 47, with his crisp suit and polished pistols and deadened soul, which is why he’s been the subject of more than half a dozen Hitman video games over the last 15 years. But it’s not cool to watch Agent 47 in a movie, because the very thing that makes him a fun video game character — his detached demeanor, his singular focus — makes him a terrible movie character. He never misses and never moves at a pace faster than a leisurely saunter. He has no apparent goals or motivation, and no opinion about his violent activities because he was specifically designed not to have goals or motivations or opinions; just targets and objectives. His only discernible emotion is his deep love for posh luxury hotels. Rooting for the title character of HITMAN: AGENT 47 is like watching a baseball movie and rooting for the pitching machine.

reviews.text: The emotional core of Abbas Fahdel’s remarkable 5.5 hour documentary HOMELAND: IRAQ YEAR ZERO is the director’s twelve-year-old nephew, Haidar. He’s a precocious, thoughtful and profoundly empathetic youth trying to make sense of the situation in Iraq in the months leading up to the invasion and the subsequent American occupation. He copes with the pre-war anxiety by focusing on his immediate world and projecting excitement at the prospect of the unknown. He talks about how great it will be to have school cancelled while taping up windows to prevent shattered glass. He questions the adults in the house about what it was like during the Gulf War in 1991. He laughs hysterically when his sister brings home diapers to wear…

reviews.author: RanchoTuVu
reviews.text: The urge to see another moody gothic Italian horror film from the early 60s can be pretty intense. This almost satisfies it. Set in a medieval German castle, the wife of its owner discovers a torture chamber with an iron maiden that has a little cup at the bottom to collect blood that drips from inside. The old methods of torture are the best according to the Punisher, a deformed killer who wears a black hood to cover his face. The story kind of ties him to the aftermath of the horrors of the Nazis and sets it in a gothic horror film. Nice color photography captures the rich dark textures of the upholstery and Rossana Podesta's flowing white night gown.

reviews.author: Demdike

A nightgown-clad American woman (Rossana Podestà) roams the halls of an old German castle before stumbling upon a room full of old torture devices, then faints upon seeing a dead woman inside the titular contraption, better known as the iron maiden. Her new husband (Castle of Blood star Georges Rivière) is descended from a line that also bred the infamous lunatic "The Punisher" (not that one), who ran around in a hooded costume torturing women he considered of loose morals to death. The family castle naturally houses a museum of this creep's favorite tools, curated and caretaken by a scarfaced Christopher Lee. Hubby tells his bride she imagined the…

reviews.text: I dug this ensemble anthology piece about a day or so behind the scenes at a posh New Orleans hotel way more than I expected. And I should have known with Taylor, Karl Malden, and Kevin McCarthy appearing (among others), that we'd be entering the Twilight Zone at some point.

reviews.author: hiruko
reviews.text: Drama unfolds in a New Orleans luxury hotel. It’s played out over multiple story arcs of various hotel staff and guests, a format I personally enjoy, and backed by a cool swinging jazz score by Johnny Keating. Rod Taylor and Kevin McCarthy’s performances are standouts, and Karl Malden is memorable as a thief. May be a little dry for some, but for a typical 60’s Hollywood production, grandiose and star studded, it delivers (via room service of course!).

reviews.text: It is difficult for me to review this from the POV most viewers will bring to it. I recently read Arthur Hailey’s original novel, and I found it a superb potboiler. Hailey did a lot of research before writing his novels. His prose might have been workmanlike but he had a real gift for crafting a procedural. Hotel is the story of one week in the life of a grand old New Orleans hotel where the process of changing a guest’s room or determining what went wrong in the kitchen is as interesting to read about as blackmail, theft, and segregation.

reviews.text: Corman’s Poe cycle kickstarter is an economical and atmospheric visual feast—decorated with beautiful sets, matte paintings, and gothadelic sequences to die for... plus the murderous house in this gives off major ‘ding dong you’re dead!’ vibes to any visitor stupid enough to enter. Starting off the fall season by revisiting these movies has been an excellent decision... House of Usher is an atmos heavy winner if you ask me... complete with yet another untouchable Price performance—that blonde hair!!

reviews.text: What we know as Life is but the Larval stage of the Great Conqueror Worm. What we understand as health is but the prelude to illness. What we see as sanity is but the first symptoms of madness. There is a Vast Edifice of Negation, a Mansion with Many Rooms which descends ever deeper into the earth, farther down than even the earth can go. The vapors which weep up from the vents is but the faint stirring breath of Liberation. Strange notes bent from Unknown Instruments beckon us to hush and lean in towards the Abyss, closer, ever closer. Life is a nervous affliction for which we now possess a cure, unpalatable though it may seem to the uninitiated,…

reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: True gothic magic, anchored by Mark Damon's determinedly bland, clueless horror white guy hero Philip Winthrop, and his physical and emotional opposite, bleach-haired Vincent Price as Roderick Usher, glorying in his own noisy, performative fragility. It's wonderful to watch the two play off one another: dark and solid against pale and angular; fierce combativeness against resigned submission; bursting life against waiting death.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: Such a blast of decadence. One can complain of House of Usher dramatic limitations, the young couple is certainly weak and generic, but that misses the film central point. Price is here a mix of master of cerimonies and subject matter, the film is about aristrocacy rotten on the inside, so it presents itself as a solo performance all about Price's relationship to the decor. On those terms, it is a complete success.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: The first of what would become many more colorful, cinemascope post-Hammer old-school horror retelling collaborations between legendarily swagged out screen creep Vincent Prince, economical B-movie maestro Roger Corman and the Gothic tales of Edger Allen Poe (which I assume were either cheap or public domain) and their bleak, tortured, very evocative visions of the architecture of death. In this case, a poisonous aristocratic family legacy of violence and sin (personified in Price's blonde, vampiric patriarch) that has fatalistically manifested itself in the tangible, decaying production design of the gothic mansion itself. Crumbling stone foundations/dungeons, creaking dusty wooden furniture, vengeful fireplaces and chandeliers; all drenched in a thick layer of fog and cobwebs that make the entire environment of the film…

reviews.text: Feels less like a film and more like a sociological examination of male relationships - the relationships men have with women, the relationships men have with each other, and the relationships that men have with themself. These men are fundamentally unable to sincerely communicate grief to each other, unable to sincerely communicate their guilt and sadness, they can barely understand the world around them - not even their wives and families - because of how deeply they understand each other. They’ve created their own language of communicating with each other - through joking, through drinking, through aggression - but rarely if ever through genuine expression.

reviews.text: Don’t be fooled by the title. While it’s true that “I Am Heath Ledger” is peppered with home video footage shot by its dearly departed namesake, this somewhat hagiographic documentary isn’t a first-person account, it’s not a direct address from beyond the grave. Brought to you by the same guy who has previously claimed to be Chris Farley, Bruce Lee, and a handful of other Hollywood legends who died at the height of their fame, director Derik Murray is no more Heath Ledger than he was any of those other iconoclasts, but — nauseatingly presumptuous title aside — the newest installment of his non-fiction franchise is a tender, worthwhile remembrance for an irrepressible star whose light continues to shine upon the people he left behind.

reviews.author: Rida
reviews.text: I Vitelloni is quiet, assured, and bursting with atmosphere. The characters are careless jerks, sure, but you can’t help but like them anyway. The existential ennui they face is all too familiar. I Vitelloni captures the bittersweet aimlessness of fast-fading youth in a way that makes it seem both nostalgic and frightening. To be stuck in limbo like that for an indefinite amount of time in such a small town, regardless of how sweet and sleepy it is... it’s hard to imagine a more unfulfilling existence.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: "We talked a lot about leaving".The best among Fellini's expressions of small-town sentimentality. Probably because the mix of family relationships, male bonding and dead-end desperation combine to put it all under a harsher context. Also, a wonderful cast doing stronger character-based work than most of his filmography allows. It is the most conventional among his pantheon movies and likely the best.

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: I Vitelloni presents a form of realism that has a slight tinge of unreality. It feels dreamy at times, due to the soft music and striking shots. The film deals with a bunch of young men dealing with the monotony of life amidst non-ideal circumstances. Yet their small-time world allows them to have selfish desires and little respect for others. One womanising man spends his life wanting to run away from his troubles and his child. He only brings tragedy upon himself. I Vitelloni is a fascinating depiction of such men and their social condition. The ending is perhaps too forgiving and too full of undeserved hope, but nonetheless I Vitelloni is a beautifully simple effort.

reviews.author: Barmilliv
reviews.text: O título do filme já dá uma pista sobre o tema: “vitelloni” é uma expressão italiana usada para descrever homens jovens, já adultos, que vivem como adolescentes. Eles não trabalham, vivem às custas da família, passam o tempo à toa e evitam qualquer tipo de responsabilidade. Os cinco protagonistas, Fausto, Moraldo, Leopoldo, Alberto e Riccardo, parecem presos num ciclo sem fim, cheios de planos que nunca se realizam. Cada um deles representa um tipo de pessoa diferente, mas nenhum é tratado de forma superficial. De forma geral, o filme mostra a realidade de uma geração que cresceu durante ou logo após a guerra, e que chegou à vida adulta sem direção, sem ânimo para construir um futuro e sem vontade…

reviews.author: Edgar Cochran ✝️🍋
reviews.text: I Vitelloni is one of the most joyous and provocative celebrations of the most relevant event of our very lives: life itself. Federico Fellini begins his influential and unparalleled filmography with definitely one of his most multi-talented and elaborate masterpieces. It may have been a good technique for Fellini to resort to an autobiographical portrait rather than a completely original story precisely because he always stated that he wanted cinematic audiences to see life like his eyes did. With I Vitelloni, Fellini goes nostalgic, and in the process established most of the important bases that would determine the characteristics that latter films of the same genre had, not to mention it was an extremely obvious and strong influence for Martin…

reviews.text: A refreshing light hearted drama, soulfully uplifted by Koreeda’s sensibilities and typical humanistic elements. He has the knack of converting even the mundane moments of daily life into something exhilarating. The overly charming performances of the kids makes it all the more heartening. Their world, innocence, dreams and journey get beautifully captured. Adding more warmth is the cinematography and musical score. Especially, the guitar band portions were lovable n mellow. The optimistic montage sequence towards the end simply moves you. It’s a movie with a big heart and rich human emotions. Highly recommended.

reviews.author: Vince The Cinephile
reviews.text: Japanese master Hirokazu Koreeda is one of the gentlest directors in world cinema, whose films have always that simplistic, tender quality in them but the emotional power that it produce is overwhelmingly powerful. More so, what I love about Koreeda’s films is that they never resort into sentimentality. His films are not always perfect in terms of narrative structure, but the tone is always balanced. I Wish is a kids’ story basically. And it was pure joy to have found this film. It follows two brothers separated by their parents’ separation and how they cope in that separation. This lead to them and their group of friends to begin a journey in hopes of 'change' in their lives.

A comedy about the so-called 'ugly Americans' on a coach tour through Europe, with sly digs at their ignorance, seemed like shooting fish in a barrel to me, an easy & cliched target. But I saw the cast list, including a very young Ian McShane & cameos by the likes of John Cassavetes & Ben Gazzara (blink & you'll miss 'em), so I braved it.

reviews.author: James Patrick
reviews.text: An episodic tale of American tourists traveling through Europe. Starts slowly as the film establishes too many characters made up of cliche and caricature. Small touches carried the film forward, a cameo or two, an inspired bit of dialogue, and at some stop along the way, these characters became more richly crafted and the central romance becomes, dare I say it, something in a minor key of lovely. Ian McShane and Suzanne Pleshette make an unlikely pair, but they develop a bit of chemistry that stirs emotion. McShane in particular becomes a true focal point for the film as a tour guide for the insufferables. He’s pure charisma and when the picture intermittently enters a sloggy bit he’s the everpresent…

reviews.author: The Great Owl
reviews.text: In the 19th century, a professor, played by Maurice Chevalier (Gigi), unwittingly finds a bottle containing a note from an esteemed ship captain who is believed to have perished at sea. Along with the captain's two children, played by Hayley Mills (The Parent Trap) and Keith Hamshere (Play It Cool), he enlists in the help of a wealthy shipping tycoon, played by Wilfrid Hyde-White (My Fair Lady), and the tycoon's young son, played by Michael Anderson Jr (The Sons of Katie Elder), for a search expedition along the 37th parallel. The only obstacles that stand in the way of this enthusiastic party are earthquakes, giant condors, floods, jaguars, alligators, lightning storms, waterspouts, nefarious gunrunners, cannibals, and a volcano.

reviews.author: NotASexyVamp
reviews.text: The first half is really entertaining. Silly fantasy ideas mixed with a great quest narrative, a really strong cast (including an elderly but twinkly Maurice Chevalier and Hayley Mills, charming as ever) and some incredible visuals. Middle sequence featuring a huge tree getting flooded which the cast then have to make their home feels very Life Of Pi, a mythic, gorgeous series of images. Also features the film's best song, Chevalier's 'Enjoy It' where he makes the most of his French charm. Second half feels like a very different movie, venturing first to Melbourne Australia then New Zealand where they are captured by cannibalistic Maioris. Very uncomfortable and racist, kept longing for the simpler hours of the tree.

Not that it's relevant, but I used to think this was vastly superior to THE DEPARTED, now I think they're just different very good movies.

Flashes of yearning for a life lived honestly and openly, cut back with fury by the structures they're bound inside. The cop-as-gangster lost in chaos and violence, adrift for years, desperate for a genuine relationship, someone who truly knows him. The gangster-as-cop rising through the ranks, witnessing the fallout of his true employer's actions, enticed by the straight life in which he's camouflaged, desperate for a way out of his secret obligation. The dizzying dance between these men accelerating the stakes…

reviews.text: Inspector Clouseau is a weird one since it does not involve either Blake Edwards or Peter Sellers. However, the Mirisch Company decided to go ahead and produce the film anyway. Looking back in hindsight, perhaps they shouldn't have. Alan Arkin is cast to play the role of Jacques Clouseau, and I really did not like his performance. It feels like a flanderization of Clouseau, and Arkin comes off as annoying. He does not have the restraint that Sellers has. I generally like Alan Arkin, who plays Clouseau here, but he was not the right choice. He does better as a neurotic like in The In-Laws or Gross Point Blank. There are some funny bits, and this surely could have been better, but overall it doesn't hold together very well. A big part of this is that Peter Sellers does frustration so over-the-top and arrogance so well that it makes it funnier, while Arkin tends to play it not as big. An interesting watch anyway.

reviews.text: Fellini's love letter to the art of filmmaking. Presented through the lens of a mockumentary, and made for fans of the craft, his work, and no one else. Intervista is the perfect way to cap off the Criterion box set (there is technically one more disc, but it's not actually directed by Fellini, so I'll save it for later). This "finale" if you will, allows us to revel in the nostalgia of everything that we were treated to beforehand, and gives us a glimpse behind the scenes of what makes his films tick.

reviews.author: Gvolpe
reviews.text: Intervista is an amazing film. Or should I say...Ode to Fellini is an amazing film. It takes the shape of a fake documentary, in which Fellini looks at, and pokes fun at, his entire career. In the end it is an homage, not to himself, as other reviewers have suggested, but to film itself. Praise for a medium which never ceases to amaze viewers and film makers alike with it's capacity to project and create our dreams.

reviews.author: Zoë 🐛
reviews.text: Fellini's very sweet love letter to cinema, essentially the polar opposite of his hate mail to television in Ginger and Fred. I was reminded a lot of Varda's own cinephile film One Hundred and One Nights: both grapple with the landscape of film in the late 80s and mid 90s and how the famous actors and directors of the 50s and 60s fit into the post-television world.

reviews.author: threepenny
reviews.text: If Amarcord is the reminiscences of a man at the prime of his life looking back on his childhood, then Intervista is the nostalgia of an elder man looking back on his prime. "There is no difference between my life and my movies. My life is my movies." And so, we pull back the curtain and see how Fellini spent these years, day after day, at his grand studio space in Cinecitta.

reviews.author: BrandonHabes
reviews.text: Fellini loved making films, and it certainly shows here. Half memoir, half mockumentary, we're given backstage passes to the swirling circus that comprised his sets throughout the years. It's the usual dream-like, Felliniesque fare that wanders through a kaleidoscope of mostly uninspired moments, though there was one segment that really tugged at my heart.

reviews.author: williamfaeleith
reviews.text: If '8 and a Half' is Fellini making a film about making a film, then 'Intervista' is Fellini making a film about Fellini (played by Fellini) making a film about Fellini (played by Sergio Rubini) as a young reporter making his first visit to Cinecittà Studios in Rome to interview a revered actress. He also seems to be making a film based on Kafka's 'Amerika', and also being filmed for a Japanese TV documentary.Along the way he bumps into Marcello Mastroianni (making a TV commercial at Cinecittà) and takes him to meet a reclusive Anita Ekberg, where they (somewhat magically) reminisce about making the film 'La Dolce Vita'.It struck me more as an homage to Cinecittà Studios than a self-indulgent exercise by the maestro.

reviews.text: It takes a special kind of egotist to equate the twilight of Italian cinema with his own, but Fellini finds a fascinating throughline between both. The amount of sketches of films flowing into each other is impressive. Mastroianni and Ekberg watching the Trevi fountain scene might be the easiest sentimental moment in Fellini's career but it still works.

reviews.author: Mrtnspckr

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: In an alternate universe, the soundtrack to this is a turning point in Mick Jagger's career. He split with the Stones, dropped the blues-appropriation, killed his pop influences, and went down a drug-addled (because it's only a little different) road into the avant garde. In such a reality, he was probably banned from Italy. In this reality, this is just a blip on his radar, a hippie-fueled exploration of Kenneth Anger's homoerotic mysticism that complements Lucifer Rising as almost a behind-the-scenes thing, but not quite. It'd count as a horror film, but in fairness, I think it rude to call Anton LaVey's Satanism "horror."

The opening shot, a long digital zoom from high over Hong Kong down to a CGI-scrubbed period street as Ip arrives in town, a refugee from the Civil War, and asks for directions to what will be his first residence/school, hints at Yau's approach throughout the film. 15 years or so of post-war Hong Kong is chronicled: vicious labor wars, the corruption of the police force, a vast influx of immigrants, dire poverty, gang wars, economic recovery…

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: Herman Yau’s film about the last two decades of Ip Man’s life plays like a corrective to the bombast on the recent crop of Ip Man movies much like his previous Woman Knight of Mirror Lake tried to rescue Chinese historical film from its usual bloat. It is a very episodic film less interest in build a narrative (outside of a contrived climatic fight that justifies the regrettable title) than in just let Ip’s life breathe in the middle of post war Hong Kong’s social fabric. In Yau and Anthony Wong’s hands, he feels less like a folk hero than a stern but well-meaning dad (which probably makes sense in a biography of someone better known for being a teacher).…

reviews.author: Justin Decloux
reviews.text: More interested in the elegiac winding down of a Hong Kong on the brink of change than being a martial arts film. The fights are fun and performed by non-martial artists like Anthony Wong and Eric Tsang, but they're often cut short because they serve no purpose beyond setting a mood. I don't think the rambling narrative quite works as well as it should, with Ip Man's mistress glossed over so it can't be perceived as a moral failing, but it's nice to have a movie about older heroes whose lives reach their end without a big dramatic sacrifice.

reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"
reviews.text: "Iron Warrior" is a 1987 Italian Sword and Sorcery film directed by Alfonso Brescia, "Al Bradley" as the film presents his name in Americanized form. I won't lie that the film is not conventionally up to par with grandiose Hollywood productions that most generally know off the top of their head, but anyone wandering their way into 80's Italian exploitation knows the merger of a slightly schlocky nature but caught up in a self-serious temperament in tone. This is exactly the film you're going to get, a wonderous piggybacking of other sword and sorcery films that owned some genre prevalence in the decade.

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: This is apparently the third part in the Ator series. I haven't seen the first two, but it seems to stand alone anyway. Iron Warrior is basically a cheapo adventure yarn in the vein of Clash of the Titans et al. Director Alfonso Brescia tries to up the ante by lending the film a surrealist vibe that runs throughout, teetering on the edge of feeling like a music video. What lead actor Miles O'Keeffe lacks in charisma is more than made up for in muscle, and he gets put to…

This historical action/adventure film focuses on the siege of Rochester Castle by that scoundrel King John after he reneges on the virtues laid down in the Magna Carta. Paul Giamatti pops up to play Richard the Lionheart's brother with a quest for vengeance against anyone questioning his reign, but in truth he takes a back seat to the heroics of James Purefoy's Templar Knight Thomas Marshall. reviews.author: Wesley R. Ball
reviews.text: What stands out most to me about James White, a staggering achievement for a freshman feature, is the absence of a soundtrack. The lack of a score allows for the intense camerawork and consistent closeups of the titular character convey all the emotion it needs. Christopher Abbott gives a marvelous performance, overflowing with a poignant, human touch that radiates in his relationships. It's rare to find a drama that packs such emotional love and artistry into such a short runtime. Films like James White are few and far between- it doesn't waste time trying to utilize melodrama to convey artificial sentiments, strictly focusing on its players' emotions and their incredibly tangible development over time. It is a supremely human tour de force that gives legitimate meaning to the phrase "art imitating life."

Jane was previously separated from her love during the American Civil War, and flung into whoredom until she was able to help herself out of it. Years later there comes a thicket of embattled acrimony between various men caught in a triangle with Jane. I've seen westerns before that use flashbacks to color in some history, but I've rarely seen one so dependent and encumbered…

reviews.author: Burrows
reviews.text: JANE GOT A GUN had a troubled pre-production, apparently. In some ways, reading the Wikipeda page was on par in entertainment value with the film itself. Portman apparently had signed on to this relatively early, and Edgerton shortly after. At the time, Lynne Ramsay was supposed to direct. At the outset, Edgerton was cast as the baddie. However, by the time it went to production years later, Edgerton was recast as the good guy and had done his own rewrite of the script. Jude Law, Michael Fassbender, Rodrgio Santoro, and Bradley Cooper had all come and gone from the cast by the time Ewan McGregor finally signed on playing the baddie. Ramsay left, and Gavin Cooper got the gig. SE7EN…

reviews.author: willmoviefan97
reviews.text: Considering all the drama, and disaster this film met with during production, plus when you add in the January death slate, the final product is arguably a lot better than expected. It contains impressive production designs, it perfectly captures the feel and tone of its era, and fine performances from the three leads, Joel Edgerton in particular. However, I found a large portion of it all to also be quite uneventful, and frankly kind of tedious. There are countless of flashback sequences, that after a while start to become repetitive, and unnecessary, taking away from a lot of the suspense occurring in the present day. These sequences could work a lot more if I felt more drawn to these characters than I did, and by the time the well done finale rolls around, I felt largely unimpacted by it all.

reviews.author: Matt!
reviews.text: “What do you think?”“I think we’re dead meat.”Shoutout James A. Janisse 😘 We now return to our regularly scheduled programming. Part V doesn’t exist anymore, forget about it. Jason’s dead. Oh wait. Now he’s not. Lightning crashes. Maggot-covered eyes shoot open. A hulking figure rises from an unearthed grave. A man’s heart is punched out through his chest. A legend is reborn. Nightmares are refueled. A franchise is resurrected. This has always been my favorite film of the series. The best thing anyone ever did with Jason wasn’t making him supernaturally invincible, it was making him fun. Yeah, he’s still crushing skulls, twisting heads, and folding bodies in half, but he’s also slowly stalking people outside…

reviews.author: mumblecorgi
reviews.text: Tamra Davis' documentary about the dazzling artist Jean-Michel Basquiat provides a solid overview of his all-too-brief life. Using footage Davis shot of an interview with Basquiat in 1986, two years before his death, as the anchor of the project, the film straddles the line between hagiography and criticism, somber and celebratory. Charting his unforeseen ascent into the high art world through unusual street graffiti created under the moniker SAMO©, Basquiat, a runaway, goes from homeless to storing wads of cash in his first edition of William S. Burroughs' novel The Ticket that Exploded. Through talking head interviews with friends (Fab 5 Freddy), associates, high art world darlings (Julian Schnabel), art dealers, and critics, a complex portrait of a mercurial, prodigal…

It exhibits Clouzot’s usual misanthropic attitude in the poisonous relationship of the central couple. Maurice (Bernard Blier) is your typical noir loser: a plump, balding piano player married to a sexy singer (Suzy Delair). He is neurotic and suspicious. She is a flirt who is not above using sex to further her career, and it drives him crazy. The irony is that she loves him dearly, but his neurosis blinds him to the obvious and it almost destroys the both of them. The optimistic finale helps make…

reviews.text: With the highly controversial Le Corbeau earning him a 2-year ban on filmmaking in France, Henri-Georges Clouzot made good use of his time off, returning to the limelight with a tight little police procedural in Quai des Orfèvres (French for "Goldsmith's Quay," a title so awkward-sounding that it didn't even get an English translation, in spite of the fact that it probably leaves non-French-speaking monolinguals with aneurisms). The ban, a result of Clouzot's (and his film's) association with the German-controlled production company Continental Films, was evidently not carried out by the will of the people (several of his contemporaries successfully lobbied against the initial insane sentencing of lifetime excommunication from film production), and as a result, Quai des Orfèvres surprisingly…

reviews.author: davidehrlich
reviews.text: If nothing else, Jimi: All Is By My Side is convincing proof that the world would be better if every biopic were made without the endorsement of its subjects or their estates. Denied the rights to Jimi Hendrix’s songs and recordings, 12 Years A Slave/Undercover Brother screenwriter John Ridley had no choice but to limit his approach to the iconic musician. Rather than making a traditional biopic—tracing Hendrix’s life from his Seattle childhood to his sudden death in London at age 27 (finishing with a title card before the end credits about how his picture is on the dorm wall of every college R.A. in America)—Ridley was legally compelled to try a different tack. The linear slipstream of a film…

reviews.author: Andy Summers 🤠
reviews.text: If there's one thing that this unofficial biopic has going for it then it's the lead performance by Andre Benjamin as Jimi Hendrix. His chameleon-like portrayal of the legendary Seattle-born guitarist is impressive, but the lack of Hendrix music in the film makes most of it thoroughly pointless. We knew he arrived in England looking for his big break, we knew he was the greatest guitarist and showman the sixties ever saw, and we knew he had a complicated private life, but most of what is dished up in John Ridley's biopic has been dismissed as bollocks by the surviving participants. The supporting cast also lacked the authenticity that Benjamin brought to his role. The actors playing Paul McCartney, George…

reviews.author: anna nomaly
reviews.text: This is an entertaining western, with typically compelling work from Eastwood and Duvall, but apart from the climactic train sequence, John Sturges' workmanlike direction and Elmore Leonard's hangout sensibility feel like artists chiefly interested in resting on their laurels than in mining any new visual or intellectual territory. Although there are no real heroes in Joe Kidd, a more stimulating film may have resulted if Duvall's villainous landowner wasn't so often equated with John Saxon's beleaguered revolutionary (the casting of Saxon in this particular role is its own uncomfortable can of worms). Taking everything into account through a modern lens, it's fairly easy to pick a side; I don't need the filmmakers to agree with me, but I wish those involved had been willing to dig a little deeper into their story's politics.

reviews.author: Dan Abel
reviews.text: Louis Chama and his band of Mexicans arrive at the American courthouse with a gripe. The land of their ancestors had their claims denied and were told that all of the records burned in a fire. Justifiably angry with the Americans who coned them, they decide that violence is the only answer. When a wealthy American land owner finds himself on their bad side he hires the former bounty hunter Joe Kidd and his own band of killers to track down Chama and quell the threat. Kidd has no qualms with either side but he is forced to work. A conflicted man with a shady past is tasked with making things right as best he sees fit.

Naturally as a fly on the wall, Eastwood's character of Joe Kidd is caught up in the…

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: Clint Eastwood, John Sturges, Robert Duvall, John Saxon (sporting a huge 'tasche) and Elmore Leonard combine...for a rather disappointing western. The plot revolves around some land dispute between Saxons Mexican revolutionary and Duvall's wealthy landowner. Eastwood's drifter finds himself in the middle. The film is very short at about 83 minutes but somehow it manages to feel very long, mainly because there's no real urgency to the plot. There's plenty of gunfights and fistfights but memorable scenes are few and far between (the jug rope scene being the best of them). Eastwood's character is far from his best; kind of a watered down man with no name type. It all feels very small scale and lacks the expansive feel of the best westerns. The plot really isn't all that interesting and doesn't seem to have much of a point by the end. Definitely a weak spot for everyone involved!

reviews.author: Blank Check with Griffin & David
reviews.text: He’s the nicest bad guy in town. His last name is an adverb. And he’s got some pretty wacky bits! Sweetie pie comedian Josh Gondelman joins us to talk about 1984’s Johnny Dangerously, Amy Heckerling’s loving homage to 1930’s gangster pictures. Things we attempt to understand in this episode: the cultural legacy of Joe Piscopo; the actual joke that’s being told in the “Your Testicles and You” animated reel / is there one?; Marilu Henner’s insane memory thing; if the Danny DeVito bull scene is a parody of anything; why does Richie Rich have cent signs in his name if he’s so rich?; and most crucially - why is this movie so damned hard to see in 2025?!?! Real fans know that Blank Check started off as an investigative podcast. Maybe it’s time to bring that element back!

And yet, there are actors from my two most beloved '80s franchises in Back to the Future's Christopher Lloyd and Ghostbusters' Ernie Hudson playing a gym teacher and principal here. reviews.text: Lightning in a bottle. There's a lot here that shouldn't work. Ju-on: The Grudge doesn't really have a story, outside of the gradually unfolding explanation as to what happened to Kayako in order to turn her house into a gateway to Hell. The budget is barebones, which forces a number of stylistic choices and casting decisions that should have just strangled the film from birth. And for a movie in which (by my count) 15 people die, there's very little gore or call for practical/special effects. Given its origins in direct-to-video cinematic standards, this very easily could have been forgettable space filler.

reviews.text: The Grudge breaks with the haunted house tradition by having the haunting ghosts attach to people instead of bricks and mortar. The film also dispenses with the ideas of having a main character or telling a story, leaving it feeling more like a collection of loosely connected short stories rather than a coherent film. The film is very effective on a visceral level; there's plenty of stand out and memorable sequences and the ghosts themselves are something of a marvel - mainly due to the horrible noise they make! Honestly though it is the lack of plot or characters that ultimately harms this. Putting together a creepy sequence is one thing but without a reason to care about what is happening...i just didn't care all that much about what was happening.

reviews.text: Juliet of the Spirits is full of dreams and visions. It presents a dull domestic life and a cheating husband, then goes into the magical and unexplained in order to explore the landscape of the mind. However Juliet of the Spirits feels like a rather unfocused exercise in surrealism. There's some beautiful poetic images, executed with inventive colour schemes and evocative blocking, but ultimately it all becomes indulgent. As a female equivalent to 8 1/2, it really lacks. The introspective power of that film comes through consistency and diving ever deeper into a psyche. By contrast Juliet of the Spirits just presents a woman guided by voices and images without uncovering more layers to her inner turmoil. We get exoticism,…

reviews.text: Opened in the US 40 years ago this weekend. This Philippines-shot Italian ripoff of RAIDERS OF THE LOST ARK with a little ROMANCING THE STONE isn't top-shelf Antonio Margheriti, though it does have a fun performance by Christopher Connelly as Captain Yankee, a con man adventurer in 1938 Malaysia who gets roped into a dangerous pursuit of something called the "Ruby of Gloom." Explosions and Margheriti Miniatures ensue. Connelly has a nice rapport with the great Luciano Pigozzi as his grizzled sidekick Gin Fizz, and you get Lee Van Cleef popping up periodically as a shady government guy. Margheriti's '80s jungle adventures with David Warbeck are all better than JUNGLE RAIDERS, but it's OK.

Set in the days leading up to Halloween, the movie dives into what it's like being a kid dealing with school, parents, bullies, and all the awkward stuff that comes with growing up. We see these boys go through everything from silly pranks and crushes to getting into trouble and learning some lessons along the way. The whole vibe of the movie is a mix of funny and heartfelt, really capturing that nostalgic feeling of being a kid trying to figure things out.

It doesn’t end on a bittersweet note, but it’ll leave you with that feeling as you reel back the years. I’m so glad I peered through Coscarelli’s filmography to discover this one. Don’t miss this truly hidden gem.

reviews.text: Italians don't always do it better; I would in fact argue that they frequently do it worse. But the one thing they did do well was throwing money at British and American character actors who had some payments left on their in-ground pool or owed back taxes to the IRS, and the cast of them here assembled borders on the compellingly surreal: Lady Lyndon and the Six Million Dollar Man and the rotund dream doctor from Total Recall and the doomed other Hemingway sister and the hotter Charlton Heston replacement guy from the second Planet of the Apes movie and... Karen Black. Do we even have character actors anymore? Is the reason the Italian international film industry no longer exists is because without a steady stream of Anglophone character actors it simply starved to death like an underfed piranha?

The film is riveting, taut and memorable from the get go, and there is a plenty of tension throughout that makes this a well made feature. Umbopa, the African Prince disguised as a…

reviews.author: Chris Hughes
reviews.text: There have been many adaptations of H. Rider Haggard’s novel King Solomon’s Mines, some more successful than others. This version is less faithful to the source than most of the others. There isn’t a whole lot of adventure on offer in King Solomon’s Mines. Most of the film is spent trudging through the desert and jungle. Paul Robeson has first billing and he takes the lions share of screen time, mostly performing songs. As a singer he’s gripping to watch. As an actor less so. Cedric Hardwicke plays the protagonist Alan Quartermain. He’s fairly stiff in the role, struggling with the drab dialogue. Roland Young is kind of miscast but offers some serviceable comic relief. Anna Lee really stood out to me with a weirdly broad delivery and kind of manic approach. I feel like the movie isn’t sure if it wants to be a drama, a musical or an adventure story.

reviews.author: Blair Russell
reviews.text: I’m fulfilling requests here and clearing space off the DVR. Last summer I saw and reviewed the 1950 King Solomon’s Mines, which was a favorite of my late mother. It was a tale I enjoyed; long before that I saw the cheesy movie of the same name from the 80’s which I didn’t enjoy as much. More than one person brought this up as a movie to see; in addition, the film starring the great Black entertainer Paul Robeson was another draw, so when this played on TCM a few weeks ago, it was recorded. By my standards of waiting months to year to watch something I’m in possession of or recorded… I wasted nary a minute.

Rider Haggard’s classic adventure novel, with its pioneering on-location filmmaking (in Technicolor), but this earlier Gaumont British production may hold up better in the 21st century. Most of the credit for that goes to the casting of the great Paul Robeson as a dispossessed prince who uses a group of British explorers to reclaim his throne. In fact, Robeson, who was disappointed with the way his earlier film Sanders Of The River turned out, almost single-handedly transforms it into a deconstruction of the pro-Empire films being made at the time. reviews.text: There is a moment in this film where we see Rick Rubin in what looked like pink underwear. I am not one to criticize the sartorial or physical aspects of a person, but the directorial decision to leave Rubin in his pastel skivvies for a full two minutes of screen time is a masterstroke of transgressive comedy that will possibly never be outshone. The man is a haggard creature even at whatever tender young age he was in this film, and seeing him pantless and disoriented is a combination of surreal, silly, and sickening. And yet, it's not remotely the highlight of this film. The highlight of this film is obviously the soundtrack, which is one of the best ever…

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: Rivette has created a soundtrack composed almost entirely of the scratch of pen on paper, and it is one of the most lovely soundtracks I can name. The fact is, it's grating at the same time, much like the titular beautiful troublemaker. It's constant, rough, and lovely. When the characters move, when the artist switches to paintbrush, when something plays on the radio, when they talk, the sound of the scratching is missed. It is dominant in this slow, careful film, even when it isn't present at all. It's the sound of creation, of slow, careful creation, of failure and success, of meticulous and sloppy creation.

reviews.author: noen
reviews.text: I'm speechless… When I chose to watch this film, maybe I acted too hastily. I did it in an almost ironic, provocative gesture, like someone testing their own endurance, like someone deciding to climb a mountain out of sheer stubbornness, convinced that a work shouldn’t be judged by its length. Four hours of film, long static shots, a plot that, at least on the surface, is simply about the act of painting. It sounds like torture. And it is, but not in the way you’d expect.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: Giulietta Masina's performance here is perhaps one of the most touching and beautiful performances I've seen in recent memory. Her allegedly simple-minded character has an unspoken depth to her that is moving to watch. She portrays devotion, a sort of spiritual curiosity, emotional complexity, and naivete not so much through the words she speaks as the expressions on her face and the movement of her body. The way her face morphs in the wake of her master's blunt statements conveys more than all the speeches you can muster.

reviews.author: silntstrm
reviews.text: Giulietta Masina's expressive performance is truly one of a kind. With her face, big eyes, and mouth, she delivers Gelsomina in a mime-like, elastic Chaplin-esque style. La Strada tells a journey of a keenly curious, innocent girl, trapped in a world of aimless loneliness, forced to wander with an abusive man, her big potential unfortunately left unfolding. Fellini's desolate and bittersweet story of a potential showgirl, a soul too tender for the world she is in.

reviews.author: Criterion
reviews.text: With this breakthrough film, Federico Fellini launched both himself and his wife and collaborator Giulietta Masina to international stardom, breaking with the neorealism of his early career in favor of a personal, poetic vision of life as a bittersweet carnival. The infinitely expressive Masina registers both childlike wonder and heartbreaking despair as Gelsomina, loyal companion to the traveling strongman Zampanò (Anthony Quinn, in a toweringly physical performance), whose callousness and brutality gradually wear down her gentle spirit.

reviews.text: It's not exactly a hot take to draw parallels between Edward G. Robinson and James Cagney. They're both tiny, dynamic actors who were typecast as gangsters but who, in reality, could do almost anything on screen. They also both have very specific kinds of charisma, but whereas Cagney's is all about intense one-on-one engagement and an almost dangerous allure, Robinson's is somehow both broader and more room-sized and, also, softer, more intimate.

reviews.author: Jon Peters
reviews.text: Edward G. Robinson is “Pressure” Maxwell, and while LARCENY, INC. (1942) has all the hallmarks of potentially being another Warner Brothers gangster film starring the man that put the genre on the map for the studio, the film came at a time when Robinson was tiring of this stigma. Jay S. Steinberg writes in his Turner Classic Movies essay, “in the waning years of his tenure as a contract player for Warner Brothers, Edward G. Robinson found himself frequently spoofing the gangster persona that the studio had successfully exploited for a decade since his star-making bow in Little Caesar (1931). Weary of being typed as a tough guy, Robinson relished his opportunities to turn the familiar characterization on its ear.”…

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: Pretty bitterly grim fable of an anonymous poison pen writer undoing a small provincial French town at the seams by simply shining a light on some of its own shocking, hypocritical behavior. Unfortunately, due to being made during the Nazi occupation of France (and funded by a German production company) it was largely interpreted on release as a depiction of a corrupt French people rather than the dark, anti-informant allegory that it reads as decades later. Clouzot has an exceptional feel for the palpably tense, misanthropic atmosphere he generates and uses just about every visual tool he can (especially lighting and architecture) to show the poisonous and paranoid effect of becoming overly fearful, insular, and cruel in the face of a force of surveillance and threat.

reviews.author: Catherine Stebbins
reviews.text: A particularly unsparing look at humanity and our ability to turn on each other, Le Corbeau has been dirtied by history from the day it exited the womb. Made by the German funded Continental Films, Henri-Georges Clouzot was banned from making films until 1947 (lifted from its initial lifelong stamp). It was seen as Anti-French at the time it was made, it is now seen in a more Anti-Nazi light and more broadly an Anti-People light. The misanthropy is locked and loaded even though room is made for people to find each other and for the guilty to go punished.

Everyone has something to hide it seems and even those who don't are not spared from the disparaging eye…

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: Made in Occupied France, Le Corbeau is a powerful statement on trust and secrecy. It is about rumours spread by letters, a representation of informing on others and spreading lies. Some parallels to the Gestapo are obvious, though there is no such organisation in Le Corbeau, just a society always looking for accusations. Le Corbeau is a portrayal of French weakness, depicting paranoia, pettiness, and self-loathing from within a terrified society. The characters may talk of faith, but they fail to preserve family values. Instead they are accused of affairs, admit to drug-taking, and keep a whole world of dirty secrets. Le Corbeau is a look at a hypocritical, naïve society ill-suited to pressure and scrutiny, such as would happen under occupation. No wonder Le Corbeau caused controversy upon release. Still it's a daring and powerful film that pushes us to consider a mindset which the French people of the time had to grapple with.

reviews.author: Wesley R. Ball
reviews.text: Henri Georges-Clouzot's Le Corbeau is a masterwork of suspense. It toys and twists the audience's perception until we are unsure of which way is right. What Clouzot does best, however, is taking the viewer's expectations and throwing them straight out the window. The traditional tropes and narratives are tossed aside in exchange for a fresher, more intuitive process. The film presents certain evidences as fact, and then proceeds to fly in your face, taking us on an unexpected roller coaster of deception and intrigue.

reviews.author: Graham Williamson
reviews.text: Viewers looking for another older film with an eerily clairvoyant air after finishing Contagion may wish to check out Henri-Georges Clouzot's film. What's it got? It's got haunting deserted streets, packed hospitals, an atmosphere of broiling mutual suspicion and the chattering classes arbitrarily deciding this is all Corbin's fault. Granted, the plague here is a purely metaphorical one, of hate and mistrust created by some precision-targeted poison pen letters. But the picture of social breakdown feels extremely well-observed.

reviews.author: chavel
reviews.text: Lilith is the kind of movie that can lead you to believe that Warren Beatty didn’t have talent until he made “Bonnie & Clyde” (1967). Interesting premise is obliterated in no time: Beatty is an occupational trainee therapist with an individual emptiness. Unbelievably, he had to be talked into taking the job. (Really, is it true there was a time in history you could go to a job interview with reluctance... and still land the position?) He actually tells his bosses that he is attracted to their patient Lilith (Jean Seberg) who is schizophrenic and sexually non-selective. And yet they let Beatty continue in giving her overabundant care, with field trip privileges, all the while he appears to neglect the other institution patients. Guess what? This is a packaged love story. At the film’s disposal is splendid black & white cinematography but it cannot make up for story phoniness and the drone in Beatty’s pitch in delivering dialogue.

It's a film with a very large scale, balancing the more dramatic war elements against large battle scenes, but in the middle of it all, it captures a deeply human portrait of resistance. At the center of this story is Omar Mukhtar, who is played wonderfully by Anthony Quinn, and it's such a complex performance, one which doesn't give the man a bigger-than-life reputation but instead portrays a more human and resilient man who inspires those around him for peace.

They conditionally carry themselves in different ways, with O'Neal's character of Ferris Whitney being more from the refined lavish life and McNichol's character of Angel Bright rough around the edges. The beginning of the film even sets the two in opposition, fighting on the bus right from the get-go as it leaves for camp.
