reviews.text: Surrogate father/son bond between a man who roams China on a motorcycle, searching for his missing son who was trafficked 17 years ago, and a young motorcycle repairman he runs into who was trafficked himself as a child. It's a really nicely depicted relationship between the two leads, and shows a lot of the beauty of China, as well as the many conflicting feelings that missing people and their families have about that broken bond between parent and child. There's also a glimpse of a reality I'm unfamiliar with. It would be interesting to learn more about how prevalent child trafficking is in China, and how these networks of volunteers who hunt for missing children work.

reviews.text: This film couldn't decide what it wanted to be. A father searching for his abducted child gets to know a child who was abducted who wants to find his real parents - this becomes part road movie, part buddy movie, part social commentary, interspersed with spectacular landscapes, soaring violins and maudlin reaching. It tries to be so many things that it ends up off pace, and if it is effective at times in examining the feelings of both the children and their parents, it does so at the expense of a more thoughtful look at the causes of abduction or the society that enables it.

They go searching together and builds sort of an substitute parent/son relationship on their journey. Heartbreaking for sure, but the film wastes a lot of time to get to the core of emotions. Shi gu (2015) is still a movie I have no regrets of seeing. It's a rewarding story even if this one doesn't reach it's peak the way it should have.

reviews.author: BrandonHabes
reviews.text: A compendium of film essays developed by Cesare Zavattini, the theoretical wizard of Italian neorealism, and directed by five of Italy's most prominent filmmakers (Antonioni, Fellini, Lizzani, Risi, and Lattuada). I love the historical significance at play. The film reaches back to Vertov's Kino-Pravda newsreels from the 1920s, where fragments of actuality were captured cinematically to reveal the pedestrian realities of everyday life. It also reaches forward to set the foundation for cinéma vérité during the next decade, inspiring one of my favorite films of the era: Jean Rouch and Edgar Morin's CHRONICLE OF A SUMMER (1961).

reviews.author: teamgal
reviews.text: Hit-or-miss-ness is, of course, the burden of all anthology films and LOVE IN THE CITY is no exception. Authored by six directors this presents itself as a magazine on the titular topic, but the shorts hardly provide any insights on love. Instead they're interesting for the ways in which they adhere to, or depart from, neorealist tenets. When they do engage with the depiction of reality — as in the Lizzani, the Risi and the Maselli segments — there are moments when the veil of fiction seems to tear, ever so slightly, letting something profoundly "real" transpire on screen, whether its a streetwalker reporting that she goes through 20 pairs of shoes a year, or a mother abandoning her child…

Don’t get me wrong, I love levity and this film has it in spades, but it simultaneously deeply understands the purpose levity serves in our lives. If I’m truly connecting with Cassavetes…

reviews.author: Carlos Valladares
reviews.text: When Vincente Minnelli makes a movie about art, I sit up and listen. Playing Vincent Van Gogh, Kirk Douglas's anguish-pain-hysteria swirlingly evokes the brooding, pent-up rage of the Abstract Expressionists, the lonely avant-gardists, the romantics, the hubris-filled artists armed with such noble, radical insight into humanity and nature that their society shuns them, so overwhelming are the sun-like rays they emit. Theirs is a lonely and solemn path. They take on the tortures of emotion and make it more vivid, more lifelike than life, through art. A film of magnetic intensity, a film that transforms the way you look at a tree or a person in a purple sea. And yet, easy romanticizing of the artist's hermit-like destiny is avoided. As is the case with Minnelli's works, ambivalence creeps up behind every silver lining. Those final words of Van Gogh's will haunt my dreams. I'm still tearing up.

reviews.text: Metrocolor's cheaper results don't push this to the same heights that Technicolor could have, but Minnelli pushes the process to its limit as he builds his film from establishing shots that contradictorily communicate suffocation through distance to the more intimate ecstasy unleashed when Van Gogh finds his true calling. Kirk Douglas seems such a mismatch for the artist, his cut physique not particularly suited for a troubled weakling whose violent temper exploded from a body only fit enough to hurt itself. But Douglas does not so much play against type as channel that type into a new outlet, and by God I ended up completely invested in his performance. So much of the movie is fades from "reality" into photographs…

reviews.author: Sam Van Hallgren
reviews.text: Taking his cue from Van Gogh's boldly painted canvases, Minnelli's biopic has a vivid emotional power that more than compensates for the by the numbers biopic storytelling. Once you get calibrated to its emotional pitch, the film - along with Douglas's extraordinary performance and Miklos Rozsa's potent and emotional score - packs an operatic wallop.

This was inspiring and entertaining, and so absolutely warranted for a masterpiece like Taxi Driver.

reviews.text: Manon by Henri-Georges Clouzot is, to put it simply, an insane film. Set in the post-war period, it follows a French resistance fighter who gets tangled up with a woman who had gotten a little too friendly with the occupying Nazis. The film is full of the director's usual pet themes, namely sexual power dynamics. Clouzot and Hitchcock have been compared ad nauseum over the past few decades, but for my money the Frenchman has the advantage when it comes to psychosexual drama.

reviews.author: ZubinShy
reviews.text: “Manon” is a genre shapeshifter of the special kind. It’s an adaptation of a 1731 novel whose story Clouzot transferred to post-war France and thus created a peculiar mixture of melodrama, film noir, tragedy and fantasy. It tells the story of the doomed love between two wildly different individuals that are fatalistically drawn to each other. Clouzot is often dubbed “the French Alfred Hitchcock” due to his suspense films from the 50s (namely The Wages of Fear and Diabolique), but I think with “Manon”, this was the closest he ever got to make a Hitchcock film, for no other reason than the melodrama. But in the end, it turns into a true Clouzot film: bleak and horrifying.

reviews.author: Kerry Maxwell
reviews.text: An interminable death march, operatic melodrama shoehorned into bleak cynical noir, replete with a massacre of Jewish refugees. I was familiar with the plot from the several operas based on the Prévost novel, so there were no surprises in the overall story arc, just bafflement at Clouzot's choices in blunt object symbolism. Entirely unsympathetic leads, combined with Clouzot's standard misogyny, made this entirely unpleasant for us, but seeing the dead body of a nazi collaborator dragged across the desert was apparently a big hit with audiences at the time.

reviews.author: La Boscaiola
reviews.text: This was my second Clouzot after "Le Corbeau", and once again I was struck by his deeply pessimistic view of humanity. I appreciate that fundamental distrust, his refusal to cast heroes and instead exposing everyone’s weaknesses. Yet some of the film’s moral valuations no longer align with my own: Robert’s possessiveness and the poetic attribution of guilt to Manon for her brother’s murder seem far more troubling to me than her turn to sex work. For Manon, a life without material comfort is simply unthinkable, and sex work appears as an economic necessity rather than a moral failing. I was reminded here of Fassbinder’s "The Marriage of Maria Braun", with its protagonist whose subversive notions of sex and love also…

reviews.author: Jesse Mitchell
reviews.text: Manon is a strange movie about an insane love story, but Clouzot's stylish direction is apparent throughout and the film is oddly captivating. The film has war, crime, Parisian brothels, murder, and a march through the Palestinian desert; while none of these elements are particularly well integrated tonally, some of the sequences are masterful, including the unforgettable desert scene at the end of the film.

reviews.author: Willow Maclay
reviews.text: Romero's saddest film? Depressive in the way most of the best Vampire stories are, but by placing Martin's vampiric struggles in the real world and outside of cinematic lore Romero humanized the character. Martin is a pervasive creep in the way vampires should be, but he's also unlike most characters of his type. He's a victim of circumstances, eternally stilted and ultimately made tragic by family. Romero took the apocalyptic locales of a decaying Pittsuburgh and applied them marvelously to Martin. Everything in this movie is slowly dying and only trudging along until finally death seeps in from all sides in blood splattered horrorific finale, but it isn't beautiful, and it doesn't end with a bang, but a slight tremble. A death knell.

All those narrow halls, blue carpeting, cork wallpaper and fold-out closet doors with the wooden slats on them. We have those exact closets here and I love them. Anyway. reviews.text: First off this should not ever be referred to as 'Attack of the Mushroom People' anymore, it creates expectations of a straightforward "monsters attack" (let alone kaiju) movie, which this is not. This I'd argue is far more interesting if you go in willing to be surprised. Body horror, cabin fever, social commentary (though that isn't new for Honda), it's got a bit of everything and there's an eerie, brooding vibe throughout the entire thing that would've been wasted on a less patient movie. Matango shows you the mold of human nature, knowing there's no way to fight conformity.

reviews.text: There can’t be that many movie directors who brought as much pure joy and entertainment to so many viewers as legendary Japanese monster maestro Ishiro Honda. But as much as I love and admire all his incredible giant Kaiju bashes and his imaginative sci-fi space operas, there is one film of his that will forever hold a very special place in my heart. I’m talking of course about his masterpiece of mycotic surrealism, his slice of outrageous mushroom madness, his hallucinogenic fungal mind-fuck, his psychedelic Pop-Art fairytale, the unbelievable, the unforgettable, the one-and-only Matango. This movie could not look any better if Mario Bava, Terence Fisher and David Cronenberg took a trip to Japan to direct a feature length Twilight…

reviews.text: For how good John Wayne has been in countless Westerns and in comedies like The Quiet Man and Hatari!, McLintock! is a combination of those two genres that doesn't really succeed. As a Western, its plot is largely an afterthought that doesn't have much in the way of momentum or action, and it really only serves as a setting for its slapstick comedy gags. That's a shame when the humour here is neither very funny nor even particularly charming in my opinion, since its brand of comedy is rather dated (much more than those aforementioned John Wayne comedies) with lots of pratfalls and most of the bits are just centred around humiliating the two main female characters. It's just not an amusing comedy when that's all McLintock! has to offer and doesn't provide a plot or characters that distinguish it within the Duke's filmography.

reviews.author: Alice Stoehr
reviews.text: "So what do two black folks do on a Sunday afternoon?" asks Joanne of her new friend Micah. Well, if they just got acquainted through a drunken one-night stand, they might check out each other's MySpace pages, exchange a few barbed remarks, then wander San Francisco together. They might discuss gentrification or "Ice Ice Baby" or their passions—his is aquariums; hers screen-printing t-shirt tributes to female filmmakers. They could get high, go out dancing, and eat tacos. Medicine for Melancholy's scenario is finite: once the credits roll on Monday morning, these two may never see each other again. But within this one day lie unlimited possibilities. Music drifts in over the action, the action breaks up into montage, and moments stretch out like they're yawning. Shallow focus and a desaturated palette soften the actors' bodies and their sun-drenched surroundings. The film relaxes, sprawling out across the city, as it develops into a romantic snapshot of this particular place and time.

reviews.author: bileygr
reviews.text: Incredibly charming or, more to the point, quaint really. Old-fashioned and spry, and at an extreme from Manon right before it, enough to give you whiplash. Its every moment is charged with whimsy, gaiety, and romance, and these facets of Clouzot – present even elsewhere in degrees – have exclusive rights to the stage; the result is somehow even better than you’d anticipate, vaudevillian and picturesque, a lovely, if modest, romance to melt the hearts of the most lecherous marquises and sing the truth of beauty in naïveté. Elsewhere I’d find this perhaps sickly sweet, but Clouzot’s got exactly the sense of poise to land it with more effervescence than schmaltz.

reviews.author: James Keith
reviews.text: There are moments of broad comedy in this lightweight farce that feel like Clouzot is gritting his teeth through it, balanced out by other moments of wonderful mile-a-minute dialog and perfect comic timing. There's a sweet gentleness to some of the romance that feels of-a-piece with similar stuff from earlier films where Clouzot co-directed/wrote, but on the whole it's more uneven than I'd like. It's not quite hyper-specific local comedy (it's mostly generally accessible and the comedy tracks), but maybe farce is a little harder to enjoy when you're whipping your eyes back and forth between the subtitles and the image.

After this film had finished, I made my way upstairs to brush my teeth and get ready for another meaningless night of sleep, only to wake up to nothing and nobody once again. When I got to my bathroom, I immediately looked in the mirror. Something stared back at me, something I have been repulsed by for so many years now...but it looked different this time. Without even thinking about it, I smiled. In that moment, a moment so rare in my life, I was proud of who I am.Mister Lonely did this. Harmony Korine, you did this.

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: Korine approaches obsession with fame through a suitably strange lens, highlighting the concept of celebrity impersonators to capture a group of misfits whose simultaneous hero worship and appropriation manages to embody a post-postmodern crisis of culture. Arguably the first seeds of Korine's modern phase, in which his garish, lo-fi character portraits as Dorian Gray snapshot of America morphed into a more direct-facing examination of mainstream decay. As with all of Korine's work, it is ferociously empathetic, and even at its most cerebral and plotted is a work of character study so intuitive and hands-off you sometimes forget this is scripted.

reviews.author: Devan Scott
reviews.text: • Oh wow. Completely fascinating. Shockingly ambitious in like eight wildly different directions, which is simultaneously the most compelling thing about it and its greatest liability. Remember how AMERICAN GRAFFITI used the greatest soundtrack conceit in history to unify the four story strands? Well, nuts to that! Each strand takes place in an entirely different time and place from one another and is realized in an entirely different style! And not surface-level "they used different film stocks" stuff: I'm talking four entirely separate cinematic languages, at least one of which is overtly avant-garde. It's not like watching four movies, it is watching four movies!

reviews.author: Jono
reviews.text: More American Graffiti trades that warmth of the original for something far more experimental. The decision to split the narrative across four New Year’s Eves, each with its own visual style, gives the film a unique structure that mirrors the chaoticness of the decade. Steve and Laurie's drama feels flat and repetitive, but Toad's Vietnam storyline offers grounded satire and absurdity. Debbie’s dive into the hippie movement is wild and vibrant, while Milner’s drag-racing arc is the most poignant, his joyful day shadowed by a tragic inevitability. It’s far from perfect, but its ambition and refusal to be a soulless cashgrab deserves real credit.

I found this one a bit of a chore to get through its entirety as it dragged through parts, but regardless it still has plenty of quality moments. I can't say I'm a big fan, but it is a creative film in certain aspects, like the use of changing aspect ratios and the way it told entirely separate stories successfully. reviews.author: Greta T. Narrator
reviews.text: I love American Graffiti so much that I was skeptical this would be able to live up to its combination of silliness and too-much-to-bear melancholy. But it does. It even effectively complicates the original's downer ending, letting the sweet and sour aspects of each character's conclusion coexist without pushing the viewer towards one or the other. And as a bonus it's one of the more formally audacious American studio movies I've seen, like if I'm Not There was greenlit as a light nostalgic romp.

reviews.author: RAFIF
reviews.text: Mother is a landmark film in the history of cinema, directed by Vsevolod Pudovkin and based on Maxim Gorky's novel. This silent film is a powerful portrayal of the 1905 Russian Revolution, focusing on the story of a working-class woman who becomes politically awakened during a time of social unrest. Pudovkin direction in is marked by innovative editing techniques and compelling storytelling. He masterfully uses montage to create emotional impact and convey the intensity of the characters experiences. The film cinematography and visual composition are striking, capturing the harsh realities of the time.

reviews.author: V. Lepistö
reviews.text: And her soul wanders to the heaven and the flag still stands... (or stood). I'm very glad that Pudovkin doesn't approach the themes sentimentally since this kind of edge is needed in a film like these. It's no Eisenstein but it works on very different levels; dare I say that it is more poetic? Some say, how can propaganda be poetic? If there's a truth to it, it can be poetic. Ice breaks as soul releases from its prison through hope and sacrifice; the spring comes even if it means that some paths are going to melt. Not everyone can stand on firm ground, some have to find the ground first. Perhaps its ideals are too simplistically portrayed to certain people considering the history behind it but such pathos could not be possible without sensitive aesthetic cinematic sense that understands the movement of film, its vibrations and turns. For those longing for freedom...

reviews.text: The major difference between this USSR classic and Sergei Eisenstein's 1920s films is the emotion involved; it too is a fiery, brilliantly edited story of life in the midst of the 1905 Revolution, but because it zeroes in on a specific family's struggles, it manages a kind of direct, unfiltered resonance rarely seen in propaganda films. Astoundingly mounted and indelible as the imagery is, the movie lands today because of Vera Baranovskaya's aching, utterly believable performance as the mother of a revolutionary and the wife of an abusive man who gets killed in a revolt. reviews.text: Well, here’s a potboiler if there ever was one. Working-class Yankee Robert Mitchum marries Janis Carter on the rebound after he’s been manipulated into thinking genteelly impoverished Southern aristocrat Ava Gardner jilted him. In the meantime, Gardner learns that she has inherited a lot of money from the family of her black-sheep grandmother, and in order to win back — or is that get back at? — Mitchum, she decides to adopt her grandmother’s bad-girl legacy, too. She convinces her oily cousin Melvyn Douglas to seduce Carter while she tries to re-seduce Mitchum.

reviews.text: Early precursor to the Giallo with some obvious Krimi influence. Antonio Margheriti directs from a script co-written by Mario Bava. The plot focuses on an all girls school where some black gloved killer is picking off the students and staff. Despite the lurid title, Naked You Die is a rather tame affair - preferring a quaint mystery to a blood soaked murder spree. The film has a relatively high body count but the primary modus operandi is strangulation so not a lot of blood is spilt. It's a single location movie with a small cast which gives it something of a claustrophic feel with plenty of red herrings....though disappointingly it becomes obvious who the murderer is really early on given…

reviews.author: Ian Kemper
reviews.text: You want to make your eyes happy? Give them this to look at. Eye popping purples, greens, and pinks from the get go along with sumptuous set designs and a cool location give this Bava inspired giallo a leg up on most of it's pre giallo-boom contemporaries. Director, and miniature car lover, Antonio Margheriti, takes a discarded (but fully prepped) Mario Bava project and along with a camera operator that would soon be cinematographer for every Sergio Martino joint, and makes something that is a perfect bridge between the genre's beautiful but stately past and its gorier flesh-filled future.

reviews.text: In the hands of an average filmmaker, this particular story of a prostitute desperately seeking true love could be a downright sentimental mess. But this work of Italian master Federico Fellini is a testament how a great director can turn this problematic story into an unforgettable film. Nights of Cabiria relies 101% on the strength of its tiny-footed, but giant-hearted leading lady Giulietta Masina. In this, Masina embodies Cabiria in all of her glory. She’s a woman of contradictions. She knows what she wants, but not exactly sure how to get it. She’s insufferable, selfish, and sometimes self-pitying, but then she’s open, full of life, fierce, and most of all, a survivor.

reviews.author: laird
reviews.text: The original Fantomas novels by Marcel Allain and Pierre Souvestre were, according to pulp fiction legend, produced by the authors working independently of each other taking writing duties for alternating chapters. While there was some pre-formulated overarching plot and resolution, the two authors were free to tear through pages and pages of incident at a high rate without the burden of traditional structure or, frankly, cogency. reviews.author: Nick Langdon
reviews.text: One Night at McCool's is absolutely a product of that immediate post-Pulp Fiction (1994) moment in American quasi-indie cinema, when Quentin Tarantino was a literal god and Hollywood was suddenly awash in non-linear pop culture-savvy scripts about ultra-hip criminals with all the needle drops that would hit at key moments already penciled in. This movie feels like the product of one of those screenplays, just one that sat in some bottom draw for several years gathering dust, before finally being dug out and put into production. How else to explain not only the dated concept but also the very specific references to two of the hottest movies of 1993? Hardly fresh material by 2001 as even this film's defenders (if…

reviews.text: We all have those movies we vaguely remember from childhood, recalling actors or characters or moments without fully remembering the film itself. One of Our Dinosaurs Is Missing happens to be one of mine, my most vivid memory being Peter Ustinov running around the Natural History Museum... yet how exactly did I forget he plays a 'ching chong' Chinaman? Perhaps my mind blocked it out given how unbelievably dated and un-PC his performance, and much of this 70's Disney farce is. Robert Stevenson's movie, beyond harmlessly offensive, is also best described as amiably silly.

reviews.text: Edward Southmere (Derek Nimmo) escapes China with the valuable secret of "Lotus X", and is followed back to London by agents of the Chinese government. In a desperate attempt to protect the secret, he tucks it in the bones of a dinosaur and leaves the information with his former nanny Hettie (Helen Hayes). While Hettie and her crew of local nannies try to recover the Lotus X microfilm from a desiccated plant-eater, the London office of China's security force, led by Hnup Wan (Peter Ustinov) and Quon (Clive Revill) are also in pursuit. Hettie's current charges realize what all the adults could not, triggering the slapstick third act.

Along with Rio Bravo, the quintessential Hawks movie for not only its rhythmic patterns, attention to a very subtle structure in its mise-en-scene, but always carrying a certain existential weight to why the hell are we doing this? that always remains unanswered, unchecked, and unwritten. But as in all the great Hawks, there is the group, a certain social democracy that remains a base ideology that could never be challenged. It's both the tragedy and the greatness of the American ethos.

reviews.text: Without naming it (and possibly without realizing it), a lot of OPERATION MAD BALL is actually about sexual harassment. What constitutes it, what the consequences should be, whether the recipient has a say in it. I’m not sure if Jack Lemmon’s character lands on the right side of it, but it’s interesting to see in a 1957 comedy. Despite all the weird, outdated sexual dynamics, I thought it was funny. The plot is that all these soldiers are plotting to throw a party without the higher ups finding out, so it kind of reminded me of an 80s comedy, but less crass. It’s a little bit too long, but I liked it.

reviews.text: Take a dip in Kore-eda’s touch of tenderness, covered in pale pink petals and breathe in the sisterly love. I’m not crying because I’m sad, it’s because of the puff of air that blew into my eyes. The breezes of gentleness, smooth like butter and sweet like honey, carry me home and let me curl up into a soft ball. They remind me how generous life can be, even when the road gets rough. Every meal shared is a joy, every glance is a touch; how every-day contains a bittersweet revelation as tears are evenly meshed with laughter. The intricate fabric texture of the familial world is a pleasure to hold onto. Our Little Sister’s kindness is a glimmer bright in the distance, as the cherry blossom trees are blooming. You just have to close your eyes and enter the tunnel of embrace.

reviews.text: What a waste of a potentially great cast. This film gets so much wrong, it's too painful to record it all. But it starts with the title. The last time I checked the dictionary,, "paranoia" meant "an irrational suspiciousness or distrustfulness of others." Yet, this film has nothing to do with that. Every fear of main character Adam Cassidy (Liam Hemsworth) is grounded in real danger. There's no psychosis here, no irrationality, no seeing boogeymen where there are none. Some very specific people are really out to hurt him and his friends if he doesn't steal trade secrets as instructed.

reviews.text: Passion is a prime example as to why I have such a love for film. I love film so much because it's subjective. Film is like art. Art is also subjective. There could be this painting and I could think it's one of the most hideous and ugly paintings I had ever seen; then there could be someone else who thinks that same painting is stunning and beautiful. Many people think Passion is trash and a convoluted mess, while I think it's brilliant and polarizing. From the fantastic performances to the solid direction to the crisp cinematography; Passion is incredibly well made with an interesting premise that will keep you guessing from start to finish.

reviews.text: Pauline at the Beach is a trivial film, but utterly charming. Mostly it is just talks of love, all between a small group of characters. At first it is a film of kisses and dances. Then love and sex. Finally it becomes a film of deceit and confusion, bringing conflict at last. Although Pauline at the Beach is just about a few characters working out their relationships during a small holiday, it is oddly engaging. This is a film just about watching people make mistakes, especially as in the end the film find villains in its scumbag men. Pauline at the Beach may merely be a collection of amorous escapades, but it presents love as insanity and creates something moving despite the slight presentation.

But, making allowances for that, I thought this was pretty genuinely harrowing true-life melodrama, by the time our hero is sitting in his car shooting up through his neck with his infant daughter sleeping in the passenger seat the film doesn't really feel remotely like a Tropic Thunder sketch anymore. reviews.text: Things do not usually end well for teenage girls who run away from home in 1970s movies. Bonnie, played by Candice Rialson, finds this out the hard way when she escapes from her brother on the streets of Los Angeles. During the days that follow, she becomes the unwitting accomplice of a double-crossing robber, played by Teri Guzman, and she becomes the kept object of desire as a model for a female painter, played by Joan Blackman. A possible salvation presents itself in the form of Vincent, an immensely wealthy and worldly art gallery owner played by Ed Bishop, but Bonnie soon discovers that Vincent collects much more than art.

reviews.text: Although they are linked, this is essentially a trio of exploitation shorts on the subject of possessiveness. We have the stylish black lady happy to humiliate and rob the well off white man, the lesbian artist who takes in a model and the gallery owner who keeps a very special zoo in his basement. Candy Rialson is perfect in the lead as she is used by them all, even if as in Voltaire's Candide, she gets a fair bit for herself along the way. This is super sexy seventies sleaze and with dodgey pop psychology and all, a delightful treat. There is a cute central performance from Candy Rialson as Bonnie, chauvinism a plenty, a sublime theme song and spot on costumerie. Not to mention a girl in a lion's cage and a spot of whipping.

But I don't care about its contradictions or its sensationalist neutrality vis-à-vis the dichotomous male-female sexual feuds, this skeevy sexploitation schlock is just frisky enough to sweep you off your feet and make you oblivious to its controversial moral paradoxes. Inevitably you may feel a little guilty about enjoying many of the naughty debauched antics that our beloved lead character, the infantile gullible blonde-haired Bonnie, a voluptuous girl who is the subject of objectification by a slew of perverts, goes through. Yet Candice Rialson as the effortlessly cool Bonnie suggests she's more than just curves and no brains. Raphael Nussbaum's…

reviews.author: Todd Gaines
reviews.text: The Tall Man is back! So is Reggie; the greatest ice cream truck driver known to man. We can't forget Mike, but why does he look so different? It's Don Coscarelli's sequel to the cult classic, Phantasm. It takes the Aliens route; it's more action-packed, than horror. It makes no sense, but that's part of the charm. Phantasm II is a highly debated movie among fans of the series. Why was Mike recast? Should we blame Mr. Coscarelli? Is that really Reggie's hair, or is it the worst hairpiece ever?

The original movie’s unsung star - a shiny flying sphere of death - was going to get more screen time (and the tagline!). It’s quite a story before even getting to the film itself.

It was scary to me as a kid, but I also loved it and it’s one of my clearest early horror memories. Wonderful times.

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: Despite coming nine years after the original, Don Coscarelli's sequel to his original horror film follows on exactly in the same vein. The story picks up immediately where the first film left off; and then cuts to some years later. Mike has apparently spent some time in a mental hospital but now he's released and back on the tail of The Tall Man. Once again, the film forsakes logic in favour of delivering pure fantasy horror. The gaps in coherency are more than covered by just pure entertainment. The film basically doesn't stop from the first moment. It's a maelstrom of cobbled together weapons, creepy dwarves, murderous spheres, dueling chainsaws, Angus Scrimm, alternate universes, explosions and more. Phantasm 2 really goes the extra mile! Very much a worthy follow up to one of the most imaginative horrors of the seventies.

Her parents (Felicity Huffman and Bill Pullman) struggle to help their daughter, find time to work and keep a marriage together. The bright spot for Fanning is her drama teacher (Patricia Clarkson) who has picked Alice in Wonderland as the school play. reviews.text: adheres to the usual beat-by-beat approach of these kinds of films and is more concerned with its melodramatic sincerities at its core than it is with pushing the bounds beyond typical genre clichés in its emotional buildup. It all truly worked for me. To be honest, it's pretty admirable how much it works in-fact, considering how silly it is. but you’ve got these wonderfully rendered George Lucas-like digital cityscapes and a tale that habitually takes you in multiple directions before culminating in a breathtakingly dramatic both literal and symbolic eruption. a full cycle of destruction. Listen, I can for sure understand why some people don't particularly enjoy this kind of work; as I've stated in relation to another film recently, this is essentially an access point film; you're either completely in or wholeheartedly out, and I'm gladly very much within.

Revolving around country preacher out to steal both innocence and profits from a southern town, the story shuffles from dull episode to colorless adventure with almost zero potential to entertain. Any low-rent charm the production may offer is snuffed out by the narrative's creepy lead, a film-wide lack of energy, and a complete inability to capture attention. The results are wholly disposable.

reviews.author: Todd Gaines
reviews.text: A beautiful cheerleader is found murdered in a high school boys bathroom. The brutal killing shocks the community, and the Feds are called to investigate. There's only one clue; a note left at the scene of the crime. Why was this young lady murdered? Who killed her? Why is Rock Hudson sporting a 70's pornstash? Pretty Maids All in a Row is my type of movie. A taboo flick, that's genre bending at its most bending. Featuring a way too smokin' Angie Dickinson, a bald Telly Savalas, music from The Osmonds, a cool kid named Ponce de Leon, and Rock Hudson like you've never seen him before. This is one film, you must see to believe.

reviews.text: Kind of a crazy and horrifying film. It’s a mix of mystery and dark humor, which is uncomfortable throughout. Starts off like a fairly normal crime thriller but slowly turns into something much more unsettling, especially in how casually it handles some serious ideas. Rock Hudson is quietly creepy, which makes the whole movie feel off in a disturbing way. The pacing is all over the place, but that actually adds to the "what did I just watch?" feeling I had by the end. You can tell this was made by a director who’s completely sick in the head, it keeps on switching between a thriller and exploitation. There are parts where I felt like I was too high. A messy, borderline disturbing and unpredictable film, with a horndog Angie Dickinson and Rock Hudson yelling, "You are a bunch of pussies."

reviews.author: David W
reviews.text: I’m well aware of the knocks against Prince of the City. Some say the film runs overlong and mires itself in unnecessary detail. Others criticize its poor structuring and concomitant confusion over motivation and what exactly is going on. Still others charge Treat Williams (playing Danny Ciello, the film’s lead) with overdramatization at best and shitty acting at worst. And still others take the film to task for its self-seriousness. These criticisms are not without merit. On the contrary, the film provides evidence for rendering such verdicts.

reviews.author: chavel
reviews.text: Prince of the City is the not-as-thoroughly gripping as you hoped docudrama on New York City police corruption, a subject of obsession for Sidney Lumet. Treat Williams is Danny Ciello, a narcotics detective with no filter who blathers to internal affairs of past impropriety at the twenty minute mark. He was cocky enough to be unafraid that his boasting was inconsequential, but then he spends the rest of the movie paying for it. City prosecutors never get off his back, and they even try to pin the French Connection scandal on him and his closest colleagues (yes, this is information that can be seen as supplemental material to William Friedkin’s 1971 classic). Williams is induced to wear a wire for…

reviews.author: DallasFrance
reviews.text: Prince of the City somehow manages to be both a grueling and brisk watch, as legendary director Sidney Lumet chucks Treat Williams into a psycho-emotional wood chipper. “I know you’re a character actor, but can you carry this three hour c-opera for me? I’m gonna need you to careen from arrogant to terrified, level-headed to frantic, and reliable to erratic-sometimes in the space of ten seconds.” Williams is up to the task, and buoyed by a bevy of other great character actors like Bob Balaban, Jerry Orbach, and Lance Henriksen.

reviews.author: Eliecer Gaspar
reviews.text: For my cents, the best film of Sidney Lumet's ’s police corruption quartet. An experimental film if we take into account its division into chapters introduced by slideshows of identification cards and synoptic quotes. And Brechtian, as Bordwell once suggested, in the sense that every element in the film is engaged dialectically with every other element. Fordian, even: "In tracing Ford’s pictures (particularly Judge Priest, How Green Was My Valley, This Is Korea!, The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance) we have seen how people (and governments) act from feeling, not from logic. People are made of dreams as much as reality." - T. Gallagher

reviews.text: Got to see this in IMAX and it was nothing short of a party. I had a blast experiencing this electrifying concert movie where I was joined by a packed theater full of die hard Prince fans, cinephiles, and people simply looking to enjoy the work of one the greatest artists ever. It felt like a real show with the audience cheering, clapping, singing, dancing, and chanting alongside Prince and friends on the largest screen possible with a rocking sound system to match. It should go without saying that the musical numbers are fun, creative, and endearing, even if you may not be familiar with the songs, but the phenomenal performance Prince puts on showcases his wide range of talents in being a natural-born entertainer with contagious charisma and hypnotic aura. Interested in checking out more of his work as well as watching another concert film in cinemas soon. Definitely a theater viewing I’ll always cherish.

reviews.text: Renny Harlin auditions for the Nightmare on Elm Street sequel he'd eventually make in this lean and mean debut, a supernatural revenge-horror prison film starring Lane Smith and a baby Viggo Mortensen. Cool to see that before eventually taking his talents to action films Harlin actually already had pretty solid visual control of cramped space and explosive, gnarly violence. The prison itself has an eerie, grimy look to it and the FX-heavy murder setpieces by the vengeful spirit of a wrongfully executed convict are wonderfully gross. Was not surprised to see regular Stuart Gordon cinematographer Mac Ahlberg was involved.

reviews.text: Van Sant’s camp recreation of Psycho is commonly criticized for not adding anything to Hitchcock’s film. But this criticism overlooks the fact that we must be knowing audience members for it to be true, which is a fact Van Sant readily anticipates. To me, this always felt more like a camp recreation of Psycho than a remake, despite its fidelity to the source. I would argue it works entirely because we know Hitchcock’s film inside and out; it’s clear from the final shot of Marion’s excavation juxtaposed with the title “In Memory of Alfred Hitchcock” that this film does not intend to bury its predecessor. I've found myself thinking about this film a lot recently, even before watching it for the first time. I am so fascinated by the nature of this picture and I heavily enjoy reading whatever I can about it.

reviews.author: sarah
reviews.text: This was so good. It suffers from some clunky pacing and dialogue in the beginning, but it eventually finds its footing, settling nicely between the voyeurism of Rear Window and the skewed morality of Double Indemnity. Having a cop be in the center of the moral ambiguity is always interesting, because the film can simultaneously explore the inner workings of a crime while also watching the criminal one step ahead. Pushover is definitely not perfect and doesn’t really delve deeply into Fred MacMurray and Kim Novak’s relationship and intentions, but it builds the tension well and kept me highly entertained. Probably my favorite of the Criterion Channel’s “Columbia Noir” collection, so far!!

reviews.text: There's shades of Double Indemnity all over Pushover - from the major plot points to the casting of Fred MacMurray in the lead role. But what the film lacks in originality, it more than makes up for in terms of style and execution. Pushover is a tightly paced thrill ride - getting going right off the bat with a bank heist that sees the bad guys get away with 200k in cash. Fred MacMurray's dim police officer falls for lead hoodlum's girl....and anyone that has seen Double Indemnity won't have too much trouble guessing what comes next. Director Richard Quine delivers a real slick thriller. The crisp black and white cinematography looks great, and the way it all focuses round…

MacMurray plays one of cinema's dumbest cops, but he is less manipulated than so dirty that there's little to do than fall for a trap, not of a duplicitous dame, but his own hubris. Novak is indeed really good and there's something very effective of just watch how MacMurray's certainties go out of control as the movie tights its knot. It is a bit mechanical written for sure, but its self-aware knock off status makes the recognizable trappings more effective.

reviews.text: Henry Hathaway's made some good movies in his career (like "True Grit," just two years earlier), but this sure isn't one of them. "Raid on Rommel" begins with a premise borrowed from "The Guns of Navarone," in which a desperate behind-the-lines mission is mounted to take out some shore guns before they can disrupt an allied invasion fleet that's already in motion. Originally intended to be a TV movie, the quick three week shoot was spiced up with action footage from 1967's "Tobruk" in a last-ditch attempt to make the film suitable for theatrical release ... which explains why Richard Burton's hair is dyed blond, so that he'd pass for George Peppard in the long shots.

A gun-stroking orgy of jingoistic Cold War carnage starring a gaggle of Spokane teens fighting back the Soviet forces who've invaded their hometown, Milius' original film plays like an unholy cross between Battle of Algiers and Gleaming the Cube, streaked with scarlet paranoia and sticky with misspent testosterone. A few years ago, someone who hates money decided that this NRA fairytale was ripe for an update, proving that even alternate histories are doomed to be repeated. The only problem? reviews.text: I can only imagine what it must have been like to walk into a theater in 1948 and experience the debut of a new kind of actor in Montgomery Clift. Sure, there's something of the doomed male beauty and Method quality of James Dean in him, but here, in his first role, Clift conveys a reticence about the whole idea of appearing on celluloid—when John Wayne growls "You're soft," I don't think he's acting. The two men, as well as Dimitri Tiomkin's score, convince you "Red River" isn't a story about a cattle drive but about America, and the clashing of two very different masculine codes.

Its black-and-white sequel, Return of the Fly, which the original is often confused for thanks to endless parodies, is a cheesy, cash-driven exercise made with none of the class of its predecessor. It's also very entertaining. The narrative is basically identical to the original, only with more trashy b-movie murder and mayhem. In place of the scientist Andre (played nicely by David Hedison) is his son Philippe (Brett Halsey) who picks up where his father left off, even copying the exact same experiments. The moods vary with some tense stories, lighthearted comedy, and melancholy. The two best entries are from HG Clouzot and Jean Dreville. Clouzot’s story is about an escaped POW who, after returning home, harbors an escaped German POW only to learn that the man was in charge of torturing prisoners in a concentration camp. reviews.text: Quentin was right. The theatrical cut of Revenge is an immorality play of the nastiest order, an existential exploitation movie driven exclusively by bad behavior and worse consequences. Its biggest transgressions would probably be indefensible if it didn’t conclude as soberingly as it does, but it does, and the result is one of Tony Scott’s most intimate movies, with languorous pacing that gives the characterization room to breathe and allows him to place the story—visually, if not geographically—within the brutal pantheon of spaghetti westerns. I bet Costner doesn’t want anyone on the planet to see this.

reviews.text: Probably Ed Wood's most competent, "normal" movie (at least that I've seen) in that basic dialogue conversations and shots/sequences flow with a more consistent old-school haunted house horror mood to them rather than the usual barely strung-together subconscious surrealism that feel like half-remembered dreams of the genre movies he loved as a kid. It's sad he didn't get to make much of anything for nearly a decade after this because you could actually see him starting to polish his weirdo obsessions into something a bit more understandable and accessible here; even his delightfully lo-fi special FX which are certainly present have a baked-in textual reason to be so since it's a story about a bullshit swami psychic staging creepy seances... Speaking of which, sort of surprised Ed Wood's psychic friend Criswell agreed to be in this one lol.

A fake Swami named Dr. Acula is in love with the “White Ghost,” who is also his girlfriend. Together, they scheme old biddies out of their life savings by running a séance scam in which spirits from the dead play the trumpet. That is, until the real ghosts catch on. Starring faux-psychic Criswell and Swedish wrestling legend Tor Johnson as Lobo (his character from Wood’s earlier Bride of the Monster) this movie plays out like a greatest hits mixtape…

Revenge of the Dead) is no exception. From a quality perspective, it is certainly on par with other Wood's films (Plan 9 from Outer Space, Glen or Glenda…), but the problem is the fact that it lacks the unintentional laughs that make some of his other films so entertaining. What you're left with here is seventy minutes of annoying characters played by annoying actors reacting to annoying situations, making the whole friggin' thing…well, annoying.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: In Rio Bravo, Wayne acts to do his duty; in El Dorado, he is in town to pay his debts; and in Rio Lobo his motivation is revenge. There's lots of comedy, but this is the least hangout late Hawks movie, and there's a meanness to it that's unexpected (and anyway, in Hawks, comedy is usually a shield for his more destructive side). I get why people don't care for Rio Lobo; on paper, it sounds like a Rio Bravo retread, but it plays more like its reversal, the most romantic of westerns just gone sour. Rio Lobo is an ugly, beat-down town, and most of the emotions, even among our good guys, are petty. There's lots of respect thrown…

reviews.author: Sam Jalali
reviews.text: Fellini just kind of lets the city wash over you. Given the episodic nature of it all, it feels incredibly similar to Amarcord in certain regards, just swapping out a nostalgic childhood town for the chaotic sprawl of Rome itself. For Fellini, everything about this movie is really just an excuse to capture the messy, unfiltered soul of Roman society. He spends plenty of time mining the waste, the casual sex, and the rampant prostitution that defined the eras he’s jumping between. It’s all a sprawling look at the changes tearing through the city. Still, it’s a perfectly chaotic vibe. Probably the best moments come from just watching the traffic jams or the sheer volume of people packed into a…

reviews.author: Sam
reviews.text: Roma is an utterly brilliant and beautiful film which seems to transport one into a dazzling and deeply personal portrait of Rome through the eyes of Fellini's past and present. It's constructed as a series of fantasies, recollections, and spectacles which blend more autobiographical notions of Fellini's childhood with invention until they combine together. The result is a largely surreal and heartwarming love letter to a city which defined Fellini throughout his life. From the opening moments, you're presented with a city experienced with feeling, and we slowly see the traffic, crowds, and noises. You move through brothels, restaurants, and all sorts of entertainment throughout the city, but it's always brimming with life and fun. There's no main protagonist here,…

reviews.text: Monument versus motion appears to be a central theme to Federico Fellini’s Roma, an abstract homage to the city itself that contains characteristically semi-autobiographical and self-deprecating elements in its amorphous narrative and episodic structure. More of a highly-personal, coming-of-age vision of the Eternal City than anything as directly self-referential as his more lauded works like 8 ½ or La Dolce Vita, Rome in all its contradictory glory is the true star of this endearingly bizarre, encoded love letter. Though I’ve only seen 3 ½ Fellini films, I’m not prepared to say it isn’t my favorite of them so far—while still exemplifying hallmarks of grotesquerie and hyperbole, Fellini also manages to flesh out his relationship to Rome and its identity as…

I personally just found it to be meandering and tedious; routinely having to stop myself from getting distracted, and eagerly awaiting for the credits to roll.

reviews.author: TajLV
reviews.text: Fellini's "Roma" is a homage to the city the director dreamed of as a boy, discovered as a youth, and experienced fully in a lifetime of filmmaking. Harrison Ford is less creepy than Humphrey Bogart, Greg Kinnear is more natural and lovable than William Holden, and, most importantly, Julia Ormond has far more complexity than Audrey Hepburn’s version of the character. This version of Sabrina lives up to the reputation of the original movie — it’s funny, charming, and very, very romantic.

reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: Written and directed by Federico Fellini, Satyricon is a fantasy drama broadly based on Petronius's Latin work of the same name and encompasses a spirit of the late sixties when the chaos of the era was forcefully impacting the balanced of both the artistic and political; where satisfaction was momentary, and magnificence was continually vanishing. The movie has no discernible plot and consists of a series of episodes; every scene petitioning images of either monstrousness or salaciousness, or frequently an uneasy combination of both. The source material only exists in fragments and Fellini deliberately gives rise to the impression that this is an incomplete movie, one that commences at a midpoint and stalls mid-communication.

The costumes and set design were immensely engrossing and helped me to forget how uninterested and lost I was in the plot. I also think this is Fellini’s best shot film, clearly he took a lot of influence from unsettling biblical paintings. There were certainly movies made in the genre afterwards, but they feel in a way like its final statements. This comparatively feels stodgy and inessential. There is enough in the way of classic genre elements, with the line between literal and perhaps less literal realities of the movie dissolving. But there is little of the viciousness of the other…

It's unforgiving, brutal and violent in equal measure, and a truly compelling watch, but like most modern day westerns it struggled to find an audience. reviews.author: More_Badass
reviews.text: In which Pierce Brosnan warms his freezing hands by sticking them into the steaming entrails of a fresh corpse…and the frontier violence doesn’t get any nicer than that. Really surprised by how little I see Seraphim Falls mentioned among modern westerns. Neeson just before going full old man action, Brosnan in his post-Bond prime, a feature-length vengeful pursuit across the Wild West from snowy mountains to grueling desert with First Blood-intense survival action and cat-&-mouse ruthlessness usually involving a giant Bowie knife. I probably know why it isn’t talked about much; the final act taking the men’s perpetual cycle of violence into the realm of allegorical purgatory likely ends this on a sour note for many. With this very overdue rewatch, I appreciated the suddenly unmoored thematic boldness.

reviews.author: Gregor Kreyca
reviews.text: Sergeant York is widely considered a propaganda movie. And it is undeniably that. In fact, it just may be to most effective one when it comes to influencing public opinion about the US entering WWII. But I also think it is unfair to reduce the movie to that status. It is for one, a very well-made and entertaining film. But it also treads its themes (the duality of men especially when their faith is in opposition with their patriotism and the moral complexities of war) with not just pathos but also with a surprising amount of sincerity. The fact that the film is based on the real story of a real man who was still alive and involved in the…

reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: Howard Hawks' Sergeant York starts competently but gets additionally more self-righteous as it develops. It is based upon the true story of World War I combatant Alvin York (played by Gary Cooper) as a man who evolves from a poor young farmer to a marksman, before discovering religion and then becoming a conscientious objector when the war arrives.

reviews.author: Channing Pomeroy
reviews.text: “Soft lands breed soft men,” Herodotus tells us in the last line of his Histories, “wondrous fruits of the earth and valiant warriors grow not from the same soil.” Hawks wants to show Herodotus was right by framing Alvin York’s story as a mythic hero’s journey from the hardscrabble hollers of Appalachia to the machine-gun torn Argonne Forest. York’s transformation from conscientious objector to hero and his miraculous single-handed victory has the feel of the Old Testament tales of Jehovah giving over the Canaanites into the hands of Joshua or Samson striking down Philistines with the jawbone of an ass. Modern myth-making just in time for America’s entry into WWII

reviews.author: Rick Burin
reviews.text: If Ball of Fire is Howard Hawks' best film - his most enchanting, entrancing and affecting - then Sergeant York has a claim to being his greatest: an astonishingly ambitious piece of storytelling, with sweep and style and a tremendous universality, that's also rooted in the personal. Though the DVD cover features Cooper in full-on battle mode - tin hat on, revolver out, face fixed in stoicism, a hero for the Father's Day market - Sergeant York is much more than a mere war movie.

reviews.text: This film is a mess but it's such a beautiful mess that it's easy to forgive the many flaws. Nearly every Giallo cliché is on display along with some ridiculously surreal elements (gorilla suit in particular!). The plot encompasses family curses, murder, lesbians, secret passages, vampirism and a whole host of other stuff. It has to be said that the plot often meanders and can even be a little boring - but the Gothic locations and lush cinematography are always enough to keep things at least interesting to look at. The plot really reaches fever pitch in the final ten minutes and the ending is a bit stupid but it really fits with everything that went before. This is by no means the best of the genre but it has plenty going for it.

Jane Birkin and Doris Kuntsmann definitely make quite a pair. Kuntsmann's a stone classic giallo queen IMO. It is cool how the real personalities of the characters in the film materialize as the film moves along. A theme of sexual liberation and an undercurrent of sexual repression delicately intermingle, so this gets fairly saucy at times. There's also the castle setting for a taste of Gothic horror, especially a crypt scene and another scene in the castle's burial ground. Birkin's terrifying nightmare hints at the supernatural as well. But it's greed that kind of drives the film's plot more than anything else. The other stuff are but tasty distractions. Directed by Antonio Margheriti, it has the flavor of his "Castle of Death"..

reviews.text: This independently produced teen comedy means well and fitfully casts a charm, but it can’t settle on a consistent tone. Stylistically (due perhaps to its budgetary constraints), it seems to be offering a low-key slice of life of middle-class American adolescence during the 1980s. From time to time, however, its tone and content indulge in misguided and poorly executed flights of whimsy. Were Jane Bernstein and director Linda Feferman’s screenplay to dispense with those flourishes and focus on the mundane realities of its three central characters, it would be a solid, if not exactly polished, little film.

This is probably some famous story everyone knows, but I was unfamiliar. I must say, there's something improbably delightful about the questions that scenario creates--how did he get her shoes off? Why her shoes? Wouldn't some other item been easier? I'm sure I can find the details somewhere, but I prefer the mystery.

Elsewhere, the great pleasure of this taboo-breaking feature is how unself-conscious it is about presenting confrontational subject matter, treating its characters as being normal (as they, of course, are) and sublimating its racial tension through subtly, deftly performed scenes like the aforementioned one. Displays its makers' filmmaking inexperience at every turn, but also how they used that to their advantage.

Nonetheless, it is a wonderful contribution to the independent cinema branch.

reviews.author: Criterion
reviews.text: An international breakthrough for neorealism, Vittorio De Sica’s Academy Award–winning film is an indelible fable of innocence lost amid the hardscrabble reality of 1940s Italy. On the streets of Rome, two boys—best friends Giuseppe (Rinaldo Smordoni) and Pasquale (Franco Interlenghi)—set out to raise the money to buy a horse by shining shoes. When they are inadvertently caught up in a robbery and sent to a brutal juvenile detention center, their loyalty to each other is severely tested. A devastating portrait of economic struggle made all the more haunting by its child’s-eye perspective, Shoeshine stands as one of the defining achievements of postwar Italian filmmaking.

reviews.author: Barmilliv
reviews.text: Um ano após o fim da Segunda Guerra Mundial, com a Itália arrasada pela crise econômica e ainda sob a sombra do regime fascista, acompanhamos a jornada de dois meninos, Giuseppe e Pasquale, que sobrevivem graças a pequenos serviços nas ruas, sobretudo engraxando sapatos. Entre os clientes mais comuns estão os soldados americanos que permanecem no país. Unidos por uma amizade inquebrável, eles alimentam um sonho simples, mas repleto de significado: possuir um cavalo branco. É essa esperança que sustenta suas forças diante das dificuldades diárias. Certo dia, seduzidos pela influência do irmão de Giuseppe, acabam envolvidos em uma atividade criminosa, o que os conduz ao reformatório e, mais tarde, a uma condenação formal. Nesse tempo de clausura, a lealdade…

reviews.text: In the 2nd century BC, Syracuse, on the island of Sicily, was a neutral city-state geographically situated between the warring powers of Rome and Carthage. When Rome got the upper hand over Carthage, however, it set its sights on Syracuse, resulting in the siege of 213-212 BC. One of Syracuse's prominent citizens was Archimedes, the physicist and mathematician, who invented weapons of warfare used by Syracuse against the Romans. Based on these historical events, this film is basically a fictional romance in which Archimedes is torn between his betrothed, the daughter of Syracuse's king, and a beautiful dancing girl/prostitute played by Tina Louise (Ginger from Gilligan's Island).

reviews.author: Simon
reviews.text: [insert dumb joke regarding the protagonist being named Simon in a film titled Simon Killer here]Won’t deny I had trouble writing about this one given how unordinary it is, but I’m quite shocked that more people don’t talk about this, as it’s one of the best films of the 2010s. Finds such a perfect line in making its manipulative sociopath of a protagonist compelling enough to follow but also making sure that you don’t really sympathize with him. This works not only because Antonio Campos (who shares story credit with leading actors Brady Corbet and Mati Diop) seemingly has a full understanding of the character being presented, but also because of Brady Corbet’s phenomenal performance (the best leading male performance of 2013). On top of that, it’s masterfully directed, perfectly paced, and features a banging (and well-incorporated!) soundtrack. It all makes for a haunting, unique character piece.

reviews.text: Sinbad and the Caliph of Baghdad is an Italian-made Sinbad movie without any magic, mythical creatures, and only one sword fight at the very end, making it inferior to just about every other Sinbad movie ever made. It's not really suitable for children, either, because the Caliph of Baghdad is a psychotic serial killer who murders dancing girls. It is established in the first five minutes that Sinbad and the Caliph are dead ringers for each other (both are played by Robert Malcolm), so it's very clear from the beginning where the plot is going, but it takes forever to get there. The acting is bad all-around, particularly by the two buffoons who offer comic relief. The film's one saving grace is that it's a very good-looking production that doesn't skimp on the sets, costumes, and location shots. Shot in Cairo, it features some beautiful Islamic architecture.

reviews.text: How many really good stories do any of us accrue in a lifetime? Mike Birbiglia has a great one: the very funny, kinda sad, mostly true tale of how his anxieties about his relationship began to manifest themselves through increasingly bizarre sleepwalking incidents. The stand-up comedian started telling this story years ago, first in abbreviated form as a 2008 This American Life segment. From there, it grew into a one-man Off-Broadway show, then a nonfiction bestseller, then a live comedy album. Now, at last, it comes to movie theaters, with Birbiglia himself starring as the not-so-creatively renamed Matt Pandamiglio, and Lauren Ambrose appearing as his long-term (and long-suffering) girlfriend.

reviews.author: Will Menaker
reviews.text: All Brian De Palma movies are essentially about two things: metacinematic commentary on artifice of film itself and being horny. Of his works that aren't adaptations or genre exercises, De Palma's more personal films are constantly reminding the viewer that what you're seeing isn't real and that you can never fully trust what your own two eyes are looking at. The act of looking at something is always inherently sleazy and obsessive, and the viewer is always implicated in the peeping and creeping on screen.

reviews.author: Maxvayne
reviews.text: Antonio Margheriti delivering some juicy 1960's Italian Sci-Fi kitsch, full of color and in a scene particular - pure poolside swank. In the first hour Snow Devils has padded breaks yet keeps our engagement with hairy monsters, colorful bright additions - including 1960's fashion and Space-Age flair, a Angelo Francesco Lavagnino score, and a fistful of schlock. However after the hour point and our heroes leave the baddies in the dust, this all goes to dirt. Padding out galore! Everything stops until a space battle involving miniature figures and glowing and glittered wired asteroids. No doubt it all sounds exciting, but unless you travel in light-speed with a futuristic glaxtus digitized remote equipped with a fast forward button it'll never be worth it. For shame.

reviews.author: Marty McKee
reviews.text: The fourth and concluding chapter of Margheriti’s unofficial Gamma I series of space operas—following THE WILD, WILD PLANET, THE WAR OF THE PLANETS, and WAR BETWEEN THE PLANETS—SNOW DEVILS is also the most obscure. It doesn’t seem to have played as often on television (even on TNT and Turner Classic Movies, which aired the other three regularly), it never came out on videocassette anywhere in the world, and it was the last of the series to receive a domestic DVD release (courtesy of the Warner Archive). It also spends less time in outer space, though the antagonists are definitely extraterrestrial in origin.

reviews.author: Matt Singer
reviews.text: This is not a very exciting film; at times, it's downright boring. It feels weirdly sedate for something by Oliver Stone, particularly since Edward Snowden's story touches on so many of his favorite themes: Abuse of government power, paranoia, conspiracies, and young idealists learning brutal lessons about the world. Stone's channeled all of these ideas into some of the most aggressive and intense Hollywood movies of our times. Snowden has very little of that anger. For a movie about our free country's slide into a surveillance state, it's awfully chill. Even Peter Gabriel's plot song, "The Veil," is mellow. Where is the urgency? JFK, a 25 year old movie, feels modern in comparison, particularly in terms of editing and voiceover.

reviews.text: For all its intellectual probing, Tarkovsky’s film fails to get at the nature of humanity for the simple reason that none of its characters are remotely human. Soderbergh’s version supplies two eminently human characters, then charts their slow, painful journey into the beyond. Our memories betray us—unless it’s the other way around... Pictures don’t come much better than this.

Soderbergh's version is more about Kelvin's relationship with his wife rather than the existential issues involving identity, consciousness, etc. It also looks very nice and definitely brings in some influence from 2001.

They work the same stories and motifs over and over again (what was the fascination with college sports?) of mild domestic and social issues. Most importantly, they feel magical. SON OF FLUBBER is no exception.THE ABSENT-MINDED PROFESSOR was a big hit for the studios and it set the template for what was to come. reviews.text: A wild and somber interpretation of Captain Harlock, infused with sharpness and boldness, takes us into uncompromising and thrilling waters steeped in discomfort and darkness—lingering with the viewer long after the film ends. The animation and CGI are quite literally out of this world, visually stunning in every sense. From the amped-up, seductive costumes that the characters skillfully use to appear cool or “badass,” often enhanced by well-placed slow-motion effects, to planets that feel massive, grandiose, and monumental, the film continuously evokes awe and spectacle with every appearance on screen.

reviews.text: Pay no attention to the LB ratings, friends: Star Pilot is an unmitigated delight. Trapped chronologically between Mario Bava's Planet of the Vampires and his Danger: Diabolik, the film acts as something of a bridge between the two, combining the former's prioritization of space style over all else with the latter's irresistible delight in bright colors and all things youthful pop culture. At one point, there's even a comment about how much like a comic book everything looks, something which is so on the nose for Bava’s masterpiece that one could be forgiven for suspecting director Pietro Francisci and his co-writer Fernando Paolo Girolami of witchcraft.

reviews.text: A lot of you probably weren't around for this, but after Return of the Jedi was released, Star Wars took a bit of a dive. reviews.text: I've always been of the opinion that if you have similar movies all fighting over the same box office dollar, there will always be one of them, regardless of its quality, that'll be ignored. 1990 was one of THE years for crime films, we had Goodfellas, Miller's Crossing, The Godfather III, King of New York, Miami Blues, and even Internal Affairs, so the deck was stacked when Phil Joanou's film was released in the September of that year. Joanou's previous film, U2's Rattle & Hum, was one of my favourite ever music/concert/documentaries, and State of Grace has a similar quality with a terrific cast all buying into Joanou's vision of Hell's Kitchen and the Irish Mob that ran it.

reviews.text: In Still Walking, people don't change; their familial relationships won't change, or at least in any dramatic, fundamental sense. Avoidance always overcomes confrontation. As for communication, whether it's interpreted through coded words or physical action, silence will more than likely prevail. No closure is offered; resentments are left unvented, problems remain unsolved, but they are collectively acknowledged, and even understood by these characters. Kore-eda is so good at conveying affection through the minutiae of delicate gestures, expressions, and awkward interactions that he makes me long for a day to go back to my sweet home. I'm always like that. I'm always a little late.

reviews.author: StrangeRobo
reviews.text: Style Wars doesn’t necessarily *support* graffiti, and it gives fair time to critics – politicians, concerned moms, irritated locals – but there’s no doubt that the film is deeply fascinated by the spirit and energy of these artists and their need to be seen and heard. The film’s style is just as spirited and energetic as its subjects, attuned to the ballet of noise and movement that makes both hip hop and city life so alive and exciting. But what really cements the film as an essential cultural profile is that it records the exact moment when this movement was co-opted by big money art galleries, which had the mercenary sensibility and financial savvy to recognize the potential for profiting off this new sense of "cool". It’s an invaluable document that manages to preserve all that grassroots passion before it was ossified into corporate buzzwords.

reviews.text: I'm not crazy about the word "slop," but it's a useful descriptor for certain cultural products. Another one might be "pure entertainment." Something like this feels so formulaic, designed by committee, shallow, full of craft but not of art, and like it is trying to appeal to everyone. Another thing about "slop" is that it is forgettable. What really happened in this move? A train, a horse, a jail cell, a cantina brawl, a dog, and lots of cowboys. Was there an event? Was there a drama? Or just a series of flashcards telling you what kind of movie you're watching?

reviews.author: FakeVoorhees
reviews.text: A fun 80s survival adventure from Don Coscarelli that features a great lead performance from Lance Henriksen and early roles for Catherine Keener and Dermot Mulroney. Henriksen leads a group into the wilderness for a survival adventure weekend that turns into a nightmare when a group of paramilitary survivalists begin hunting them. It's more of an adventure movie than a thriller as it focuses more on the wilderness survival aspects than the human threat and takes its time showing the challenges the group faces at the wilderness survival school. When the military group does start chasing them down, it makes for an exciting, fast-paced final third. It never gets too intense though and feels more like a family friendly adventure film than you would expect from its R rating. It's actually similar in tone to something like the Karate Kid including highlighting the different philosophies of the two groups and Henriksen as a mountain man Miyagi.

reviews.text: Rugged survivalist/teacher Lance Henriksen eats and tells others to eat earthworms. Survival Quest is a rock solid forest survival movie from Don Coscarelli. A group of individuals (including Catherine Keener and Dermot Mulroney) from all paths of life sign up to take a survival class led by Lance Henriksen. Of course, there's a group of douche bro wanna-be soldiers romping around in the woods with rifles and idiocy, and after some particularly idiotic idiocy they decide to hunt down our poor group of learners. It's straightforward, which is surprising considering it's from Coscarelli. There are plenty of "we did it together" moments that'll fill your heart. This feels like a title that could be put out by Vinegar Syndrome.

Worth checking out even if it doesn't have the bite of movies like Southern Comfort or Rituals.

reviews.author: Lexzilla
reviews.text: Sometimes all a documentary needs to succeed is just a real enthusiasm for a fantastic subject. And while this might essentially boil down to talking heads and film clips, it works because it’s about hyping movie-treasure Dick Miller. A man who even if you don’t think you know him, you probably do. He’s been in that many things. It’s a light potted history but its crammed, somehow also becoming a bit of an overview of Roger Corman and Joe Dante too, as he was in that many of their works. As a film, this is a feel-good experience, all charm and delight. All hail Dick Miller.

reviews.author: Brian Saur
reviews.text: Still one of my favorite documentaries of the last decade. I adore Dick Miller and not only is it delightful to see a highlight reel of some of his best parts, but also to see him as part of his marriage to Lainie. They are a truly charming couple and it is so sweet to see them together and to hear her perspective on Dick and his career. On top of that, there are so many great folks in here that are more than happy to talk about Dick. I also like the energy and the little animated bits as well. Just a lovely doc. Rewatched via the new Dekanalog Blu-ray.

reviews.author: UncleChoppa_
reviews.text: Dick Miller has to be the most contagiously likable character actor of his generation. He’s your neighbor that comes to family parties, or the cool uncle who takes you fishing and on the dl, as a secret between just the two of you, he slips you your first beer. From his days with the Corman crew to becoming a Joe Dante staple, as far as character actors with genre and indie cred rank, Dick Miller has to be at the top of anyones list.

reviews.author: Evan “Raymond Gun-Virus” Pincus
reviews.text: Rest In Peace to Dick Miller, one of the all-time greats and a national treasure. Of course, you can't tell the Dick Miller story without telling the Roger Corman story, and you can't tell the Corman story without telling the story of the American B-picture, and you can't tell that story without touching on Dante and the B-movie revival... so needless to say, this is a packed doc, but it's informative and endlessly lovable. Dick Miller may be gone, but the legend lives!

reviews.author: Cinematic Underdogs
reviews.text: The pop art, Andy Warhol-esque, vintage-style comic book aesthetics of The 10th Victim are a sight to behold — from the sleek opening NYC chase sequence to the elegant Roman Coliseum finish. Starring Fellini’s beloved Marcello Mastroianni and a super sultry Ursula Andress, this futuristic, swinging-sixties satire on media/paparazzi culture is flimsy in plotting but salacious in theory. It’s very much an ironic product of its own ire — a kitschy middle finger to the very Ming Tea/advertisement-adjacent superficiality it playfully parodies. A hell of a fun time, regardless — but there’s definitely brains behind its dimwitted bimbo vs. himbo premise.

reviews.text: Gaudy post-modern murder-game mixup. I think I prefer Petri when he is operating outside of genre conventions, although that’s not to say there isn’t a little sociopolitical scathe here—an examination of the inseparability of reactionary ideologies and bourgeois pop-art and -culture—but Petri is either disinclined or prohibited from plunging into these ideas in any real meaningful way, which may have something to do with the notion that this is clearly meant to function as a b-picture—a kind of proto-Italo-Austin Powers with a too-faint tinge of leftist philosophy, and while it doesn’t totally falter as a political film or cult film, it doesn’t exactly thrive either. At least the music was groovy.

Doesn’t quite top that opening high and a vulgar LA conspiracy neo-noir parody with a shock comedian at its center doing a cartoon rock industry private dick performance will either appeal to you or not, but huge credit needs to be given to Renny Harlin who cranks this with enough Bruckheimer/Scott/Bay music video style to actually get this into Real Movie territory if not quite the Last Boy Scout one I wish it would at times. The Diceman is a lot more comfortable in its relaxed toxic macho riffing mode than the unhinged action one it occasionally threatens. However, also includes surprise appearances by Robert Englund, Gilbert Gottfried, and David Patrick Kelly which I very much appreciated.

By the Capital Records scene when they fall off the side of the building and Dice says “Oh my hair”, my mom walked out, she’d had enough. My Dad and I stayed. reviews.text: Siegel's punchy, macho direction is an unexpectedly perfect match for a hothouse psychosexual melodrama. The arrival of a wounded, vulnerable Clint Eastwood in his prime at the doorstep of a girls' school immediately broaches fears of his rapacity, only for the women themselves to lose their composure around him. The film unfurls as an extended fever, claustrophobic and sweltering as colors fade from heat and visions intersect in deranged blurs. The net effect is not one of eroticism but fear, of McB, of repressed desires, of each other as sexual competition. McBurney himself revels in the attention, and his predatory behavior to adult and teen alike has a deviant mastermind quality to it, with his seductions specifically tailored to each…

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: The Best Years of Our Lives is classical Hollywood at its finest. Here is a humanist film, with sympathies for the ordinary man. It comes from a point in time when society was transforming. The American economy and way of life was drastically affected by World War Two. This was a rare time when the West embraced a belief in helping individuals and sharing economic prosperity. Yet returning to civilian life, soldiers found their years spent away prevented them from getting jobs. Injuries and nightmares plague those who return. The Best Years of Our Lives depicts these realities. It must have been incredibly affecting for those who saw it on initial release.
