reviews.author: Scott Kelly
reviews.text: Though almost forgotten today it seems, La notte brava is a truly undersung once influential film from a key period in Italian cinema. In the late fifties, director Mauro Bolognini collaborated with novelist/poet/screenwriter Pier Paolo Pasolini a number of times before Pasolini would slide into the director's chair with his impressive debut Accattone. La notte brava, scripted by Pasolini and loosely based on his 1955 novel Ragazzi di vita, is set over the course of a single action-packed evening and the result is a somewhat episodic film that employs an impressive and highly attractive ensemble cast. Its concerns are typical of Pasolini; the wild morally bankrupt youth of the Roman slums, the brawling, thieving, pimps, prostitutes, hustlers and black marketers.…

reviews.text: They always say that certain film genres come and go depending on what audiences want to see. Back in the 1930's, 40's, and even the 1950's, Pirate films were regular releases from the major studios, and although as time went on the swashbucklers, just like the Westerns, faded in popularity, some filmmakers tried to rejuvenate the genre by throwing money into big budget productions. If we ignore Richard Donner's The Goonies as a pirate film, it was decades before Renny Harlin's Cutthroat Island attempted to put pirate films back in the spotlight. Harlin certainly did that, but for all the wrong reasons, losing more money than a Bitcoin entrepreneur, and almost bankrupting Carolco Pictures, and we'd have to wait for…

reviews.text: I have been listening to the theme song for this film for years. I assumed when I heard it that it was connected to the film, and I was delighted to learn that it was right there in the opening credits (complete with overlong instrumental intro). It's just pure, campy, wholesome easy listening harmony, cheezy in the best possible way. I am a little obsessed with finding the best of easy listening. It's an awful genre full of the very worst qualities of pop music, but in there, amongst the welling strings and the soaring, empty voices, there are gems, pure beautiful gems. Even Perry Como manages to have a good time somehow. And "The Blob" is one of those…

I even think I may have seen it on Elvira’s Movie Macabre which was huge in my area when I was young. So because of the nostalgia I’ve got for this one, I can’t really say for sure that it’s a great movie, but watching it now, I gotta admit I was kinda riveted. It’s not the most original concept, an evil car going after anyone and everyone it can. Christine became a much more famous version of a similar story, and the idea of a singular object/beast terrorizing people is nothing new, but this one scratches a certain itch for me, and I suspect it’s one that always will.

reviews.text: I can imagine the pitch for this movie: “American Beauty” meets “Donnie Darko.” That’s exactly what this is, suburban teen angst drama about parents who ignore their kids, teenagers so reliant on drugs, and one guy who sees his dead friend. It’s bizarre, all right, but it’s endlessly fascinating and rather absorbing, thanks mostly to the clear-eyed vision of first-time director Arie Posin, as well as his spectacular ensemble. Standouts are Jamie Bell, Ralph Fiennes, Carrie-Anne Moss, Glenn Close and Allison Janney. Not all of the numerous plot strands work, but as a whole, the message is clear and Posin’s craftsmanship shines through.

reviews.author: Mike Kennedy
reviews.text: This film, which Fellini made for Italian TV station RAI, was released in cinemas the day after its Christmas Day screening on national TV. It gave Fellini the chance to go for broke with his fascination with the circus and with clowns which have featured, in some way or other, in all his films that we have seen so far in this retrospective.

reviews.author: BrandonHabes
reviews.text: THE CLOWNS is stuck somewhere between fiction and documentary, with Fellini himself at the fore entertaining his favorite subject: the circus. Fellini was fascinated by the circus, he saw it as a metaphor for life. Even his earliest neorealist work possessed a lyrical quality that favored spectacle and showmanship, often depicting life as a shabby festival. This film makes a lot of sense in his filmography, a kind of memorial to his childhood dreams filled with clowns and circus performers looking back on their lives. With his production team on deck, he interviews famous retired clowns no longer working in the business, juxtaposing their conversations with thrilling circus performances that intersect with the larger story at hand. It's a colorful…

reviews.author: threepenny
reviews.text: After doing a project ("Fellini: A Director’s Notebook") for NBC, Fellini ran out of excuses to not do one for Italian television as well. And so he agreed to do five shorts for RAI, which in the end became two movie length productions, of which "The Clowns" was the first. It continues his exploration of the documentary form in fiction that runs throughout his filmography, but only for the second time (after A Director's Notebook) includes himself as himself in the production. I find the term "mockumentary" to be wholly inadequate to describe the work. Rather, it is something of a collage of styles brought to bear to explore his theme, which is, the death of the clown. So, memories…

reviews.text: I like the flavour of these things enough that I didn’t have a bad time, but this is not helped at all by the amount of twists, double-crosses and contrivances it piles on. You still have the sweaty jungle vibes and casting to enjoy, but these things go down a lot better when the plot is easier to follow and the ratio of talking to shooting leans in the latter’s favour, which is not the case here. There’s one unintentionally amusing sequence that brings to mind the end of The Departed, but as this recycles footage from Code Name: Wild Geese in the climax, you’re better off rewatching that one instead.

Для сыгравшего Ефима Быкова "Комиссар" стал не первым и не последним фильмом, оказавшимся на полке: в "Андрее Рублёве" актёр играл скомороха, и Ефим тоже сначала появляется в фильме этаким шутом, причитающим о шестерых детях, хотя в рассказе Гроссмана героиню окружали семь оборванных ангелов, как будто отсылкой к апокалиптическому откровению. В тёмном подвале похожее откровение переживёт сыгранная Мордюковой комиссарша Вавилова, наблюдая за кружением семьи Магазаников, и заговаривающий страх танцем Ефим, напомнит уже заговаривающего войну анекдотами партизанского командира из "Проверки на дорогах", которая тоже вышла только в 80-х. Впрочем, для мирного жестянщика, привыкшего…

reviews.author: Alena
reviews.text: Придумала себе новую игру: смотрю полочное кино глазами нормального кинозрителя и думаю, чем оно напугало советского чиновника. Здесь причина абсолютно очевидна — люди, и даже Комиссары, которые от гражданской войны страдают, сомневаются в своём выборе и не отдают Родине без раздумий каждую капельку пота. Гражданская война в глазах Аскольдова не достойна романтизации, как и любая другая война. Поэтому «Комиссар» — история о небольших людях и их больших выборах, детях, впитывающих контекст жестокости с самого раннего возраста, солидарности, вере в лучшее будущее.

reviews.author: Tim Brayton
reviews.text: Gorgeous black-and-white anamorphic cinematography, plus some amazing subjective sequences and quasi-nightmarish vision. The film's actual plot is a bit hemmed-in by the limitations forced on it by the censors - who went on to ban it for 20 years anyway - but the parts that work are truly stunning, and the parts that don't are squirreled away in the corners. Nonna Mordyukova's performance as the titular official, a patriotic Bolshevik broken and made tragic by the needs of the Civil War is one of the best I've seen from this era of Soviet filmmaking.

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: It may not be as good a movie as No Country for Old Men, but it does strike me as a better adaptation of Cormac McCarthy. In fact, McCarthy's screenplay (and Ridley Scott's unexpectedly vibrant, at once overcooked and understated treatment of it) possibly lays out his strengths as an author more visibly than even his greatest novels. You can see here how his approach of constant digressions and a dialogue style that is deep on philosophy and abstract observation but short on exposition, nonetheless uses its various open-ended distractions as the mechanism for which he propels what eventually reveals itself to be, however many complications it has, a fundamentally simple story.

reviews.author: noen
reviews.text: One of the best films of Soviet cinema I’ve ever seen, is a seminal work that spectacularly creates a visual symphony that transcends the limits of a narrative we’ve already seen in other films. Each piece of this film is so detailed, with cinematography that masterfully accompanies the deep immersion of the raw emotions of love and loss in the midst of the tumultuous and destructive World War II. Director Kalatozov presents us with a frighteningly yet beautiful narrative about the fragility of human feelings and abandonment, but also about the power of hope in the face of an imminent disgrace.

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: The lonely cold of war. The Cranes are Flying is an essential piece of Soviet cinema, a film which allowed an entire nation to weep for their dead. Made over a decade after the war ended, The Cranes are Flying is a melodrama calibrated not to propagandistic patriotism but to a specific feeling of loss felt by a nation that had lost so many. Young love everlasting, millions of lovers will never age as their bodies are buried under the muds of Eastern Europe. The Cranes are Flying presents war reaching the streets of Russian cities, with buildings burning and gunfire rattling. Our lead is a woman constantly lost within crowds, as her life becomes spiritually numb. There is nothing…

One is Tatyana Samoylova’s Veronika, the heart of the film whose expressive face speaks with more clarity than any line of dialogue. reviews.author: Edwin 🦦
reviews.text: Rewatching The Cranes Are Flying felt like confronting something I wasn’t ready to face the first time. I genuinely don’t know why I felt underwhelmed on my first viewing because now it feels almost undeniable. Maybe that’s what certain movies do: they wait for you to catch up to them. Watching I Am Cuba last year definitely played a part in that shift. It recalibrated how I look at this kind of filmmaking, but more importantly, it made me more patient with it. This time, The Cranes Are Flying didn’t feel like a story I was watching unfold but rather a meditation on time, loss, and the fragile nature of human connection. World War II exists here, but not as…

reviews.text: Whenever I’m feeling off, I always have this tendency to look up into the sky; it doesn’t matter whether it’s day or night—the sight of clouds or stars never failed in making me relaxed. Today, before watching this film, I went outside, looked up, and saw a flock of birds flying past our residence. It’s a sheer coincidence, considering that I was planning to give this film a rewatch after buying apples to eat while watching. At that moment, a sudden realization hit me—maybe this feeling of relief and seeing something novel is exactly what the audience felt after watching this film.

By day, he is a garbageman; presumably, the only career in his world with any sort of job security. But at night, he truly comes alive. As a stand-up comic, Marty has the chance to not only escape his miserable existence, but bring others with him; to a world of laughter and escapism...if only he had something to laugh about. The only person more disinterested in him than his agent, is his girlfriend, and his best friend is ready to sell him out in a second. And that's not even the worst thing going on…

reviews.author: Ben Hibburd
reviews.text: "The Desert Rats" is a fairly standard 1950's World War II picture. The film focuses on a theatre of war that doesn't get covered nearly as much in cinema, with the action taking place in North Africa, and primarily the siege of Tobruk where the British and Anzac forces are forced to repel Rommel's forces, wave after wave over the course of eight months, using every trick in the book to make sure that the German forces were unable to reach the Suez Canal.

reviews.author: Andy Summers 🤠
reviews.text: I'd only seen director Robert Wise's 1953 WWII film The Desert Rats just the once, back in 2010, not that long after I started my movie diary. Maybe it had caught me on the wrong day and in the wrong mood, but I wasn't that impressed with either the film or the performance of Richard Burton, who plays the lead here. That poster there is also quite misleading, as James Mason has just two scenes in the film as Erwin Rommel, both fictional it would seem, probably a ploy by 20th Century Fox to capitalise on the success of their 1951 WWII film, The Desert Fox: The Story of Rommel, which had Mason in the lead. Henry Hathaway's film was…

reviews.author: Ben Neild
reviews.text: The Desert Rats was produced just twelve years after the events depicted therein, Robert Wise’s WWII drama centring upon the Siege of Tobruk where Allied forces won a significant victory in the Western Desert campaign. The tone of the film is remarkably downcast for long stretches of the runtime as a group of Australian soldiers under British command endure constant attacks from both land and air, the characters forced to devise a number of elaborate strategies to see off the encroaching German Army. Richard Burton stars as Captain "Tammy" MacRoberts as he struggles to reign in the group of delinquents with which he has been saddled, although the ongoing animosity between officer and enlisted man is never quite interesting enough…

reviews.author: Doctor_Doughnut
reviews.text: Pretty standard 1950s British plucky Second World War flick retelling the Siege of Tobruk in Libya by Rommel’s Afrika Korps against the much smaller force of Australian, British & Indian forces during seven and a half months of 1941.Not much is very accurate apparently and, even though he gets second billing, Mason (playing Rommel again after The Desert Fox) is barely in it, so the whole show is left to a gruff Burton shouting at people and continually being shot in non-essential areas of his body.Scarf fans should look out for Rommel’s actual scarf being worn by Mason (this doesn’t have appeared to have helped his German accent unfortunately).I was standing to attention saluting for the whole runtime.

reviews.text: I never watched this when I was young but I remember it being considered a classic British war film. I can see the appeal although I don't think it's aged too well overall. But otherwise it's an old fashioned yarn about stiff upper lips and the UK/Australia relationship. James Mason is the best part about it and his scene with Richard Burton makes the whole film worth watching.

reviews.author: Fint
reviews.text: The highlight of the film is obviously the single scene act-off between James Mason and Richard Burton, although Mason's tones are disguised by his Teutonic accent as Rommel. It is the only moment for Mason to shine in what is inevitably Burton's film, commanding his Australian troops with an unrelenting and utterly unsentimental edge. When you think of the deleterious effect booze had on Robert Newton, there is a palpable sadness to his performance as Burton's soused former teacher.

reviews.text: The Dogs of War is a bit of a mixed bag. It’s undeniably cheesy, but in some ways, not as bad as I expected. That pacing choice makes it feel a little lopsided—spending a lot of time setting things up, only for the payoff to be less exciting than it should be. Imagine an "Expendables" movie where a solid 50 minutes of the runtime is given over to the meticulous planning, logistics, and resource gathering that must take place before a black ops mission can even begin; director John Irvin's dispassionate, almost documentary-like style and eye for detail mean we're even more invested once the pyrotechnics go off and, good Lord, do they ever go off during "Dogs of War's" grand finale.

reviews.text: "The Dogs of War" is a 1980 War film directed by John Irvin. Not particularly directed at a major war in the worlds view eye, the film rather makes its focus on guerilla warfare in Africa, particularly centered around the ownership of valuable platinum deposits. The film itself is based upon a 1974 novel of the same name written by Frederick Forsyth, a prevalent espionage and military writer who wrote other books to film such as "The Day of the Jackal", which actually got two major studio releases on the same book. Forsyth himself was in the Royal Air Force and also a military journalist before writing international espionage thriller fiction, so there is an apt amount of real-world realism…

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: Total B-movie junk from Charles Band. The Dungeonmaster features an incomprehensible plot that has something to do with an athletic computer whizz who finds himself having to complete various tasks in some kind of alternate dimension at the behest of an evil wizard....for some reason. The film is put together like an omnibus, though none of the individual "stories" would work on their own. There's seven sections in total, each one directed by someone different. The quality of each really varies, although they are somewhat charming and feature those wonderful cheapo eighties practical effects. We've got segments involving little demons, a huge aztec statue, zombie things, frozen villains from the past, an urban slasher, a mad max inspired futuristic car…

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: Weird and mostly charming low-budget fever dream mix of just about every trashy 80s genre b-movie you can think of (sci-fi, fantasy, horror, etc) bridged together by an episodic (sort-of) anthology kid's adventure structure so that Charles Band could hire as many of his friends as possible and let them show off as many of their diverse and ambitious cheapo FX setpieces as possible. One minute there will be a sorcerer summoning zombies and then in the next, we'll be laser-fighting giant stone golems followed by a dune buggy chase shootout. How good they all are is up for debate but it's basically 7 movies in 70 minutes. What a deal! The new Arrow restoration of this looks quite nice too.

reviews.text: The Fu Manchu series is the crowning achievement of producer Harry Alan Towers, with the five movies showcasing some of the best elements of his productions. He was competing with Hammer horror films, German Krimi films, and even James Bond, all in this one series. Remember the very first James Bond picture, Dr. No, features a western actor in yellowface with plans to take over the world. In fact, Christopher Lee was once even recommended for the role. West German producers got on board with the idea and supplied two popular actors: Karin Dor and Joachim Fuchsberger. reviews.author: Bart D'Alauro
reviews.text: Maybe not a fitting end to Sellers' career, but not nearly as bad as I'd been led to believe. Sellers provides some big laughs as both Fu and Smith, and Helen Mirren skillfully carries the movie through some of its drier patches. Sure, Fu's makeup and accent is a caricaturish nightmare and the number of "they all look the same"-type jokes is appalling. But, on the plus side, all the "yellow peril" ugliness of the original stories and previous adaptations is ridiculed and subverted, and the yin-yang/mutual respect thing between Fu and Smith make the characters a bit more interesting than I've found them before. And there are some bizarrely brilliant touches, like replacing the Dr. Petrie character with a beloved lawnmower that Smith can't function without, that tipped the scale in this movie's favor for me. It's just too bad that its racism prevents me from calling for a critical re-evaluation, because it almost deserves one.

Aber der hier……?!Als Argento-Fan kann man ja viel reininterpretieren, von politischem Kommentar auf Blablabla bis pessimistischer Sicht auf Dadada oder was auch immer.Auch wenn dem so ist, das vorliegende Mischmasch aus nicht zündendem Humor/Slapstick, unspannendem Revolutionieren und katastrophalem AufdieNervengehen zündet einfach nicht. Eine ständig heillose Karikierung mit politischem Ausrufezeichen, ein beißender, aber zahnloser zynischer Gesellschaftskommentar oder kurzum gesagt eine äußerst nervende Sache und nicht die angestrebte entlarvend zynische Politsatire. Auch wenn es Regisseure gibt, die in mehreren Genres zu Hause sein können, Dario zählt nicht dazu. So sehr man es auch schön reden will.Aber der Argento-Komplettist hat die Scheibe so oder so im Regal, wenn auch nur in der hinteren Reihe.

reviews.author: williamfaeleith
reviews.text: A bit of an uneven oddity, this.Dario Argento's only non-horror/thriller is a strange picaresque comedy drama about the 1848 Revolutions in the Italian states, specifically the Milanese uprising against the ruling Austrian Empire.It starts out as slapstick comedy including a scene where our two heroes help a pregnant woman give birth, which is like a Laurel & Hardy sketch, complete with jaunty piano accompaniment. It becomes more serious as it goes on, making political comment about the Revolution and why it failed.There is a clever comedy section in he middle, where a conversation is viewed from under a table and all that is shown are the shoes of the participants.The film's episodic structure, and some quite disturbing scenes played for laughs, makes it feel like a not wholly satisfactory experience.

reviews.author: Corey
reviews.text: loved this. bookended by the animals trilogy and Deep Red, this oddball/screwball revolution comedy blends a multitude of filmic languages along with the already-developed giallo flair from the director’s hand, finding a way to meld the occasional 70s horror-tinged zooms/pans into a historical war drama. the comical overtone is an ace, bouncing between sequences akin to silent film slapstick skits and witty, snappy back-and-forth dialogue between the lead characters excellent rapport; then to this whiplash of deviance behind gunfire and mutiny where stakes become fabricated almost out of thin-air, and the fragility of it all beneath the punchlines and farce suddenly could not be less palpable. bittersweet that this was a bomb for Argento—on one hand (albeit, a far greater upper one), the failed reception brings us the best installments Italian horror might’ve ever saw, but on the other, we get a tremendous scan and release from Severin decades later, preserving a gem buried within.

reviews.author: Mads Ej
reviews.text: This was an interesting documentary about two of the most interesting Danish directors: Lars von Trier and Jørgen Leth. Lars von Trier asked Jørgen Leth to remake his classic short film “The Perfect Human” five times and each time with some new challenges and limitations. The idea was interesting and they were both very likeable in their conversations with each other but we mostly just followed Jørgen Leth and saw him make the short films, which had some interesting moments but also got a bit boring at times. The short films were interesting to watch, as they showed a great amount of creativity from Jørgen Leth, but as Lars von Trier predicted from the start none of them reached the same quality as the original short film. It was overall a fascinating watch and it was funny to see Lars von Trier mess with Jørgen Leth, while they also had some interesting talks about moviemaking.

With Leth's 1976 short The Perfect Human as the blueprint, von Trier provides Leth with a few simple (yet devious) rules for each Obstruction which Leth then must abide by as he remakes the original piece.

reviews.text: Lars Von Trier tortures his personal hero, because of course he does. My patience for LVT's brand of self-righteous bullshit is always thin, but there's something compellingly upfront about his impishness here. When he challenges Leth to remake his movie with no shot lasting longer than 12 frames, the other director's resultant movie, at once avant-garde and thoroughly coherent, is so exciting and watchable than Von Trier visibly looks upset to have actually inspired Leth. It's also a wry touch that one of his "obstructions" is total freedom, which he actually administers as a punishment for failing to follow other rules to his satisfaction. It's a blunt but nonetheless well-made point about the necessity of limitations on art, and if…

reviews.text: For what? All that trouble and for what? That's the bitter feeling you're left with after watching The French Connection, an intricately framed, austerely striking crime thriller that quickly reaches a boiling point and keeps going at an unrelenting pace until it plainly but painfully deflates. It is a turbulent and feverish observation of one's obsessive behavior, an obsession that becomes consuming for its bearer as it is viewed from a distance, through a safety net. The invisible safety net consists of an impartial perspective that implies active examination rather than immersion, thus placing the characters in closer inspection while still allowing for tension and anticipation to build up.

reviews.text: The Ghost Breakers, directed by George Marshall and released in 1940, is a classic horror comedy starring Bob Hope and Paulette Goddard. The film follows the adventures of Larry Lawrence (Hope), a cowardly radio host who flees to a haunted castle in Cuba after a series of mishaps involving underworld boss Frenchy Duval (Paul Fix). Along the way, he meets a mysterious woman (Goddard) and together they must battle the ghosts that inhabit the castle. The Ghost Breakers is a delightful blend of horror and comedy, with Hope and Goddard providing excellent performances. Hope is a comedic legend who has delighted audiences for decades. The Ghost Breakers is a classic horror-comedy full of dialogue and sight gags. Hope's comic timing…

There’s a bounty of beautiful shots in this picture, with great performances, sets that drive me crazy because I wish I lived in them, a breathtaking score, Vincent Price doing exactly what he does better than just about anyone (he’s so Evil in this movie), and the perfect shady small-town foggy New England atmosphere.

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: I'm a big fan of this film. God knows how many times I've seen it. This is part of Corman's Poe cycle but it's actually a loose adaptation of Lovecraft's classic The Case of Charles Dexter Ward. The story is essentially a distilled version of the original novel and focuses on a warlock put to death by the local villagers and returning for revenge. Everything in this film is so brilliantly hokey. I love the way that the descendants of the original townsfolk are all played by the same actors as their ancestors, and how they are all the same age as their ancestors at the time of burning! Roger Corman augments all the action with some scrumptious horror tropes…

This fits perfectly together and results in a pleasantly enduring eerie atmosphere. Vincent Price is Vincent Price again and I just like it when Vincent Price plays vincentpricely. Unfortunately, the movie lacks of a few highlights and a greater breeze of suspense for the big hit. Nevertheless, I still felt well entertained.

reviews.author: Will Sloan
reviews.text: For boomer teenagers at the drive-in in 1963, there was nothing spookier than a 52-year-old man standing around in a castle. Just kidding folks, I love the Corman/Poe movies, of which this is perhaps the most median and least "notable" example, despite actually being based on an H.P. Lovecraft story. You've got fog, ripe colors, pleasingly fake-looking cemeteries, a big spooky castle, and Vincent Price hamming it up like Satan himself. All the stuff you like in one of these.

reviews.author: Sam
reviews.text: A generally creepy gothic horror which is very slow in approach but very scary and chilling in execution. It’s great to watch Roger Corman direct an actual scary adaption of an Edgar Allan Poe story and Vincent price is better than ever playing two characters one more sinister than the other. The town setting and the palace here are so incredibly spooky and atmospheric and that’s honestly the movies main selling point. The raven is better with entertainment value and humour while this one is generally more spooky acted and better directed.

reviews.text: One of the funniest, most pathetic and anxious depictions I've seen of male ego/self-destruction. Grodin has this perfectly-pitched awkward confidence of a man who can't help but treat every impulsive decision and interaction as an active sales pitch, and very impressed by May's stillness and control with the camera. reviews.text: Another very effective piece by Ishirō Honda, this time not involving any monster but instead being a science fiction crime movie. Honda's trademark special effects work, while not as elaborate or impressive as some of his other films, is still nothing to scoff at and features a few memorable scenes utilizing dry-ice vapor and blue animated clouds to creatively convey how a person made up of gas would get around. The character work, specifically for the main star of the vapor man, is really interesting; his turn to misanthropy and life of violent crime as a result of being turned into a guinea pig in a horrific science experiment is very tragic, yet is never excused and serves to examine…

Really enjoyed the dynamic between the leads and Mizuno, The Vapor Man himself is a really well-written antagonist and drives the story by controlling the mysterious gang robberies and the news. The special effects here aren’t Honda’s best work but they are still very impressive for the time and are a fun way of showing of The Human Vapor’s abilities using the effects of the time. It’s theming of the use of experimentation through the army to “heal” Mizuno’s cancer only…

reviews.author: Andy Summers 🤠
reviews.text: One of the first things you notice about Kirk Douglas is his physicality, he was as fit as a butcher's dog during his Hollywood heyday. He arguably made his name playing the boxer Midge Kelly in Champion, back in 1949, but Douglas had bigger plans than simply being a star, he wanted it all. Forming Bryna Productions at the end of the 1940's, Douglas fancied himself as a producer and a director, although he only directed two films during his lifetime, Posse, and Scalawag, both of which he also starred in. The Indian Fighter was Bryna's first production, and Douglas brought in Hungarian born, American director Andre De Toth to shoot it in beautiful Oregon.

He doesn’t belong to the whites or the natives, so all he can do is move toward a muddled idea of honor and a love that is sweet, while still being unsure that the filmmakers truly sold that element. A film as troubled and conflicted as its characters. If a dude wore an eye patch at one point or another, than it’s almost guaranteed he made some good films.

reviews.author: Christopher Moore
reviews.text: Another Andre De Toth western I'm not crazy about. The more I watch in the western genre, the more I get acquainted with a rotating cast of directors. De Toth strikes me as a dynamic and action-oriented filmmaker, and one who could use CinemaScope to his advantage. In Indian Fighter this is masterfully demonstrated by the siege on the fort. Just not sure I find the storylines in his films to be thematic and persuasive enough for my tastes. He's a director of westerns who saw the genre as solely vehicles for technique, not as displays of feeling for the West and its mythology.

Anchored by a captivating and hair-raising performance from William Shatner, Corman’s film never pulls its punches. Its narrative makes it abundantly clear the blame for the town’s actions doesn’t solely rest at the feet of a right-wing opportunist like Adam Cramer, but with the town’s citizens as well, since they are ultimately open and responsive to his dangerous rhetoric. reviews.author: Jayson Kennedy
reviews.text: There's showing the monster too much then there's this astonishingly stupid choice. A doctor travels to Orloff's castle despite warnings from townsfolk and weary residents within the stone abode. Meeting his daughter, claims of ghosty activity prove true when the professor details creation of an invisible man. Revenge against graverobbers, superfluous nudie violations, and closeups of Howard Vernon's physiognomy ensue. Eurociné as a production company weren't exactly known for quality over quantity. Yet this pap of a multitude of cuts and nonsensical titles is like their offals cobbled into a somewhat merciful seventy minutes. Even then Orloff meanders to reveal a terrible ape costume as the entity too happy to get handsy. Why not have Vernon be the reveal? Would've made just as much sense. This disc's presentation matches the feature's quality; assailed by print damage and missing frames to the backing of a stylus raking over melted vinyl. Watched via Image Entertainment's DVD.

reviews.author: Scott Tobias
reviews.text: Ben Gazzara's performance here is one of those that so captures an actor's essence that it would be pointless to think about anyone else in the role. Beyond all the Cassavetes grace notes-- the dingy texture of the nightclub, the evident affection for his cast of outcasts and rogues, the dread-inducing inevitability of the title-- there's Gazzara, a wannabe big-shot who lacks the means, the common sense, and the luck to lead the kind of life he feels he deserves. His gregariousness becomes tragic.

reviews.author: mia lee vicino
reviews.text: (1978 version)hm! probably one of my least favorites from cassavetes, but the artistry of the intimate camerawork, ben gazzara’s subdued performance as club owner cosmo vittelli, and the swirling atmosphere of his beloved burlesque house is undeniable. here, cassavetes explores the frustrating paradox of cosmo’s wanting to make meaningful art, as shown by his relentless dedication to the quality of his girls’ act rather than their Tiddies, versus his needing to use their Tiddies to draw customers into the club in the first place. it’s essentially the same issue that many indie filmmakers face, especially cassavetes himself.

reviews.author: Brett Wright
reviews.text: With the exception of Mabel in 'A Woman Under the Influence,' I don’t know if Cassavetes ever gave us a better "self-portrait" — with so many of his personal insecurities and struggles on display, as well as his singular drive for creative freedom — than he did through the characters of Cosmo and Mr. Sophistication in 'Killing of a Chinese Bookie.' Cosmo finds freedom through putting on his act. As he says, he only feels like himself when he is playing a part. His club is where he can be who he wants to be: that self-styled man of comfort, the cool master of ceremonies who writes all his own skits and holds creative control over the productions. He makes…

Robinson in a Lang movie, yet Cassavetes keeps finds ways to surprise us until hitting that destination. The movie is three long traps, Cosmo falling in bed with the mob, the title hit and how he deals with fallback which often is conduct with precise but lively manner. That makes The Killing of a Chinese Bookie…

reviews.text: I, uh, sort of loved this. It's terribly serious and methodical, framing vampirism as a louche addiction — once, it's specifically referred to as a cult — that deprives good people of their children and turns hunting them from the intellectual exercise it is for Van Helsing into a terribly personal, tragic one undertaken by a man who knows no other way to go on. I also, oddly, appreciate the almost complete lack of lore. Why can these vampires be out during the day? Why does alcohol and fire somehow remove the danger of a vampire bite? How can people who have been turned be magically reclaimed? The film has no interest in answering any of these questions, instead assuming…

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: A standalone vampire film from Hammer, with no link to the Dracula series. After an opening involving a spade and blood gushing from a coffin, we focus on a honeymooning couple who find themselves the attention of a vampire cult after becoming stranded when their car breaks down. The first hour or so is very much a slow burn, as director Don Sharp takes his time in setting up the situation and characters. The village at the centre broods a real eerie atmosphere, while the indoor locations boast the usual lavish Hammer sets. It's a very colourful film and beautiful to look at. The Kiss of the Vampire includes some genre clichés, but is keen to set its own rules…

reviews.text: "The Kiss of the Vampire" does its own unique thing from the killer opening of a funeral with blood coming out of the coffin all the way through to a whacky ending of flesh ripping vampire bats. It's one surprise after another, though kind of done in subdued ways. It has a lot of the atmosphere associated with gothic vampire imagery such as a castle and ground fog, but it twists the plot around. The bloodbath that it leads you to assume will happen, actually does happen but it's totally different than what you were expecting.

reviews.text: The thing about having Howard Hughes produce a movie is that the man never seemed to know what kind of a movie he wanted to make. He wanted a musical, no he wanted a noir, no he wanted an adventure, or maybe a comedy, no no he wanted a murder mystery. It must have been like being supervised by a hyperactive Pekingese. This worked well at least once, with the lovably strange HIS KIND OF WOMAN. With THE LAS VEGAS STORY, despite Hughes’ purported desire to showcase the gambling mecca he was heavily invested in, what you get is a film about how great Jane Russell looks in 1952 dress bodices, occasionally accessorized with the plot’s MacGuffin, a Cartier diamond…

reviews.text: This is less fun than Antonio Margheriti’s jungle mercenary shoot ‘em ups, in part because it lacks any memorable performances. In those movies you had a nice and sturdy, if not particularly showy, lead in Lewis Collins, and you had guys like Lee Van Cleef, Klaus Kinski and John Steiner looking sweaty and miserable in the tropical heat. Here, the main guy looks like Peter Coyote but has none of the presence. But also in part because this aims for some level of seriousness, but has nowhere near the dramatic chops to justify its veneer of cynicism. Not to mention that some of what transpires strains credulity.

After about a half hour of watching the hardass Captain callously send his men off to slaughter, his best Green Beret sergeant rebels and ends up AWOL. Exploding huts, exploding helicopters, exploding trains, exploding toys, exploding people, and soggy rat attacks ensue as the Captain chases the Sergeant across the entire nation of Vietnam. Margheriti's entertainingly lowbrow exploding hut opus gets an extra half-star for its pointless and laughable bummer ending. For maximum sleaze ambience, view on a decrepit Lightning Video videotape.

reviews.author: Sam
reviews.text: I sort of really enjoyed this one and also kind of hated its lack of ambition and honest waste of Redford. It's a military prison film, which by itself felt quite refreshing for a different take and offers insight into the power struggle and character conflict in such a place. Unfortunately, it's a bit too by the books since it follows the typical tyrant vs. moral hero structure, and it's all been done loads before, but what does elevate it is very strong performances from Gandolfini and Redford. The tension and atmosphere of the prison feel great too, and it feels the right amount of oppressed, and that last 30 minutes is arguably as fun as any other prison film. It's disappointing for sure since it could have offered a bit more insightful examination into military prison and its leadership but goes for more of a typical action flick, but at least it's still entertaining and has good performances.

Most of the film is spent humiliating Gandolfini's colonel/warden, who is more a military fetishist than a real soldier to Redford, who correctly surmises that Gandolfini was a desk man and never set foot on the battlefield or put a bullet in a man's head like any good god-fearing soldier. reviews.text: Stylish, sexy, bloody and super atmospheric Spanish Gothic/Vampire Horror film. It’s one of the best of this kind I have seen so far. The Legend of Blood Castle gave me everything I could ever hope for from a 70’s Euro horror. It has a good cast, the story is quite interesting and well told and music, sets, costumes and the production design in general all fit the setting perfectly. But the real star of the show is the cinematography. Compositions, framing and lighting are so well done, it reminded me of the Gothic Horror films of Mario Bava at times. And I can't think of a greater compliment than that.

reviews.text: This is a somber, serious film that relentlessly plods onward about fear, suspicion, manipulation, and virgin blood. In the opening scene a naked boy on a special horse leads a procession into a graveyard to open the tomb of a suspected vampire by torchlight. It's pretty awesome and establishes the slow, steady inevitable pace of doom that's pretty hypnotic and riveting. The trial of the dead body for vampirism is carried out in all seriousness by the leaders, and followed by the carrying out of the bizarre sentence (on a body that's dead) for the mollification of the living. Ignorance reigns kind of supreme. The belief that virgin blood restores the skin to youthful beauty is the main plot used to show the visceral reality plus its symbolism of nature in a repressed society.

reviews.text: "The Little Shop of Horrors" is perhaps one of Roger Corman's better directorial efforts in terms of his script choices and style of filmmaking. Unlike its 80's counterpart, there's not a single musical number to be found. This movie is pure, unadulterated B-movie cheese. It's a film where every aspect is turned up to eleven and every situation is played for laughs. The characters are all zany and outlandishly hyperbolic, especially a young Jack Nicholson who pops up for a brief dentist appointment in one of his earliest and most bizarre roles.

reviews.author: Will Sloan
reviews.text: Famously shot in two days, which will have any attentive viewer asking: "What did they do on the second day?" But seriously folks, the behind-the-scenes lore that this was thrown together at lightning speed to take advantage of some standing sets is a vital extension of the text. Well, I suppose a lot of people who discovered this on late-night TV in the '60s and '70s obviously gravitated to its oddball humor without knowing about the production - Charles B. Griffith's script is full of funny lines ("Liver oil... wonderful for the colon"), and there's no denying the screen presence of Mel Welles - but I think knowing the behind-the-scenes story helps let the viewer in on the infectious just-goofing-around…

reviews.text: A deadpan comedy, a film that lets its humor live within the absurdity of its premise and characters, making the giant carnivorous plant more menacing by having every human being more ridiculous than the monster. The soundtrack knows this is a horror movie, but the dialogue knows it's a farce, and so you keep finding the humor sinking in as the next goofy thing is said. In the midst of this is the horror not of the plant itself, but the willingness of the plant's "owners" to do its bidding. While some of the jokes don't work (it punches down a bit, especially when it comes to women), some of them (infamously, Dick Miller eating flowers) are so weird they only elevate this to another level.

reviews.text: This first screen version of "The Lone Ranger" deviates from the then-popular radio program.The suspense of The Lone Ranger's identity is a big part of the serial, as he is one of five Texans fighting a ruthless outlaw named Jeffries, who is impersonating a government official and bleeding the people in the region dry.The action and photography are first-rate in this serial.The five "Ranger suspects" — played by Lee Powell, Herman Brix (later Bruce Bennett), Lane Chandler, Hal Talifiero and a young George Letz (later George Montgomery) — are very solid.The musical score adds to the serial's excitement as the 15 chapters gallop by.The serial was the second directed by the team of William Witney and John English and already shows how strongly they work together behind the camera.

reviews.text: This movie definitely thought I was more interested in its unlikable characters than I really was, spending the entire first half on all their intrigues as to why they ended up on a dodgy boat heading out into a hurricane. But the second half more than makes up for it as they get caught in the Sargasso sea, becalmed on man eating plants and attacked by Spanish Conquistadors in balloon vests. It's all a feast for the eyes and fires the imagination, logic be damned. Apparently based on a Dennis Wheatley novel though I always thought it was based on the Sargasso Sea stories of William Hope Hodgson, a great weird fiction author and a favorite of mine. I can only assume Wheatley took his inspiration from there. Not a great movie by any means but it is unique and the back half a complete joy.

reviews.text: The Lost Weekend stages with amazing modernity the physical and psychological travails of a man prisoner of his addiction to whiskey. The protagonist loses consciousness on the stairs and ends up in the alcoholic ward of a New York hospital, a real infernal circle governed by sadistic nurses and populated by pathetic outcasts of society who scream and writhe in delirium tremens. After reading Charles Jackson's best seller, Billy Wilder secures the movie rights to the work despite Paramount not being enthusiastic about the raw pragmatism of…

Speaking of which, I think the character of Don Birnam is a really well written one, and one of the best from this era. He has a lot of depth and good reasons to really care for him. reviews.text: Boris Karloff stars as a mild-mannered scientist, Dr Laurence. Whilst researching and experimenting on the human mind and soul, he soon finds a way that'll allow him to switch a patient's mind into another's body. And as the experiments become more successful, he begins to lose his own mind and morality, transitioning into a 'quote unquote' mad scientist.

reviews.author: Ben Hibburd
reviews.text: Man, there's nothing like a Boris Karloff jam to shake me out of a funk. I swear these old-school horror yarns have some kinda mystical healing power that aids in alleviating the cloud of melancholia that forms over me. I don't know why it does, but what I do know is that when all else goes to hell, these movies act as a respite in the squall of swirling shit that threatens to bring me to my knees when I get bogged down by pain, tiredness, apathy and seemingly perpetual hospital visits. The soothing, resonant tone of Boris Karloff acts as a mental opiate, tranquillising the white noise and dissipating the myopic mind-chatter.

reviews.text: The Man Who Died Twice is basically the last gasp of Republic Pictures before they shut down production entirely. It starts off incredibly strong with an explosive opening sequence. Within the first few minutes, you get a fiery car crash, a massive brawl on an apartment balcony, someone getting thrown over the railing, and a shootout. It grabs your attention immediately. The camera work is honestly a lot better than you would expect for a cheap B movie. Jack Marta shot it in this black and white widescreen format called Naturama and it gives the whole thing a really polished moody look. There is even this weird visual distortion on the edges of the frame from the lenses that accidentally…

reviews.text: Brightly colored gothic horror inspired by Poe (and coming a lot closer to the original story than, say, The Raven), this is an eerily beautiful film. I actually was a bit shocked when Vincent Price outright declared his allegiance to Satan; I expected some sort of work around, some sort of avoidance of the topic. Instead, Corman's film embraced the villainy, declared Satan the master of the universe and the death of God, and then toppled it all with the most gorgeous grim reapers ever (fuck off, Gaiman). This is pre-psychedelic kaleidoscopy painted on the grimmest classic horror. Vincent Price seems to relish his role here, which turns what would be hammy into the exquisite.

Speaking of which, it's so easy to forget just how much of this is practical. Fine, set aside the dated digital doubling in the Burly Brawl fight; the remainder of the sequence is damn near a miracle, spinning the camera around 5-10 performers at a time, with as few as maybe 15 cuts a minute. I won't even go into the freeway sequence.

reviews.text: 100-word review: The Mechanic serves up classic Jason Statham fare: gritty action, and his signature portrayal of an ultra-competent antihero. The movie delivers on its promise of adrenaline, but of course it falls into the trap of predictability that often characterises Statham's films. While it's undeniably fun, the plot follows a familiar formula, leaving little room for surprises. One notable drawback is the frenetic editing. With an excessive number of cuts, the film sacrifices visual coherence, making it challenging to fully appreciate the choreography and impact of the stunts. This editing style detracts from what could have been more immersive and memorable action sequences.

reviews.text: So, how does one tell the story of Muhammad and the beginnings of Islam while respecting the teachings of the Quran, thus keeping the prophet offscreen entirely? By placing your focus on the people who surrounded him and on the struggle Islam faced to be recognized as a religion. The Message handles this challenge very well, with the direct stares into the camera from characters when they speak to Muhammad break the fourth wall of this historical epic in a really fascinating way. It practically demands the viewer to engage with the film in a different manner than other films of its genre. There's also some gorgeous camerawork, and it captures the vistas of the Libyan and Moroccan deserts quite…

It is a widely-acknowledged truth among movie enthusiasts that this production—one of the most successful ever created—explains the Islamic faith and the prophet Muhammad (pbuh) in three hours and does it justice. reviews.author: davidehrlich
reviews.text: What made Tom Cruise a movie star? It wasn’t his toothy smile or his all-American dimples. It wasn’t that he was cocky enough to be loved, but also vulnerable enough to be lovable, although that certainly helped. It wasn’t even the fact that the way he runs on screen tells us more about the fundamental nature of cinema than anyone has conveyed with a stride since Eadweard Muybridge trained his camera on a galloping horse. No, Tom Cruise became a movie star because he possessed something that galvanized all of those individual qualities into something special — a need for quality control.

A veces vemos a ambos hombres trabajando juntos, y en esos momentos la película pasa de ser una mirada del trazo como pensamiento irracional, volátil, a convertirse en un experimento cubista donde el placer de hacer se observa a sí mismo. Una escena así, en particular, expresa con una genialidad insondable el estilo de Clouzot. El rollo se está acabando y Picasso tiene sólo cinco minutos para un dibujo más. reviews.text: Intense social paranoia magnified until it's manifested physically, the very shame of being found out something which becomes both the haunt and the refuge. There's a strange undercurrent beneath the entire thing which lends the film an uncanniness in all but its heroine, a social pariah who finds herself lying low within the strangeness of suburbia. It's more likely that the town is an exaggerated expression of contemporary social norms (which haven't much changed) but the way Fuller presents it portrays said suburbia in its cruelest form: acceptance until that acceptance is needed. Even at its most conventional is there that creeping unease, a lamp in the middle of the room that can't quite light up the corners and so…

reviews.author: Liz
reviews.text: I had a pretty good idea of where this was going by the end of the first act, but what surprised me so much is just how gross it was willing to be. This is pure pulp, a high-class roughie that actually empathizes with its female lead, without all of the requisite sexual violence and the sordid, pervy gaze. The plot is a fever dream assemblage of tropes -- the woman trying to escape her past, the hardboiled cop, the saintly businessman with a dark secret, the brothel -- but what makes this so special is how it uses all of these stock elements in a way that (sadly) feels progressive even today. Bad girls don't go to hell, they go to suburbia.

reviews.text: The Naked Kiss defies easy explanation. To which genre does it even belong? The closest thing we can call it is a “neo-noir”, and while Stanley Cortez’s brilliant cinematography does at times recall the sharpened spaces of something like The Night of the Hunter, the nebulous tropes of the noir don’t really stand out at all in Fuller's yarn. Noir is known for the ambiguous morality of its complex web of characters; Naked Kiss, on the other hand, tells you right straight-out where each character stands in big, honkin’ caps-locked letters. Its seedy story is told in signature Fuller fashion: through a series of increasingly looney scenes that add necessary pieces to the film’s overaching message. Its opening sequence—which ranks…

reviews.text: Watched in honor of Robert Redford, with two friends who had never seen it. One of my all-time, life-long favorites. The final images hit harder in the immediate wake of Redford's passing - we have lost a legend. The movie is not so much about baseball, but instead is part fable, part myth about talent, weakness, mistakes and redemption. Acting, writing, directing, cinematography, editing, and music are all Oscar-caliber, and the seemingly simple story hides layers of depth and wisdom. The movie's moments of triumph and loss somehow feel suspended in time, captured in amber.

reviews.text: The Outcast is packed with enough incident, which, if not handled right, could have resulted in a frenetic and bloated picture. However, the directness and the seeming simplicity of Witney’s approach corrals the narrative into a sharp, economical, and well-observed study of human behaviour. The acting is exemplary and, as is customary for a Witney picture, the stunt work is breathtaking and brilliantly edited.

reviews.author: Evelyn Rose
reviews.text: Hamlet with horsies in Republic's Trucolor. By the end of 1953, Republic's staple product, the B series western, had gone with the stage, so this 1954 production is a revealing example of a studio in transition. It opens with former series cowboy veteran Bob Steele rolling into town and greeting bright young thing John Derek, and what follows retains, thanks to its suggestive source material, the resonance of a contested passing of torch within genre confines. Unfortunately, for all that, the movie just isn't much good – pretty boy Derek wasn't in Hollywood because he had Shakespearean stage training, and the bright visual palette, chosen so to show off Trucolor, clashes with the script's chiaroscuro needs. Pair with Edgar G. Ulmer's far better Strange Illusion for a Poverty Row Does Hamlet double feature.

reviews.text: The Ox-Bow Incident marks an important turning point in the history of American cinema, being the first western to deal with a social issue in a realistic way and without indulging in the heroic and Manichean tones typical of the genre. William A. Wellman creates a cutting-edge work, a social drama that uses the context of the Wild West to criticize the distortions of modern society. In this sense The Ox-Bow Incident is the progenitor of that series of psychological westerns of the 40s and 50s, among which Wellman's Yellow Sky, Henry King's The Gunfighter and of course High Noon by Fred Zinnemann.

reviews.text: Revelling in its film noir roots, The Pavement manipulates expectations from the outset. Directed by Taylor Angel, who confidently handles the thoughtful screenplay by Christopher Connors, the short film accomplishes some neat results thanks to a narrative that takes advantage of a looping history that holds a potency in its simplicity. Classic noir elements are present, such as a gun, guilt and a femme fatale, along with a narrative trick that continually replays the same few seconds with additional information being revealed and the soundscape shifting for each repetition. The Pavement is a fascinating example of short filmmaking that is both tidy as well as accomplished.

reviews.text: "The People That Time Forgot" is a 1977 adventure film directed by Kevin Connor. Connor made an assortment of bright and somewhat campy fantasy adventure films in the 1980, with many based upon infamous works of literature. "The People That Time Forgot" was notable a 1918 novel written by Edgar Rice Burroughs about a selection of travelers that are on a rescue mission for another grouping of travelers lost in a unknown prehistoric land. Obliviously to me before starting this film, "The People That Time Forgot" is actually a direct sequel to "The Land That Time Forgot" (1974), also directed by Kevin Connor. Either way it didn't really make or break the film for me, because ultimately, it's a schlocky…

I just read "war" in one of the descriptions and thought they were soldiers, that's my bad folks. Seriously though, you will never guess what this is actually about, like where the plot goes after the first act. I had a feeling it would be sci-fi-esque but not to the extent it turned into. It's a good flick, it looks beautiful of course, I enjoyed the plot's evolution despite the sudden whiplash of info. If you've seen Shinkai's more popular works like Your. Name, the ideas in his feature debut here will feel familiar. It's a nice and brisk watch.

reviews.author: Tim Brayton
reviews.text: It's no surprise at all that Shinkai Makoto's first feature would run into exactly the problem it runs into: the first 27 minutes are an exquisite mood piece, darting around warm feelings of melancholy and longing, using music, light, and pacing to generate a kind of free-floating affect. And then the script cracks its knuckles, and announces that we're going to start digging into the narrative, and it just gets so obtuse and boring. One gets the persistent feeling that Shinkai cares about emotions & not about story so much, and while of course that can be sustained for 90 minutes, the director hadn't figured out exactly how to do that just yet.

reviews.author: Karl Janssen
reviews.text: This black and white biblical epic out of Italy was made before the peplum film explosion, so it doesn't fall into a lot of the formulaic clichés that mark so many of these ancient epics. I don't know how faithful this is to the Bible's telling of the Queen of Sheba, but it's a pretty interesting plot. King Solomon captures too ambassadors from Gat who are on their way to a war conference in Sheba. Since Sheba is an enemy of Israel, Solomon replaces these diplomats with two spies of his own, including his son Rehoboam. Espionage is complicated by romance, however, when Rehoboam falls in love with Balkis, the Queen of Sheba.

reviews.author: CinemaSerf
reviews.text: I think the fact that this is in black and white helps it enormously. So often the poor quality of the image distracts from these Italian-made adventure films and tends to render them all but unwatchable. This one benefits also from decent story to underpin the, admittedly, pretty mediocre acting. The young prince "Rehoboam" (Gino Leurini) finds himself posing as an agent of Gad (not God) at the court of the legendary Balkis, Queen of Sheba (Leonoro Ruffo) who has sworn never to feel the touch of man. Of course the two fall in love, much to the chagrin of her army commander "Kabaal" (Franco Silva) and from now on in, the film follows a fairly predictable route of deceit,…

reviews.text: This movie is (apart from its cast) cheap and deeply silly, and it embraces both with such pride that the result is an unadulterated delight. It's so funny and so ridiculous that it's just utterly winning, and a complete pleasure to watch. It admittedly took me at least 50% longer to watch than it should have, but that wasn't because I was bored or distracted — no no, I just had to rewind basically every Vincent Price scene, so that I could admire his line delivery and wonderful expressions all over again.

Feels more like gothic horror for kids and I kinda loved hanging out with all my grandpas making funny faces at each other in their goofy outfits/elaborate castle sets. reviews.text: This is a weird one! The switch from intense Gothic horror to goofy comedy is jarring to say the least. Edgar Allen Poe's famous poem is brought to life in the first five minutes and what follows is pure imagination from writer Richard Matheson, as we focus on a battle between wizards or something. The Raven fits the bill in terms of style; the aesthetic of the film very much ties in with the earlier Poe adaptations but tonally it is a completely different animal. The plot really is a mess and jumps from point to point with reckless abandon. The cast, however, is great with series regular Vincent Price hooking up with Gothic horror favourites including Peter Lorre and…

reviews.author: Ben Hibburd
reviews.text: If I had the choice to inhabit any cinematic world, I'd have to choose somewhere in the Roger Corman "Poe-verse." As per usual, this film is beautiful to look at. The set design is detailed and packed to the brim with unique macabre trinkets, elegant robes, and dusty dungeons filled with all kinds of lotions and potions. Watching a Roger Corman film is like watching a game of Dungeons and Dragons come to life, and I love every minute of these films. From the exuberant lighting to the goofy effects where you can clearly see the wires holding items up, there's an effortless charm about these films that I've yet to see replicated. Corman's stories are a bit naff, and…

reviews.text: Dwan breeds a semiology equal parts biblical and ecological, thereby inherent in the narrative itself. A parable governed by (a)morality and the rule of nature, that is to say, indifference, in which genre is fluid, even liminal, and which resembles a scale with fidelity on one side and treason on the other, tipped by both divine and natural law; and, in this context, money is no longer the proverbial root of evil, having been reduced to stained slips that will burn up or float off long before they can be spent.

Notice all that pink; it is a mean, hard film, full of betrayal and…

reviews.text: Honestly earnest, The Rocketeer is the kind of innocent, pristine, warm adventure that takes place in a picture-perfect, dualistic America. Out-of-work pilot Cliff Secord lives in Los Angeles, but his world rather resembles a Smallville-type of town, with diners and a friendly crowd that rallies behind him unconditionally. His girlfriend Jenny, an actress, belongs to Hollywood. When he stumbles upon a jetpack, he finds himself entering her world of fame and a conflict larger than anything he could ever imagine. Both the FBI and the Nazis are on his trail, but all Cliff wants to do is fly and be with his girl, and he becomes a hero by staying true to himself.

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: Relatively unreconstructed and a brisk 88 minutes. Even if there's not much to this it's nice to see a straightforward revenge western with few revisionist tendencies. The doses of grisly violence, South Africa standing in for the Old West, the international cast, the simple narrative, and the vague anti-capitalist threads all place this pretty squarely in the German strain of spaghetti western offshoots. It's easy to imagine this with, say, Klaus Kinski and Gianni Garko. Although Nieves Navarro (just to pick a name at random) would never have been able to pull off what you get here from the increasingly incomparable Eva Green.

reviews.text: The Savage Innocents, or "Ombre Bianche" (White Shadows in Italian). Is this a nullification? Or maybe it's a contradiction? An irony? Notably, "Savage" is first, followed by "Innocents." Hiko dies, and then Papik is born. The Missionary and the 2nd trooper are killed, and then Peter O'Toole and Inouk live. In this order, it is the most recent that is preferred and remembered. This is also an uncivilized outcome, as the book never forgets. It's like a tense note without resolution. "Killing never solves anything," Fritz Lang would say. To wipe the book, to reclaim power from the book and words is what Nicholas Ray has done with The Savage Innocents. A movie that uniquely reimagines what it means to…

reviews.text: Some kind of fantasy documentary deeply fascinated with the eskimos’ culture and its contraposition to western civilizing morals and rules. Some very beautiful sequences (the old mother’s farewell scene is unforgettable) and a very humanist eye. A weird but very remarkable exercise from Ray, that replaces his usual telluric dramaturgy by a more descriptive, observational construction of a world, and also a bit far from his usual motifs (violence here is unwanted rather than inevitable, values are analyzed more through an ethnographic approach rather than a moral one, it is cold instead of hot, it is anti confrontational rather than angry…).

reviews.author: MJsays
reviews.text: Toying with humour and sadness in film is such a difficult balance to strike, but The Savages is by far one of the best examples of how to do it. Taking universal themes that loom over all of us like a dark cloud, such as growing old and facing death, we go on the journey with a pair of middle-aged siblings who are confronted with the harsh realities (and responsibilities) that this daunting yet unavoidable stage of life can bring. Laura Linney and Phillip Seymour Hoffman build such a brilliant dynamic as brother and sister, and to no surprise, are able to match the humanity and heart of Jenkins’ screenplay with an expert level of comical timing. A funny, brutally honest and beautifully-realised story about the importance of family and learning when and how to prioritise them around the life you’ve built for yourself.

reviews.author: David W
reviews.text: In 1970, a robotics professor at the Tokyo Institute of Technology, Masahiro Mori, published an article on the relation between robots’ resemblance to us (as humans) and our affinity for those robots. To wit, as robots look more and more human, we like them more and more—but only up to a point. When robots begin to bear legitimately close likeness to humans, yet remain not quite human, Mori hypothesized that our encounters with them would begin to provoke a sense of eeriness, or creepiness. This dramatic dip, from affinity to revulsion, is what Mori termed “the uncanny valley.”

reviews.text: Henri Georges-Clouzot’s choice of Maisons-Laffitte as location for this farce on international spy intrigues wouldn’t have been arbitrary. The wealthy suburb of Paris was, and is, home to a large expat Anglophone community. So, in a film that edges towards British mordancy, the Cold War mapping of the Berlin Western Powers - UK, US and France - against a MacGuffin of an enemy in Dr Malic's microcosmic hospital, makes unspoken, satiric, sense.

Henri-Georges Clouzot is fast becoming one of my absolute favourite directors.

reviews.author: Jeremy Milks
reviews.text: Director Antonio Margheriti is a classic example of an Italian genre director for hire. His filmography is all over the place in every category with approximately zero classics, yet most of his films are pretty fun, starting with the ridiculous Yor Hunter From The Future and a few other mid-range gems like The Last Hunter and Cannibal Apocalypse. He has one really good Spaghetti Western - the Kinski starring And God Said To Cain, but mostly his stuff is forgettable. I think this is the 3rd time he'd use Lee Van Cleef as his star and what we get is a dreary (almost depressing), clever crime movie set in NYC. It really droops in the middle but Van Cleef is so great to watch no matter what. He's an eagle in human form.

reviews.text: Il Bidone is often forgotten among Fellini's work because it fell between two of the most beloved works of his career. It's also a departure from his usual style, yet still distinctly a film that feels right at home among his body of work. It admittedly doesn't quite reach the emotional heights of La Strada and Nights of Cabiria, but it's still a good film that deserves respect among his early filmography.

reviews.author: Joe
reviews.text: I appreciated this as the overwhelming action spectacle it is the first time I saw it but on second viewing I felt more keyed into its metatextual game, a violence bonanza in CGI and bullet-time about old stories evolving into new formats across generations, like a utopian vision of how the blockbuster could be used to connect people with their ancestors, and vice-versa. Tsui Hark shoots all the action scenes like he's doing The Matrix: 1946, and then caps it all off with a mid-credits sequence that reimagines the climax in an even more fantastical, superheroic fashion, feels like showing off but in a thematically productive way. You could do worse than this if you're looking for something to scratch that RRR itch, this one even has its own man vs tiger showdown. I'd love to be able to see this in 3D on the big screen someday!

reviews.author: Joe
reviews.text: The framing device here places this in a very specific thematic context: That even in these carefree times, you should make the effort to appreciate and honor your forefathers whose heroism and sacrifice during wartime made your life possible. Fair enough, but Tsui Hark comes close to subverting this theme by making this gleefully entertaining and exciting, World War II era combat shot with bullet time and geysers of CGI blood. The bad guys are larger than life too, starting with the main antagonist - Lord Hawk, a supervillain who's pretty much Oswald Cobblepot reimagined as a Chinese warlord.

Righteous defenders of the common people, the PLA set-up base in a ravaged village and try to take down a gang headquartered at a former Japanese fortress and arsenal on Tiger Mountain. Nevertheless, it's epic wuxia/war-film filmmaking, it's got all the bigness and all the exciting you could ask for.

reviews.author: proofrock
reviews.text: Barry Shear's best feature, and all of them are good. '70s psycho downer that just piles on the hopelessness, as a small town's youth are wooed, sexually assaulted and murdered by its rank-spoiled older son (Richard F. Lyons in a rare lead role). There seems to be so little going on there that the kids just go along with Skipper for lack of any better outcome, irresistible to his power even if it means their lives. The party sequence in this is burned into my brain years after the fact, a truly bad trip that boxes out the more obvious nods to what's going on with palpable frustration and inchoate terror. Watching Skipper eventually cave in leaves no trace of satisfaction; the damage is already meted out.

reviews.author: Moronic Inferno
reviews.text: The Angry Samoans wrote a 39-second song about this movie. If that’s not a valid reason to watch it, I don’t know what is. The film itself is a fictionalized account of real-life serial killer Charles Schmid (aka The Pied Piper of Tucson). It’s well-produced, though I had trouble finding an entry point to become fully engrossed. I think the problem is that it’s played too straight tonally, too cooly nonchalant. Fans of true crime stories and the dark side of the free-love era may be interested though. Folk singer/activist Holly Near appears in a small role. She must’ve had a good agent in the late 60s and early 70s.

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: The Trip is just a film about a guy taking LSD and tripping. That is the entire plot. But it's really compelling oddly enough. Roger Corman was at his most experimental here, layering the film with a psychedelic atmosphere and hallucinogenic visuals. It is incredibly impressive what he achieved on a low budget. The cool, disconnected imagery and rapidly edited montages are very evocative. They're boosted by the colourful sets and great re-use of old material to make the journey feel larger. The Trip is very 60s, capturing the zeitgeist of drugs and hippies, and embracing that trend. It's also very funny and a fair depiction of drug taking which neither glamorises or demonises drug use. It's a groovy film.

reviews.author: Eddie White
reviews.text: A remarkable and relatively hidden film by French master Clouzot, La Vérité is a stack of lethal dominoes; love, lust, jealousy and infidelity, that begin to fall from its beginning and never cease with each highly charged scene that follows. Bardot as Dominique, brandishes her sensuality like a sharpened dagger, transforming from pouting, petulent temptress to an enraged and heartbroken soul in a performance that shows what she was capable of as an actor. The film has an incredible rhythm to it, an operatic feel that ties in with the conducting talents of Dominique's lover, Gilbert. Throughout the film I was struck by its anxiousness, through its direction, editing and performances and couldn't help but think of it as a rapidly beating heart, ready to explode. In an uncanny parallel to this noticeable vibe, I then read that Clouzot's wife in real life, died of a heart attack shortly after its release and his life and career never recovered.

reviews.author: maneleeo
reviews.text: That ending just hurt me a lot you know. The whole film, I mean. It's like Fellini regarding everything he has done, thinking about all of his themes, all of his sadness, all of his excentricities, and I could go on and on and the list would be endless. Fellini's films are many many many things. They are a joy to watch. This one was different. It felt like Fellini, the circus-like insanities, surrealism, funny characters, these were all there. But it wasn't the kind of swan song I expected, nor it was something I would imagine Fellini doing. It indeed felt like a swan song, but one without intent of going out in glamour, it's all about expressing the thoughts of a man that kept his entire life expressing himself. And that final shot says everything, the world is a crazy crazy place.

reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: Henri-Georges Clouzot’s The Wages of Fear is an exceptionally gripping thriller about the corrupting consequences of capitalism, faintly camouflaged as an adventure movie. It’s based on a novel by Georges Arnaud and placed Clouzot on the international stage after it won the Palme d'Or at the 6th Cannes Film Festival. There’s a strong and active energy to its cinematic compositions, masterly provided by Armand Thirard (Les Diaboliques), which assists in this being a marvellously constructed politically soaked noir that’s overcrowded with anti-corporate views and opinions.

This film is a…

reviews.author: Matthew Christman
reviews.text: Watching this intense existential suspense film about vagbond ex-patriates in a South American backwater driving highly unstable nitroglycerine through dangerous mountain passes, one thing that jumps out is the brilliant use of sound. While most films made during this period (and most made nowadays, actually) tend to punch up moments of tension with a bombastic or manipulative score, The Wages of Fear creates unbearable tension with no external soundtrack whatsoever. It's amazing that so few filmmakers have figured out what Henri-George Clouzot knew in the early fifties: silence, or the rhythmic beats of nature, heightens tension far more than an artificial musical accompanyment. This film is chock full of rivetting sequences, but its also filled with clear-eyed commentary on capitalism, masculinity, and death.

reviews.author: chavel
reviews.text: The Wages of Fear is as exciting and nerve-rattling now as it must have been 65 years ago. Just be patient for the first hour while it establishes character background. It’s worth it since the next eighty minutes keep you pinned to your seat. In South America, four men have to navigate a transport truck over mountainous terrain while carrying lethal nitroglycerin. The roads are narrow and narrower, and increasingly hazardous – the slightest bump can blow them up. They want to move slowly, but on necessary occasions they have to crank up the speed. And other times, they have to move across shallow but untrustworthy streams and motes. Do you really think all four will make it? This Henri-Georges…

reviews.author: Edwin 🦦
reviews.text: I was not expecting Henri-Georges Clouzot’s The Wages of Fear to take place over the course of just a few scorching hot days, so watching it during a heatwave here in Southern California felt weirdly perfect, like I had accidentally signed up for a sensory experience rather than just a movie. I could practically feel the dust sticking to my skin and the sweat pooling under my collar as the tension climbed higher and higher.

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: There is so much tension in The Wages of Fear. At any moment things may explode, whether that be through violent confrontations between men, accidents in unsafe terrain, or literally explosive cargo. The enemy here is man, where survival depends on co-operation and people are forced into dangerous circumstances through desperation. The Wages of Fear relies on a lot of cruel dramatic irony, meaning none of the main characters have any guarantee of living to the end. For its time the film is unsparingly brutal, sending characters into an inferno they have little chance of surviving. But people need money to live, and will provide their own blood to get it. The Wages of Fear builds so much atmosphere, creating…

reviews.text: Fellini’s first solo effort allowed me to correct a misconception: no, he didn’t begin with neorealism in The White Sheik. However, it’s possible that the film’s poor reception inclined him toward the neorealist wave, where he found success with I Vitelloni, Il Bidone, La Strada, and, naturally, Nights of Cabiria. Thus, Fellini took time to mature his work and master his craft before returning to that “art of unpredictability” already budding in his 1952 debut.
