reviews.text: Roger Corman is just a fabulous director. In The Wild Angels, he cuts the camera loose to follow the action on the ground, to take in the horizon, to move with line of sight, to capture the chaos of a gang brawl or a bacchanalian church desecration. Corman dug that he was making a Biker Western, and used the beautifully sparse, polluted spaces of the Southern California desert. Monte Hellman edited this, too, so everything is jagged, vibrating, quick pans, zoom-ins, pull-outs. A real sense of exposure, of danger, of imminent violence, is present in every moment of The Wild Angels. This is New Wild Hollywood before it was A Thing, not Cool, but Hot, a Cinema that really expresses…

reviews.author: Joe
reviews.text: If the people of Earth ever decide to shoot a biker movie into space to explain what biker movies are all about to extraterrestrial life, this would be the obvious choice. All of the genre tropes are here (naturally, since this movie essentially created the genre), and surprisingly artful in their presentation. It's easy to make fun of Peter Fonda's big "we want to be free to do what we want to do" speech when you hear it out of context, but the movie surrounding it is surprisingly ambivalent towards Fonda's character and every single other Hell's Angel in the movie.

The incident later lent itself to the title of David Stratton’s autobiography: “I Peed on Fellini: Recollections of a Life in Film.” The book was published in 2008.

reviews.author: RanchoTuVu
reviews.text: The biker flick The Wild Angels at first looks like Corman is trying to have it both ways by mixing rowdy Beach Party vibes with a tough biker flick. I could see the audience they were going for was white middle-class teens at the drive-in but Corman and the cast gave them more than their audience likely bargained for as playfulness turns into violent insane desecration of sacred American middle class symbols. It's exploitation done right with rad fuzz guitar accompaniment and quieter more pensive guitar tunes. It features Bruce Dern as The Loser playing the character as he lived and then as he died and became a symbol for the movie to hang an insane final funeral scene on showing that Corman wasn't fooling around with the Beach Party stuff by the end.

reviews.text: Film director Andrew V McLaglen sadly passed away on the 30th of August of this year. Best known for a host of Westerns and an exceptional reputation directing the television series Gunsmoke and Have Gun-Will Travel, he may not have been one of those star names that attracted award attention, but he sure made entertaining films. He was 94 years old, but left some real gems among his filmography with this 1978 film probably his best. This is an action film with a real taste of the seventies to it. reviews.text: Boots and saddles. I am really not sure how I could address this masterpiece. There is so much going on here, its bloody letter to capital, its inconceivable formal sophistication when dealing with comedy, action and drama, the complex idealistic tropes towards ideals and glory, the shift from the war of secession to the war against indians, brothers and enemies, drinking to stop the drinking, killing to stop the killing. Somehow what seems most essential to say about this without sounding too superficial is that there are two instances in this film where Havilland’s face is focused that achieve monumental pungency: once while she eats onions unwillingly, out of love for a man, after she just heard the tea tell her that he was coming into her life, and later when she hears that same man breaking a love chain and she tells him goodbye, as both of them knew he wasn’t coming back. For ideas live longer than bodies.

reviews.text: raoul walsh is the most dynamic and zestful of classic hollywood auteurs, his narratives dashing at impossible speeds. warner bros in the 1940s was a haven for no-nonsense directors like him, hawks and curtiz -- but unlike those two, walsh didn't believe in an intellectualized distance between himself and his material. the films of hawks are more stimulating than exciting, and curtiz is the model of efficiency, not efficacy -- between them, walsh feels unique in his pugnacious and heedless hurtling through a variety of adventures and genres. the dialogue tracks of his movies can barely keep up with the pace of his camera movement, as if his characters rarely have a moment to distinguish between speech and action; these…

Finalmente, as guerras indígenas fazem com que ele recupere o comando de um forte perdido nas terras selvagens do oeste: segunda juventude de Custer, mais estimulante e mais calorosa ao coração, menos louca e muito mais comovente, como um desafio contra a sua época, contra o mundo moderno. - Michel Marmin, Raoul Walsh

Recordemos no sólo su impetuoso adiós al cine, (Una trompeta lejana), sino, sobre todo —tal vez las más hermosas escenas de su dilatada carrera— el del nuevo campeón y el derrotado John L. Sullivan en Gentleman Jim y el de Custer y su esposa —«Pasear a su lado por la vida fue muy agradable, señora»— en Murieron con las botas puestas, escenas sutiles y delicadas, prodigios de ritmo y modulación dignos de Ford o Mizoguchi.

reviews.text: Time Runner is another entry on the long list of "baffling career choices Mark Hamill made". I'll say this, early on I was reduced to tears laughing at one of the choices the film makers made. One of our characters, a scientist, arrives at a crash site to examine the mystery craft Hamill has arrived in. They look up to see a government helicopter arriving. Dramatic music plays as the copter lands. We see an interspersed shot of boots hitting the ground. Cut back to the scientist. Cut to the 'badass' villain being introduced. Cut to the same shot of boots. Cut to the scientist. Repeat cycle a few more times. This keeps happening as the scientist and the villain walk…

reviews.author: Matthew Christman
reviews.text: This movie is one of the most egregious wastes of a premise in film history. You've got a police force chasing criminals through history to stop them from changing the course of world events. The first two scenes, with the Confederate gold hijacking and JCVD throwing the stock broker out of his window in 1929, tease the viewer with the idea of Van Damme teaming up with Da Vinci and face-kicking Hitler. Then, after that great set-up, JCVD spends the next hour going FIVE YEARS INTO THE PAST. Wow. ZZZZZZZZzzzzzzzzzzz. Another tragic case of a cool comic concept being thrown out the window as an excuse to provide a plot.

reviews.author: Branson Reese
reviews.text: I just cannot bring myself to care that this movie wastes its own premise so hard. So what? So they didn't go back in time to see Benjamin Franklin or Cleopatra or Genghis Khan. I don't think the movie would've been that much different if they had and I think you're kidding yourself if you think otherwise. Jean-Claude Van Damme would still have done the splits with his butt out. I guess it would've been nice if he did it in front of Charlemagne but you need to understand that not everything you think should happen is going to happen. Be serious if you're going to be taken seriously. Try to enjoy how ludicrously wrong they got "what cars in 2004 will look like" like the rest of us in the real world.

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: Gloriously fun Sci-Fi action romp, taking place in an extremely futuristic 2004! As is often case with time travel films, this one is absolutely riddled with plot holes - some of them are so big, Van Damme couldn't do the splits over them - but it really doesn't matter too much, as the fast paced plot and numerous action scenes are enough to keep things entertaining, and it's much more fun not to worry about the things that don't make sense. Jean-Claude Van Damme makes for a likable lead and certainly he knows his way around an action scene. There's some good fight stuff, including a few imaginative schlocky scenes such as the guy who gets his arm frozen off…

reviews.author: mumblecorgi
reviews.text: There aren't many films noir from the classic period that deal effectively with the drug trade. My favorite about the subject is Litvak's Sorry, Wrong Number, starring Burt Lancaster and Barbra Stanwyck, which fuses a tale of marital deceit with a drug smuggling angle. To the Ends of the World, though nowhere near as good, gets props for tackling the subject when relatively few people in the US outside the bureaucrats working for the Federal Bureau of Narcotics (the predecessor of the DEA--or the Drug Enforcement Administration) would know about. (We even get a cameo from FBN Commissioner Harry J. Anslinger.) Dick Powell stars as an agent who tracks major shipments of raw poppies before they are converted to opiates…

Robert Stevenson is no Hathaway not to mention Anthony Mann.

reviews.author: Ripplin
reviews.text: Commissioner Michael Barrows (Dick Powell) is a U.S. Treasury officer, specifically from the Federal Bureau of Narcotics. It's 1935 and he's looking to bust the opium trade. To that end, he goes in pursuit of the Kira Maru, a ship leaving California that they suspect is involved, and it rushes toward international waters. From a distance, he sees an act that really shocked me (seriously! *shudder*), and from that moment on, he's fully devoted to ending this scourge. His investigation will have him travelling the world, meeting fellow officers and also people that can't be trusted. Or can they? (No, they can't. Or can they?)

reviews.author: lemonski
reviews.text: I first saw To The Ends of the Earth sleeping on a friends sofa; bleary-eyed in the early hours of the morning I happened to tune in part way through, and was immediately hooked. To a teenager who hadn't travelled anywhere much except in the pages of Tintin, Dick Powell's globe-trotting detective hunt for a gang of narcotics smugglers was immediately compelling and completely enthralling. From San Francisco to Shanghai I was riveted - director Robert Stevenson sets a cracking pace, the plot twists and turns, and Powell is cynical and charming as he doggedly follows the trail. By the end, I was convinced that this was the greatest movie ever made.

And when the scenes DO have sound, that sound is often the voice of Powell making speeches in florid style about good and evil, etc. But this story of a narcotics agent's trip around the world trying to stop a massive shipment of opium from reaching its customers is compelling in a number of ways. It's a strange little picture, sure to be called noir (because it's in black and white and…

reviews.text: Not at all a particularly riveting watch. It is, however, a unique look into a particular period and place in history. This film is a 1940's take on an 1857 novel about the state of higher education in England in the 1830's. So, while being a very dated coming of age flick, it's also a unique window in time to a time and place that is both similar and incredibly distant to what we experience today. The story is a stark lesson against bullying that takes place in a period as early as exists in any film about higher education. Most of the acting is competent, and while there's no real enthralling part of the film it was an interesting enough watch. As a history minor I probably found it more interesting than most, even so this one wasn't bad.

reviews.author: Carlos Valladares
reviews.text: What would a compromised Cassavetes film look like? It's amazing that even when Cassavetes had an even moderate control over pictures (even those made for Hollywood studios), they would inevitably turn out more "his" than "theirs" — an astonishing feat. This Paramount flick about a jazz pianist's (Bobby Darin) and a could-be jazz singer's (Stella Stevens) struggle to remain faithful to their art has showier camerawork, glossier made-up faces, and more moody trick shots than John uses on a good day. It wants to be like Faces/Husbands/Shadows, but never gets there. And yet, shades of Woman's razor slit, Faces's shower resuscitation, Chinese Bookie's runt against an oppressively commercial system, Love Streams's jazz structure, Husbands's pathetic glorification of drinking (the only…

reviews.author: Rizki
reviews.text: Cassavetes knew how to compose with the wide range of human emotions, like so many notes on a jazzman’s partition, showing them at their rawest with a fascinating mix of razor-sharp precision and cool jazzy detachment. However, the virtuosity that made Shadows such a revolutionary classic, breaking new cinematic ground, seemed lacking in Too Late Blues — a sincere story, but without the face-slapping intensity that became the director's trademark.

reviews.author: Sam
reviews.text: It's definitely a step down from Shadows, but it's still a moody, soulful drama from Cassavetes, which blends emotion throughout, even if not to the extent of his later films. You can tell Cassavetes is trying to make this film more raw and more than a studio picture of the time, but it's obvious to see studio interference. However, it's still a human-grounded enough story. Bobby Darin is also surprisingly great here, bringing an emotional weight that I honestly didn't expect, but sometimes his performance feels dull. It's a shame you can't see his full vision with this film, but it still feels sincere, and it easily has more potential than it pulls off.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: So hopeless compromised that the moments when Cassavetes manage to slip in in the middle of the more standard elements really have a charge. Fascinating in how it very much doubles on itself, a movie that is always about its own making and the negotiations there in. One wishes the main actors were more comfortable on Cassavetes rhythms.

reviews.author: BrandonHabes
reviews.text: The story of an artistic visionary wary of selling out, unwilling to compromise his art to the smoldering bribe of Hollywood, feels like an ironic placeholder for Cassavete's entire career. It's almost as though Cass is imagining on screen, through the life of a jazz musician, where this soul-selling path may have taken his own career, had he been more concerned about success than the promptings of his artistic muse. This is the story of Ghost capitulating his art into the seductive, wealthy arms of the boozy, beautiful Jess Polanski (i.e. crass commercialism), but it's really the story of Cassavetes spending his entire career fighting against this metaphor, yet yielding to it when it gave him enough currency to make…

reviews.author: nitrate74
reviews.text: Fascinating if inevitably compromised attempt by Cassavetes to smuggle as much of his evolving post-Shadows freeform style (and repertory company both past and future) as possible into the confines of a glossy Paramount production. The tension keeps things interesting, and he's got the right studio-approved leads for those maverick sensibilities: With his natural bent for moving between the pinnacle of the mainstream and various countercultures, Darin understands his character in a way not likely available to many performers, and Stevens is deeply touching in one of the few parts she ever had that knew how to properly use her air of bruised but yearning vulnerability.

reviews.author: seb
reviews.text: Whilst, admittedly, lacking the distinct visual style of a regular Cassavetes film, Too Late Blues's overarching feeling of forlornness and disillusionment more than makes up for it. It chronicles the conflict between upkeeping artistic integrity and achieving mainstream success, which comes at cost of compromising one's creative identity, a near autobiographical allegory to Cassavetes' own struggles with major studio filmmaking. But, it's much more than that. It's about obsession and its destructive tendencies, it's about adolescence and its accompanying directionlessness, and it's, at heart, about surviving and making the best out of a subpar situation. What a gem indeed.

The film begins by showing the lead character butchering a dead body and feeding it to pigs and that really sets the scene for what is to come - a dirty, nasty and over the top gore flick. While TPB: AFK is not entirely one-sided, and certainly not hagiographic, it does have a partisan bent, and you get the feeling that widespread viewership is the paramount motivation here, money be damned.

reviews.text: It’s been a bit interesting to see how the view of The Pirate Bay has changed here in Sweden over the years. Last year saw a dramatized series about the site, produced by Sweden’s public service and looking back at the 2009-trial regarding the site is a bit like looking back at a different period of time. TBP AFK is a documentary centering on the trial and as such, it sort of functions like an entertaining courtroom drama. The three defendants (the guys behind the site) range from being pretty charismatic to incredibly arrogant, but their occasionally annoying personalities only adds to the strength of the docu.

The set-up is genuinely great, but as it goes on it starts to wander all over the place. One thing about that, though, is that it does make it feel like you are constantly trying to figure out what is real or not, and it adds to the mind-bending vibes that it is going for. Unfortunately, a lot of the ideas in this one don't fully work. It keeps stacking up plot twist after plot twist, so it ends up becoming quite confusing. It comes across as trying to be smarter than it really is. Danny Boyle's brilliant visual style and the performances are still enough to save this from being a total misfire.

reviews.text: Triple Agent. A great film, based on the alternation of newsreel footage and fictional commentary on real events, and arriving at some of Rohmer's familiar concerns despite the unfamiliar approach. The film centers on the mystery of the protagonist Voronin: he spins elaborate tales of White Russian politics (Rohmer wrote this remarkable dialogue out of thin air), speaks enough truth to be persuasive, yet complicates his self-presentation by acknowledging the possible stragetic function of selective truth-telling. His wife Arsinoe's struggle to understand his motives makes her a surrogate for the audience; Voronin himself functions both as a representative of the world's irreducible complexity and as a device to make us question the fictional conventions that would normally help us make…

reviews.text: She only does sketches on the street, applying quick images into her more painterly images once she’s home, and he does the same: accruing ideas and secrets, all in the seeming effort of cutting a well-rounded, stable figure to his wife, when he is really intently omissive, mercurial even at his best. As Balzacian a penultimate film as Rivette’s actual adaptation, The Duchess of Langeais, surveying how games of unknowability effect actual emotions, already slippery conceptions of status made more opaque by the outside world. Fiercely adjacent to the theater, but the 3:4 images mean the camera has to follow each character as best it can, mapping out a whole stage within our own limited view, bolstering the extreme proximity of this husband and wife, while also isolating them from one another on a frame by frame basis.

reviews.author: Connor Denney
reviews.text: There might be a twist ending to Triple Agent, where it turns out that everything we believed throughout the course of the film, even as we piece together the minor surprises along the way, lead to an incorrect conclusion. The film plays its cards far too close to its vest, however, for Fiodor's story to be exposed in such a manner. In the end, we know that Fiodor's life of secrecy and the guarded manner in which he carries himself even around those closest to him have deceived us, but there is hardly a way to know exactly how we have been led astray. The film has a deep understanding of its protagonist, revealing the chinks in the armor that lead to a fuller picture of his inner self, but it maintains a respectful distance and does not pry into the truth of his situation: his real political affiliations are never entirely elucidated.

reviews.author: Quiller
reviews.text: In my review of Roberto Rossellini’s Journey To Italy, I observed that many of the figures associated with Neorealism were happy to return to the studio when they got a chance to. What filmmaker wouldn’t want access to studio resources and big-name movie stars, including some from Hollywood? Most of the folks who made this adaptation of Homer’s The Odyssey had connections to Neorealism. Producer Dino De Laurentiis produced Bitter Rice and Europa ‘51, which screenwriter Ivo Perilli and coproducer Carlo Ponti also worked on. reviews.text: Roy Rogers was enormously famous way back when, making several movies every year, almost always playing himself (the singin', fightin' cowboy). Here, Rogers is seen making a movie that seems to climax with him punching a guy who then falls out of frame. He's probably dead. He then announces to the crew that he's going to celebrate his tenth anniversary (in movies, I assume) by going back to his ranch and singing with his backup band/farmhands The Sons of the Pioneers. While there, he beats up a horsenapper who decides he's going to steal Trigger, who gets second billing, as revenge. There's lots of songs, lots of fighting and dang if Rogers isn't charming as all hell. The movie isn't good, but I get why this sort of thing was popular. Worth noting that Trigger nearly kills a guy by stomping on his head.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: The premise of this film relies on the idea that Manifest Destiny was a good thing, and therefore, the entire thing just falls apart. In some ways, it's the opposite of Black Narcissus--there's no hint of apology for American avarice here. Add to that racial and ethnic stereotypes and the standard pride in the race war between whites and Native Americans, and you have quintessential Hollywood Western mythology. This film is morally bankrupt before even getting into the central conflict, which is not about the railroad (which is just a backdrop, no matter how much mythologizing the film does), but the love triangle between Stanwyck and her two beaus.

reviews.author: J. K.
reviews.text: Fellini's debut feature is a little underwhelming when compared to the unreasonably high standards he set later in his career, but it still manages to be a solid film in a general sense. It has an Old-Hollywood kind of feel, while also staying grounded in classic Italian cinema. That is in no small part because of it's colorful cast of characters, which all feel convincingly authentic. From an acting standpoint, everyone did a great job helping him get his wings off the ground, but Giulietta Masina is unsurprisingly the standout – even if she is somewhat underutilized.

And the ravine shot was right again because "Vengeance" is but another cool spaghetti western, albeit with a few lapses here and there. But they're made up for in memorable scenes, like a knife throw from across a saloon pinning a card to a seat post that a cheater was pulling out of his sleeve. Plus Claudio Camaso and Werner Pocath killed it as pale, sickly, and psychotic villains. Double pleasure there. Richard Harrison as Joko Barrett anchors things adequately as the protagonist, effectively wreaking vengeance with a rifle he saws the barrel off of. With Antonio Margheriti directing, it's got style.

reviews.author: Jeremy Milks
reviews.text: Comic book style Western from pulp master Antonio Margheriti, starring Brett Favre lookalike Richard Harrison as a man out for revenge on the five men who killed his brother. The gimmick used here is Harrison throwing a small piece of rope at each man he hunts down, the same rope used to pull his brother to pieces by being tied to five horses. We get five really over-the-top villains and the hunting of each one is like an episode unto itself, which gives us a lot of pay-offs all paced perfectly throughout the film. There's a torture scene that's memorable, where a man is tied down under the sun and has little sticks propping open his eyes so he can't blink. Right away you think of Argento's Opera or A Clockwork Orange. Great stuff here. Recommended for Spaghetti fans.

A spaghetti western I feel I should revisit more often, and it also makes me want to take a better look into Margheriti's filmography.

reviews.text: Vikingdom feels less like a finished film than like the outline of one that was never properly realized. What it presents is a fantasy world stripped of texture, replaced by surfaces that appear relentlessly artificial. The visual design aims for grandeur but collapses into something oddly weightless, a digital emptiness that never convinces for a single moment.Yusry Abdul Halim seems to pursue scale without the means to sustain it. The result is an aesthetic that appears both cheap and overdetermined, as if excess could compensate for the absence of coherence. Instead, the film becomes increasingly difficult to engage with, each scene reinforcing the sense of a production disconnected from its own ambitions.The performances do little to anchor the…

reviews.author: Hutch
reviews.text: This is Terrence Malick in full wonder mode, and while I can’t vouch for its effectiveness or otherwise on the IMAX scale, I certainly struggled with it on my merely human scale. It starts with abstract space spunk before leading into heavily CGI’d approximations of reality, mixed in with shots of real reality at its most infernally spectacular and preternaturally beautiful. The beauty of nature in Malick’s lens is overwhelming. Even the primitive humans have got perfect teeth*. Rising above its immaculate conception hovers a whispering Brad Pitt uttering banalities. This is surely the ultimate in dreadful voiceovers, operating to the logic of a random awestruck word generator. There is some great music in here by the likes of Mahler, Beethoven, Bach, Pärt, Poulenc and Kancheli, but it’s all somehow made to sound less great.

Somehow this movie is both incredibly cynical — the American people fall easily for a manufactured war against an otherwise anonymous country (sounds familiar*) — and not cynical enough. The precipitating incident, after all, is that the president was caught in a sexual tryst with a young woman. This, the film tells us, will derail his bid for reelection if his team can’t successfully distract the press. The eventual fate of Bill Clinton — he left office among the most popular presidents of the post-war era — seems to say this is nonsense. And from the vantage point of 2025, the idea that anyone would blink at a presidential affair is ludicrous. In the modern media cycle, the president’s affair would have been resolved in 24 hours! No fake war necessary.*I would bet legitimate money that this movie was a powerful influence on the Bush White House. Speaking of which, rest in piss Dick Cheney.

reviews.author: Will Sloan
reviews.text: This movie has become a minor cultural touchstone because of its provocative central idea, which is that Washington and Hollywood could conspire to create a fake war and easily sell it to us, the rube public. But because Barry Levinson and David Mamet believe in nothing except their own cleverness, the movie has only that one idea, and most of the movie just repeats it rather than complicating/challenging/building on it. Don't expect any character arcs either. While I'm not thrilled about Mamet's subsequent right-wing conversion, at least it led to Spartan, a much more entertaining movie.

reviews.text: Haven't watch this in a long time, and the thing that stands out is just how much of a Clinton-era curio it is. The halcyon days when people really thought they were living at the End of History, and their biggest concern was that nothing was Real anymore. Since then, we've been living hip deep in the Real, while at the same time trying to keep it at arm's length with the Internet. As a result, Wag feels about as relevant as a silent movie about the dangers of Jazz music. Hoffman is still funny, though. Also: there IS an Oscar for Best Producer: who the hell do you think accepts the Best Picture award?

reviews.author: chavel
reviews.text: What’s enduring about Wag the Dog is its satiric slant on presidential image buffering, with spin doctor Robert DeNiro as Conrad Brean employing Hollywood producer Dustin Hoffman as a brassy, silver pompadour Robert Evans-type to construct a phony war as a decoy strategy after the president is accused of sexual misconduct with a Firefly girl. We never see the President head-on, but we hear his audio and get enough of a sense what a phony gasbag he is, though in 1997 it was seen as obscene satire because none of us thought a President that imbecilic could ever take Oval Office.

reviews.author: Alí Jozi
reviews.text: Wag the Dog is a textbook example of a film gaining fame more for its timing than its quality. While the premise of government and Hollywood collusion is inherently interesting, the film is an exhausting, over one and half hour loop of the same narrative. It leans so heavily into "deep state" conspiracy theories that it loses all nuance, offering a cynical view of a rigged system with zero alternative perspectives. Most of the humor feels cheap and dated. Ultimately, it’s an oversimplified, anti-American satire that only stayed relevant because it accidentally mirrored the Clinton/Lewinsky scandal months later.

reviews.author: Fint
reviews.text: That Walk on the Wild Side was a troubled production is evident in the end result. Director Edward Dmytryk bristled over producer Charles Feldman's casting of his girlfriend Capucine in the central role, and ultimately gave up final cut on the picture, weary of the producer's interference. The minimally talented Capucine insisted on being dressed in the latest Pierre Cardin, despite the film being set in the 1930s. The script details of prostitution and lesbianism were hacked back to a insubstantial sliver by the Production Code. Anne Baxter was trying to hide her pregnancy from everyone. Jane Fonda made no friends by constantly deferring to her acting coach. Laurence Harvey and Capucine hated each other. And everyone hated Laurence Harvey.…

reviews.text: Walk Softly, Stranger is a curious blend of film noir and melodrama that showcases both the strengths and limitations of its era. Directed by the skilled Robert Stevenson, this film is a compelling exploration of love and redemption, albeit marred by a few narrative missteps that prevent it from achieving true greatness. The film stars the ever-charismatic Joseph Cotten as a drifter with a troubled past, who arrives in a small town with the intent to escape his previous life. His journey intersects with that of a young woman, played by the captivating Anne Baxter, whose innocence and vulnerability offer a contrast to his morally ambiguous nature. Their chemistry is palpable, effectively capturing the tension between desire and the weight…

I like how it remains a sober take on space adventure, with scene after scene of engineers at consoles speaking dryly about the proceedings. Quite enjoyable.

A talky affair where the cast hangs around the same few cave sets listening to Price quote poetry, and a climax inundated by repetitive underwater footage and questionable monsters (the aforementioned fishmen, now fully lit in all their rubbery glory). It is Jacques Tourneur's last film though, and there's some great Mario Bava-inspired stuff, so kind of worth checking out.

reviews.author: DavidS60
reviews.text: War of the Planets is a noble attempt, but is ultimately thwarted by its low budget and limited talent. Director Antonio Margheriti, the Italian equivalent of Roger Corman, throws together a sci-fi opus involving a strange life form that manifests itself in the form of gas in an effort to take over Earth. While some of the special effects are passable, others are downright hilarious, including the ultra-strange New Year's Eve dance that takes place in zero gravity outside a space station. Equally odd is the fact that the Earthlings decide to attack the alien mist with bullets and lasers when it would seem more logical to simply point an industrial fan in the direction of the fog and just blow it away. To top it off, the dubbing from Italian to English is brutal at times. War of the Planets isn't all bad, but it's not very good.

This time the threat is from green glowing lights that turn out to be some kind of mental floating microorganism type thing that can take over people's minds or freeze them like mannikins. Our heroes immediately start shooting at the pulsating lights, which somehow sort of works. Astronauts wear space suits that are lace up. The men are in corsets. The alien base has moving walkways and cabinets filled with dinner sets that descend at a press of a button. It's all marvelously nonsensical.

reviews.text: One of the medium's foremost masters of screen space has a panic attack, a full-blown psychotic breakdown when confronted with the post-9/11 horror and confusion and paranoia that comes with the realization that our space no longer feels safe. Some of the straight-up cleanest and scariest monster/disaster suspense sequences ever put to film. Watched this on the new 4K Blu-ray and felt like I was seeing a number of its gruesome images I've never been able to get out of my head for the first time again; the stylish shadows, light blooms, muted colors and grain textures all look incredible and only serve to heighten the ground-scale vaporizing, rivers of corpses and fertilized roots of human blood. Someone should scare the shit out of Spielberg again so we can get more movies like this and Munich.

reviews.text: The first two-thirds are among Spielberg’s most effective works, and one of the scariest things anyone has made in the last 20 years. (It’s basically all of my anxieties condensed into 70 minutes — thanks Spielberg, I didn’t want to sleep tonight anyway.) The pace and intensity of absolutely nightmarish images seems unsustainable — and apparently it was, because the final act shifts to something that’s much less frightening and then much less bleak. Even if that material has its roots in H.G. Wells’ original story, it still doesn’t quite fit the magnificent freakout that precedes it.

Centering around buzzing, ticking, and beeping 1980s technologies that may spell the end of humankind, the film revels in modems and two-color displays; but, more importantly, carries the classic and contemporary warning that that same technology can be humanity’s undoing. Combined with an energetic cast, a compelling narrative, and a mostly serious tone, the film’s message rewards its audience with a gripping, well-assembled drama.

reviews.text: Few Western stars had the charisma of Richard Widmark, and here he rightly shines brightest among a slew of arguably bigger names. Co-starring with Henry Fonda and Anthony Quinn, Widmark holds his own in a thrilling Western that's as complicated as it is beautifully directed by Edward Dmytryk, with double-crosses, side swapping, and characters doing the most surprising things when push comes to shove. As close to a Western noir as I've ever seen, the detailed plot nuances make for a tension-filled affair where the apparent lawlessness is replaced by something even more dangerous, especially when that comes in the shape of a hired gun posing as a marshal. The people wanted law, and nobody could stand up to McQuown…

It certainly softens the novel considerably and misses a lot of its texture while very efficiently streamlining it. The filmmakers mostly turn it into a masochist love triangle between three gunmen. The town does come up lively, and Fonda's cast adds a fascinating note with its echoes of My Darling Clementine. But his brother, played by Frank Gorshin, still rides with the cowboys, who now hate Widmark. Just that would have been sufficient but "Warlock" features Henry Fonda as a mercenary the town hires to deal with cowboys and Fonda's sidekick Anthony Quinn, who's got a clubfoot. This is a tribute to the complexity of the situation and it's really interestingly done with characters with all kinds of shades in it.

reviews.text: "We Were Soldiers" is a 2002 Vietnam War film directed by Randall Wallace. Based on the book "We Were Soldiers Once… and Young" written in 1992 by Lt. Gen. Harold G. Moore and Joseph L. Galloway, the film looks into the events of the Battle of Ia Drang which took place from November 14th to the 18th, 1965. This conflict directly is known as the first larger scale battle within the war as any previous conflicts were smaller skirmishes between patrol units. Both Moore and Galloway are displayed in the film, with Moore being the central character and played by Mel Gibson and Galloway being played by Barry Pepper in a much smaller role.

It looked to be a shot for shot reshoot of the CASTLE OF BLOOD script by the same Director, Antonio Margheriti, only now it was in color. Unfortunately, it didn’t have Barbara Steele as Elizabeth.…

Web of the Spider, as it stands, is a 1971 variant for a slightly different set of horror fans. Sure, it can be argued that the cinematography and the atmosphere suffers from the brand new visual flair, but in my opinion, it just goes to show how the creator had improved in technique and skill over that eight year period. reviews.text: Gesehen im Rahmen der Discord Challenge „Zirkus des Horrors“ „When Animals Dream“ setzt sich mithilfe von Bodyhorror und Monsterfilm Elementen mit der regressiven und konservativen Einstellung vieler ländlicher Gegenden und vor allem ihrer Abneigung gegen das was aus der Norm fällt auseinander. Dabei findet der dänische Film für mein empfinden durchaus immer mal wieder atmosphärische Einstellungen, grade wenn die Szenerie des Fischerdörfchens im Fokus steht, ist mir insgesamt aber dennoch zu träge, beziehungsweise schleppend erzählt. Nicht, dass ich slowburn und generell eher langsame Filme nicht mögen würde, aber Jonas Alexander Arnbys Werk entwickelt einfach zu selten eine spannende Sogkraft um seine Trägheit auszugleichen. Sonia Suhls Performance in der Hauptrolle hat mich auch nicht immer überzeugen können leider. Dennoch bleibt eine, zwar nicht unverbrauchte, aber immer wieder spannende Herangehensweise an diesen Themenkomplex und der ein oder andere interessante Ansatz.

reviews.author: HKFanatic
reviews.text: Pure populist cinema. The late Jan-Michael Vincent plays an army pilot who returns to his small Arizona town to start a life as an independent truck driver only to find that, you guessed it, the real battlefield is at home, thanks to a shady shipping company foisting contraband on their drivers. Effectively generates some white-knuckle suspense—it looks like Vincent did much of his own stuntwork as well—but what this captures most effectively is the idea of a corrupt but inescapable System tightening a vice grip around a good-intentioned individual until said individual has no choice but to retaliate with violence. I would not be surprised if S. Craig Zahler digs this movie.

It's fucking beautiful in every sense of the word, moving the camera in exciting and longing ways that combine the best of current technology while calling back to the past without overdoing it. Sono's film is both a homage and a raging bull of creativity, reminding of where the beloved cinematic art form came from but showcasing the powers available today.

reviews.text: John Huston belief in the poetry of loserdom can often be too much for me, but it serves him really well in this Flannery O’Connor adaptation. Huston brings an outsider perspective to O’Connor religious tale, and finds the road to martyrdom a very natural extension of his usual interests. It has a fully realized world but one full of desolation and longing. Brad Dourif is great as Motes, and the supporting cast isn’t far behind. There is probably no more Hustonian shot than the image of Dourif disappearing in the rain near the end, his work done, all connections to humanity lost.

I've always wanted to see this film solely to see Dourif as the central leading figure. On top of that and with certain prior knowledge to Flannery O'Connor's book to also see the way Dourif could play such an intriguing character that she has wrote into this southern gothic parody of religion and absurdism. It did not disappoint either.

Loath as I am to use the phrase "sicko mode" to describe any movie -- especially a very good one like this -- the proverbial shoe fits; shooting in eye-popping Godardian color and blocking his gorgeously sullen actors in homage (or parody) of Antoniennui, Clouzot not only fulfills the arty-experimental mandate of his famously unmade L'Enfer but gives the era's reigning masters of masochism, submission, and self-excoriating allegorical anguish a run for their money. As a relatively late entrant in the history of boys photographing girls, Clouzot doesn't seem come to this sort of material naturally, but his long-standing gift for pressurized and conspiratorial horror (especially the betrayals and reversals of Diabolique)…

reviews.author: Graham Williamson
reviews.text: Prior to La prisonnière - to give it its subtler French title - Henri-Georges Clouzot hadn't made a film since 1960's La Vérité. He spent half of the intervening years trying to make a film called Inferno, which would use cutting-edge experimental film-making techniques to visualise the extreme psychological states that had tormented characters in older films like Les diaboliques and Le Corbeau. There's a pretty famous documentary about Inferno which you might have seen. My main memory from it was that just as I began to think Clouzot was spending an inordinate amount of time shooting test footage of Romy Scheider's naked body, the narrator told me he suffered a coronary while filming her lesbian scene.

reviews.author: Stephen M
reviews.text: My third Clouzot, after "Le Corbeau" and "Manon". This was his last film and the only one in color. It's about kink (voyeurism, BDSM), obsession, men's erotic capturing of women via photos and film, and the gender complications when women take on a submissive role. All set against the contemporary kinetic art scene in the psychedelic 60s. It mostly works, although the relationships between the main characters keeps shifting and morphing in a confusing way. I had a hard time making sense of it until I let it all settle in after viewing.

reviews.author: SCREENGAZER 🏳️‍🌈
reviews.text: KINKY BEAUTS| | | | | | |Although Henri-Georges Clouzot enjoyed immense accolades at home and abroad, thanks to The Wages of Fear and Les Diaboliques, his life and career were marked by one setback after another. Political controversies, court sentencing, banishment from filmmaking, personal losses and illness, unfinished projects, and snubs from French New Wave directors. Despite all that, one constant in his work is his unapologetic interest in the unsavory shades of the human psyche. After a health problem put an end to a film project, Clouzot channeled his unfinished business into La Prisonnière, a.k.a. Woman in Chains while suffering from a major illness, and it became his final film before his death in 1977. Viewing…

reviews.text: French director Henri-Georges Clouzet, now 61, is one of grand old masters of suspense, horror, and the bizarre. At his best Clouzot has been Hitchcock with a touch of Bunuel: the inquisitor who only pressed harder when his victims cried, "Enough." LA PRISONNIERE, Clouzot's twentieth film and first in eight years, presents the old Clouzot working out familiar themes in familiar patterns, and a new Clouzot baffled and ill at ease with his new audience.

Going to a casino and whipping ass in poker and blackjack? Check. Becoming a sideshow magician to earn a few bucks? Check. Aiding surgeons in saving patients with internal injuries? Check. Seeing through everything around me and exploring the vast cosmos? Check. Going fuckin’ mental because my own eyelids are now transparent every time I try to sleep? Super check. Roger Corman once again churns out a “smart idea wrapped in a silly package” B-movie, but Ray Milland’s committed Invisible Man-esque performance and the tone-setting giant severed eyeball that opens the film are the type of things that set it slightly ahead of the 50s/60s sci-fi schlock pack. The ending also totally kicks ass.

reviews.text: Truly mind-expanding in its own button-down way. The unusual pace is set right in the opening, an eerie shot of a disembodied eyeball - no credits, no production logo, just an eyeball. There's more than just trippy imagery and cheap thrills here, though - the themes are cosmic, and the dialogue is richly layered with references to sight and lack thereof. Even the purpler soliloquies (like the one about "a city unborn"), which coming out of a lesser actor's mouth might seem like a simple necessary way to cut production costs (telling is usually cheaper than showing, depending on the actor), seem powerful and significant when delivered by Ray Milland.

Often directed by the same luminaries of Italsploitation's golden period in the 60's and 70's, it always struck me how badly the quality of film making dropped off. Putting aside the rise of horror legends like Lucio Fulci and Dario Argento - in fact, there were loads of great horror films from there during the 80's - and focusing on the sub genres of fantasy and post-apocalyptic films, things became pretty tawdry.

Biting irony as the movie makes you want to visit Greece as much as Deliverance makes you want to visit the state of Georgia. This is intended as a crowd-pleaser but depicts a vile, murderous, thieving village of the kind you usually don't see outside of horror movies. And when the despicable villagers are done with their murdering and thieving, the main characters who have lost the people they love go on as nothing has happened - and dance. Zorba's Dance. But both films are the 2001 movie, the latter is the butchered Miramax cut, which removed 20 minutes of exposition and character building, which had to make an already confusing movie damn near incomprehensible.
